# Uniform Airy bounds and numerically satisfactory pairs

Tools behind DLMF Table 9.2.1 (numerically satisfactory pairs of Airy solutions).

* `airyErr_bound_of_isBigO`: a big-O relation on `airySector α` with an explicit radius.
* `airyErr_wellConditioned_of_far`: for a pair with constant nonzero Wronskian it suffices to
  bound `|f g'| + |f' g|` outside a ball (compactness handles the rest).
* `airyErr_ai_uniform`: `|Ai w| ≤ C |e^{-ζ}| |w|^{-1/4}` and `|Ai' w| ≤ C |e^{-ζ}| |w|^{1/4}`
  uniformly in the closed plane `|arg w| ≤ π` for large `|w|`, including the negative axis,
  from the Poincaré expansions 9.7.5–9.7.6 and the oscillatory expansions 9.7.9–9.7.10.
* `airyErr_cross_le`: cross products `|Ai w₁| |Ai' w₂|` are bounded when `|w₁| = |w₂|` and
  `re ζ(w₁) + re ζ(w₂) ≥ 0`.
* `airyErr_far_real`, `airyErr_far_sector`: boundedness of `|Ai Bi'| + |Ai' Bi|` on the real line
  and in the closed sector `|arg z| ≤ π/3`.

The pairs themselves are proved in `DLMF.Airy.Equation`.

# Conventions for the DLMF Airy acquisition

Oscillatory integrals are stated as limits of finite integrals, not as totalized Bochner
integrals. Complex powers of the Bessel argument use an explicit logarithmic coordinate,
so that the substitution `ζ = 2 z^(3/2)/3` retains its analytically continued branch.
The sector filter contains the whole closed sector, hence Big-O statements are uniform
there. These conventions support DLMF §§9.2 and 9.4–9.14.

# Differential and connection properties of Airy functions (DLMF §§9.2, 9.4)

The Airy functions are defined through their Maclaurin series, written with Mathlib's regularized
`₀F̃₁`. With `f(z) = ₀F̃₁(;2/3;z³/9)` and `g(z) = z ₀F̃₁(;4/3;z³/9)` (`airyF`, `airyG`),

$$
\operatorname{Ai}(z) = 3^{-2/3} f(z) - 3^{-4/3} g(z),\qquad
\operatorname{Bi}(z) = \sqrt3\,\bigl(3^{-2/3} f(z) + 3^{-4/3} g(z)\bigr),
$$

which is DLMF 9.4.1 and 9.4.3 with the Gamma factors of the Maclaurin coefficients absorbed into
the regularized series. Both functions are entire, with derivatives `airyAiDeriv`, `airyBiDeriv`
given by explicit series.

## Main results

* `hasDerivAt_airyAi`, `hasDerivAt_airyAiDeriv` and the Bi analogues: Airy's equation
  `w'' = z w` (9.2.1), packaged as `isAirySol_airyAi`, `isAirySol_airyBi`;
* `airyAi_zero`, `airyAiDeriv_zero`, `airyBi_zero`, `airyBiDeriv_zero` (9.2.3–9.2.6);
* `wronskian_airyAi_airyBi`: `𝒲{Ai, Bi} = 1/π` (9.2.7);
* `IsAirySol.eq_of_initial`: solutions of Airy's equation are determined by `w(0), w'(0)`;
* rotations by `e^{±2πi/3}`: `airyBi_eq_airyAi_omega` (9.2.10), `airyAi_mul_omega`,
  `airyAi_mul_omega_recip` (9.2.11), `airyAi_add_omega` (9.2.12), `airyBi_add_omega` (9.2.13);
* `airyAi_conj`, `airyBi_conj`: both functions are real on the real line.

# Ai² as a Gaussian average of Ai

The representation `Ai(x)² = (2^{2/3}/π) ∫₀^∞ Ai(2^{2/3}(x + t²)) dt` for real `x`
(`airyAi_sq_eq_integral`), the basic tool for the product integrals of DLMF §9.11.

Proof: with `c = 2^{2/3}` and `F(x) = ∫₀^∞ Ai(c(x+t²)) dt`,
* differentiation under the integral sign (Gaussian domination from the bounds 9.7.15) gives
  `F' = c ∫ Ai'`, `F'' = c² ∫ u Ai(u)`, `F''' = c³ ∫ (Ai + u Ai')`, and an integration by parts
  in `t` turns this into the product equation `F''' - 4xF' - 2F = 0` (DLMF 9.11.1);
* the Wronskian of three solutions of 9.11.1 is constant, and that of `Ai², Ai Bi, Bi²` is
  `2/π³` (9.11.2), so Cramer's rule writes `F = a Ai² + b Ai Bi + d Bi²`;
* `x^{1/2} F(x) → 0`, `x^{1/2} Ai² → 0` and `x^{1/2} Ai Bi → 1/(2π)` (9.7.5, 9.7.7) force
  `b = d = 0`;
* `F(0)` is the Mellin transform 9.10.17 at `α = 1/2`, and Legendre's duplication formula with
  `Γ(1/3)Γ(2/3) = 2π/√3` gives `a = π/c`.

For the Mellin transform 9.11.15 the representation is rewritten with `s = t²` as
`x^{α-1} Ai(x)² = (c/2π) ∫ Φ(x, v) dv` with `Φ(x, v) = 1_{x<v} x^{α-1} (v-x)^{-1/2} Ai(cv)`;
Fubini (`airySq_double`) reduces the `x`-integral to a Beta integral, and the remaining
`v`-integral is the Mellin transform 9.10.17 at `α + 1/2` after scaling (`airySq_scaled_mellin`).

The helpers carry the prefix `airySq_`.

# The binomial in Stieltjes–Euler form, for the Airy error bounds

For `0 < a < 1` and `1 + t` in the slit plane,

  `(1+t)^{-a} = (Γ(a)Γ(1-a))⁻¹ ∫₀¹ τ^{a-1}(1-τ)^{-a} (1 + tτ)⁻¹ dτ`

(Euler's integral for `₂F₁(1, a; 1; -t)`, continued from the unit disc by the identity theorem),
and the remainder of the binomial expansion after `N` terms is
`(-t)^N (Γ(a)Γ(1-a))⁻¹ ∫₀¹ τ^{N+a-1}(1-τ)^{-a} (1 + tτ)⁻¹ dτ`. On a ray `t = r e^{iθ}`,
`|θ| < π`, the factor `(1 + tτ)⁻¹` is bounded by `1` for `cos θ ≥ 0` and by `|csc θ|` otherwise.
These give Olver's multipliers `1` and `|csc(ph ζ)|` in DLMF 9.7.17 (Olver, *Asymptotics and
Special Functions*, Ch. 7 §§3–4; Nemes 2017b).

## Main results

* `airySt_binom`: the Stieltjes–Euler form of `(1+t)^{-a}`.
* `airySt_binom_rem`: the exact remainder of the binomial expansion.
* `airySt_factor_bound`: the ray bound of the remainder factor.
* `airySt_rem_le_M`, `airySt_rem_le_chi`: the remainder of the ray Laplace integral
  `∫₀^∞ e^{-Wr} t^{b-1}(1+t)^{-a} dr`, `t = r e^{iθ}`, after `N` terms is at most `M_θ` and at
  most `χ(N+b) + 1` times the first neglected term (Olver Ch. 7 §§3–4; Boyd's method for χ).

Helper names carry the prefix `airySt_`.

# Airy functions (DLMF Chapter 9; Beals–Wong §9.9)

Mathlib has no Airy functions. This area defines `Ai` and `Bi` as entire functions through
their Maclaurin series (`DLMF.Airy.Basic`), proves Airy's equation, the initial values, the
Wronskian, uniqueness of solutions from initial data, the rotation identities with cube roots
of unity and real-valuedness on `ℝ`; and relates them to Bessel functions of order `±1/3` on the
real line, with the leading large-`x` behaviour and positivity on `[0, ∞)` (`DLMF.Airy.Bessel`).

The remaining modules acquire DLMF §§9.2 and 9.4–9.14, including Scorer, generalized and
incomplete Airy functions. The initial acquisition admits all new statements; existing
proofs are preserved. Oscillatory integrals include convergence limits, continued Bessel
arguments retain logarithmic coordinates, and asymptotic expansions use finite remainders.
The equation-by-equation inventory and source-domain qualifications are in
`AiryAcquisition.md` at the project root.

# Means, tridiagonal matrices and infinite determinants (DLMF §§1.2–1.3): definitions

Most of DLMF §§1.2–1.3 is about objects that Mathlib already has (binomial coefficients,
matrices, determinants, norms); the pointers are in
`DLMF/AlgebraicAnalytic/Algebra/MathlibCoverage.lean`. This file defines the few notions that
are not upstream:

* the arithmetic, geometric and harmonic means of finitely many reals (1.2.17–1.2.19) and the
  weighted power mean `M(r)` (1.2.20–1.2.22);
* tridiagonal square matrices (1.2.57);
* the symmetric truncations `D_n[a_{j,k}]` of a doubly infinite matrix, convergence of the
  infinite determinant, and determinants of Hill's type (1.3.18–1.3.19).

The finitely many numbers `a₁, …, aₙ` of DLMF are a family `a : ι → ℝ` over a finite type `ι`;
`n` is `Fintype.card ι`.

# Binomial coefficients, finite series and partial fractions (DLMF §1.2(i)–(iii))

The binomial coefficient `C(n, k)` of nonnegative integers is Mathlib's `Nat.choose`, and for
complex `z` the coefficient `C(z, k)` of 1.2.6 is Mathlib's generalized binomial coefficient
`Ring.choose z k` (on `ℂ`, a binomial ring as a `ℚ≥0`-module). The binomial theorem 1.2.2, the
sums 1.2.3–1.2.4, Pascal's rule 1.2.7 and the geometric sum 1.2.11 are upstream; the pointers are
in `DLMF/AlgebraicAnalytic/Algebra/MathlibCoverage.lean`. Here are the DLMF forms that Mathlib
states differently or not at all: the even-index sum 1.2.5, the Pochhammer forms 1.2.6, the
complex sums 1.2.8–1.2.9, the arithmetic progression 1.2.10, the factor `a` in 1.2.11, and the
partial-fraction decompositions 1.2.12–1.2.16. The decompositions are stated for the values of
the rational functions at points `x` off the poles, over an arbitrary field (DLMF: constants,
real or complex); 1.2.14–1.2.15 need characteristic zero for the factorials.

# Determinants (DLMF §1.3(i)–(iii))

The elementary properties of determinants (1.3.1–1.3.7, the row and column rules of §1.3(i),
triangular matrices) and the Vandermonde determinant 1.3.13 are in Mathlib; the pointers are in
`DLMF/AlgebraicAnalytic/Algebra/MathlibCoverage.lean`. This file has the DLMF forms of 1.3.6, the
alternant property 1.3.11–1.3.12, Hadamard's inequality 1.3.8–1.3.10, the Cauchy determinant
1.3.14, the circulant 1.3.15, Krattenthaler's formula 1.3.16–1.3.17 and the convergence of
infinite determinants of Hill's type (1.3.19); the truncations `D_n` (1.3.18) are defined in
`DLMF/AlgebraicAnalytic/Algebra/Basic.lean`.

DLMF's circulant (1.3.15) has rows `(a₁, …, aₙ)`, `(aₙ, a₁, …, a_{n-1})`, …, that is the entry
`a_{k-j}` (indices mod `n`) in row `j`, column `k`; it is the transpose of Mathlib's
`Matrix.circulant a` (entry `a (j - k)`). Indices run over `Fin n` from `0`, so DLMF's `a₁` is
`a 0`, and the `n`th roots of unity are `ω_k = e^{2πik/n}`, `k = 0, …, n-1`.

The formulas 1.3.14, 1.3.15 and 1.3.17 were checked numerically (mpmath, `n ≤ 6`, random
real data) before acquisition.

# Matrices, vectors, scalar products and norms (DLMF §1.2(v)–(vi))

DLMF's matrices are Mathlib's `Matrix m n ℂ` (transpose `Aᵀ`, Hermitian conjugate `Aᴴ`, trace
`Matrix.trace`, determinant `Matrix.det`, inverse `A⁻¹`); vectors are functions `n → ℂ` (or
`EuclideanSpace ℂ n` when the Euclidean norm is meant). The definitions and the algebraic rules
1.2.27–1.2.39, 1.2.53–1.2.56 and 1.2.62–1.2.69 are upstream; the pointers are in
`DLMF/AlgebraicAnalytic/Algebra/MathlibCoverage.lean`.

**Convention for the scalar product.** DLMF's `⟨u, v⟩ = ∑ u_i \overline{v_i} = v^H u` (1.2.40)
is linear in the first argument, Mathlib's inner product `⟪x, y⟫_ℂ = ∑ \overline{x_i} y_i` in
the second. Here `⟨u, v⟩` is written `u ⬝ᵥ star v` for plain vectors, and it equals Mathlib's
`⟪v, u⟫_ℂ` on `EuclideanSpace ℂ n` (`dotProduct_star_eq_inner`).

This file proves the DLMF forms of the scalar-product rules 1.2.40–1.2.42, the complex Hölder
inequality 1.2.50, the equality case of the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality 1.2.51, the limit
`‖v‖_p → ‖v‖_∞` of 1.2.48, the Leibniz formula 1.2.59 in DLMF's index order, the statements on
inverses and linear systems in §1.2(vi) (1.2.60–1.2.61), the attained maximum in the matrix
norm 1.2.67, the characterization 1.2.71–1.2.72 of
eigenvalues, the characterization 1.2.73 of non-defective matrices, 1.2.74–1.2.75, and the
convergence of the exponential series 1.2.76.

The equality case of 1.2.51 as printed ("iff `v` is a scalar multiple of `u`") fails for
`u = 0 ≠ v`; it is stated with the alternative `u = 0`.

# Means (DLMF §1.2(iv))

Properties of the arithmetic, geometric, harmonic and weighted power means defined in
`DLMF/AlgebraicAnalytic/Algebra/Basic.lean`: the limits of `M(r)` as `r → ±∞` (1.2.23–1.2.24),
`M(1) = A` and `M(-1) = H` for equal weights (1.2.25), and `M(r) → G` as `r → 0` (1.2.26).

The limits 1.2.23–1.2.24 and 1.2.26 are proved for arbitrary positive weights `p_j` with
`∑ p_j = 1`; for 1.2.26 the limit is then the weighted geometric mean `∏ a_j^{p_j}`, which is
`G` for `p_j = 1/n` (stronger than DLMF, which states 1.2.26 for equal weights only). The maximum
and minimum of 1.2.23–1.2.24 are `⨆ j, a j` and `⨅ j, a j`.

The inequalities between the means (AM–GM and the power-mean inequality) are DLMF §1.7(iii)
and are not treated here; Mathlib has them as
`Real.geom_mean_le_arith_mean_weighted` and `Real.rpow_arith_mean_le_arith_mean_rpow`.

# Green's theorem in the plane and Stokes's theorem (DLMF 1.6.43–1.6.44, 1.6.57)

Green's theorem 1.6.44 is TauCeti's `TauCeti.Green.green_ac_index_one` (credited in the
pointer file `DLMF.AlgebraicAnalytic.Calculus.MathlibCoverage`): the plane is `ℂ`, the curve
`γ` is closed and absolutely continuous on `[a, b]`, and the region `S` is the part of the
filled hull of the trace off the trace, on which the winding number of `γ` is `1`. This
covers DLMF's positively oriented simple closed piecewise differentiable curves (whose
interior has winding number `1` by the Jordan curve theorem, not in Mathlib), and more: the
curve may cross itself. This file proves the area formulas below 1.6.44 from it, and states
Stokes's theorem 1.6.57 for a parametrized surface over such a region.

# Inequalities (DLMF §1.7)

The inequalities of Cauchy–Schwarz, Hölder and Minkowski for finite sums (1.7.1–1.7.3) and
for integrals (1.7.4–1.7.6), the inequalities between means (1.7.7) and Jensen's inequality
(1.7.10) are in Mathlib (pointers in `DLMF.AlgebraicAnalytic.Calculus.MathlibCoverage`). This
file states the remaining parts: the equality cases, the converse statements, the reversed
Minkowski inequality for `0 < p < 1`, the power-mean inequalities 1.7.8–1.7.9 and DLMF's form
of Jensen's inequality on an open interval, together with 1.7.11.
The finite Hölder converse uses the normalized dual vector and Mathlib’s conjugate-exponent
and real-power identities, including the zero-vector case. The finite Hölder equality case
uses Mathlib’s equality characterization in Young’s inequality after normalizing each vector.
The integral analogue uses the same normalization and Mathlib’s almost-everywhere equality
criterion for ordered integrable functions.
The finite Minkowski equality case uses strict convexity or strict concavity of real powers
according to the exponent, with zero vectors handled separately. The integral equality proof
applies the corresponding almost-everywhere Jensen criterion; measurability follows from
integrability of the positive powers.
Power-mean order and equality
use strict Jensen and lean-codes' negative-power convexity theorem from
`ToMathlib.Analysis.Convex.NegativePower`.

**Equality cases.** For sums DLMF writes "equality iff `aⱼ = c bⱼ`" (1.7.1, 1.7.3) and
"`aⱼᵖ = c bⱼ^q`" (1.7.2); this misses `b = 0`, `a ≠ 0`, where equality holds. We use the
symmetric form of DLMF's integral statements: `A aⱼ = B bⱼ` with `A`, `B` not both zero.

**1.7.11.** DLMF prints the strict inequality `exp(∫₀¹ ln f) < ∫₀¹ f`, which fails for constant
`f`. We prove `≤` (`exp_integral_log_le_integral`) and state the strict inequality for `f` not
almost everywhere constant.

The means of §1.2(iv) are written out explicitly: `A = (∑ aⱼ)/n`, `G = (∏ aⱼ)^{1/n}`,
`1/H = (∑ 1/aⱼ)/n`, and `M(r) = (∑ pⱼ aⱼ^r)^{1/r}` (weights `pⱼ > 0`, `∑ pⱼ = 1`).

# Continued fractions: definitions (DLMF §1.12)

DLMF writes `C = b₀ + a₁/(b₁ + a₂/(b₂ + ⋯))` with partial numerators `a_n` (`n ≥ 1`) and partial
denominators `b_n` (`n ≥ 0`). Mathlib's `GenContFract K` is `h + a₀'/(b₀' + a₁'/(b₁' + ⋯))` with
pairs indexed from `0`, and `GenContFract.cfConv_ofFun h a b` (DLMFMathlib) builds it from two
sequences. `contFrac a b` is DLMF's fraction in DLMF's indexing (the value `a 0` is unused):

* `(contFrac a b).nums n = A_n`, `(contFrac a b).dens n = B_n` (the canonical numerators and
  denominators of 1.12.4–1.12.6), and `(contFrac a b).convs n = A_n/B_n`;
* `(contFrac a b).convs' n` is the nested finite fraction `b₀ + a₁/(b₁ + ⋯ + a_n/b_n)`;
  with Lean's `x / 0 = 0`, it equals `A_n/B_n` when its nested denominators do not vanish
  (`DLMF.AlgebraicAnalytic.contFrac_convs'_eq_convs`);
* `(contFrac a b).contsAux 0 = ⟨1, 0⟩ = ⟨A_{-1}, B_{-1}⟩`.

Further definitions: the nested tails `contFracTail`, the approximants `C_n(w)` of 1.12.20
(`contFracApprox`), equivalence and contraction of continued fractions, convergence, and the
elements of the even and odd parts (1.12.23–1.12.24).

# Convergence of continued fractions (DLMF §1.12(v))

* **Pringsheim's theorem** (1.12.25): if `b₀ = 0` and `|b_n| ≥ |a_n| + 1` for `n ≥ 1`, then
  `|C_n| < 1` and `C_n → C` with `|C| ≤ 1`. The proof is the classical one: the canonical
  denominators satisfy `|B_n| - |B_{n-1}| ≥ |a₁ ⋯ a_n|`, so the series 1.12.9 of the convergents
  is dominated by the telescoping series `∑ (1/|B_{n-1}| - 1/|B_n|) ≤ 1`. The hypothesis
  `a_n ≠ 0` of DLMF is not needed (stronger than DLMF). It is proved in any complete normed
  field.
* **Van Vleck's theorem** (1.12.26–1.12.28), for `1/(b₁ + 1/(b₂ + ⋯))` with all `b_n` in the
  sector `|ph b_n| < π/2 - δ` (admitted).

# Linear second-order differential equations: definitions (DLMF §1.13)

* `IsLinODE2SolOn f g r w D` (1.13.1, 1.13.8): `w'' + f w' + g w = r` on `D`, with genuine
  differentiability of `w` and of `w'` at every point of `D` (so the totalized `deriv` cannot
  make a nonsolution satisfy the equation); `r = 0` is the homogeneous equation 1.13.1.
* `IsFundamentalPair f g w₁ w₂ D` (1.13.2).
* `wronskian w₁ w₂` (1.13.4) and the `n`-argument Wronskian `wronskianN`.
* `schwarzian z ζ` (1.13.20): `{z, ζ} = z'''/z' - (3/2)(z''/z')²`, derivatives with respect
  to `ζ`.
* The Sturm–Liouville equation 1.13.26 (`IsSturmLiouvilleSolOn`), the unmixed and periodic
  boundary conditions 1.13.27–1.13.28 and the eigenvalues of a regular Sturm–Liouville system.

# Sturm–Liouville systems and the Liouville normal form (DLMF §1.13(viii))

For the Sturm–Liouville equation 1.13.26 `(p u')' + (λρ - q) u = 0` on `[a, b]` with unmixed
(1.13.27) or periodic (1.13.28) boundary conditions:

* the eigenvalues of a regular system form a sequence tending to `+∞` (admitted);
* the Liouville transformation 1.13.30 `t = ∫_a^x √(ρ/p)`, `w(t) = u(x) (pρ)^{1/4}` to the
  normal form 1.13.29 `ẅ + (λ - q̂(t)) w = 0` with `q̂` as in 1.13.31 (admitted);
* the correspondence of eigenvalues (admitted) and of nodes (proved) under the transformation.

The transformation is stated with `m = (pρ)^{1/4}`, `T(x) = ∫_a^x √(ρ/p)` and its inverse `X`
given by hypotheses, so that no new definitions are needed.

DLMF §1.13(viii) also says that periodic boundary conditions are carried to periodic ones. This
holds only when `pρ`, its derivative and `ρ/p` agree at `a` and `b` (for example for
`(b - a)`-periodic coefficients), since `w(0) = m(a) u(a)` and `w(c) = m(b) u(b)`; the periodic
statement below carries these hypotheses.

# Changes of variables and products of solutions (DLMF §§1.13(iv)–1.13(v))

For `w'' + f(z) w' + g(z) w = 0` on an open set `D ⊆ ℂ` (`IsLinODE2SolOn f g 0 w D`):

* the inversion `ξ = 1/z` (1.13.11–1.13.12);
* elimination of the first derivative by a change of the dependent variable (1.13.13–1.13.15)
  and of the independent variable (1.13.16–1.13.17); the integrals `∫ f dz` of DLMF are
  primitives `F` of `f` on `D` (hypotheses `HasDerivAt F (f z) z`), so the statements are
  branch-free;
* the Liouville transformation 1.13.18–1.13.19, stated in the variable `z` with a chosen square
  root `σ` of `ζ'`, the Schwarzian derivative 1.13.20 (definition `schwarzian` and its
  square-root form), Cayley's identity 1.13.21 and the inversion formula 1.13.22;
* the third-order equation 1.13.23 for products of solutions, and the mixed-potential identity
  1.13.25.

The chain rules and Leibniz expansions use Mathlib’s derivative API,
`iteratedDeriv_fun_mul` and the analyticity of complex differentiable functions.

Mathlib's `Polynomial` supplies the polynomials, their roots, the division algorithm, the
discriminant `Polynomial.discr` and Descartes' sign changes `Polynomial.signVariations`. This
file adds the few objects of DLMF §1.11 that Mathlib does not name:

* `hornerB f α k` (1.11.2–1.11.4): the coefficients `b_k` of Horner's scheme, `b_0 = f(α)` and

  Horner's scheme applied to the quotient;
* `dlmfResolventCubic p q r` (1.11.18): the resolvent cubic `z³ - 2pz² + (p² - 4r)z + q²` of the
  reduced quartic `w⁴ + pw² + qw + r` in DLMF's normalization (TauCeti's
  `TauCeti.resolventCubic` is a different normalization);
* `IsStablePolynomial f` (1.11.24) and the Hurwitz determinants `hurwitzDet f k`

# Zeros of polynomials (DLMF §1.11)

Statements of DLMF §1.11 that are not already in Mathlib (the upstream ones are recorded in
`DLMF.AlgebraicAnalytic.Polynomials.MathlibCoverage`).

* §1.11(i): Horner's scheme (`hornerB`, 1.11.2–1.11.4) and the extended scheme (`hornerC`,
  1.11.5–1.11.6) for a polynomial `f ∈ K[X]` over a field.
* §1.11(ii): real zeros of monic real polynomials of odd and even degree, the parity part of
  Descartes' rule of signs and its form for negative zeros, reciprocal zeros, the discriminant as
  a product over the zeros (1.11.9).
* §1.11(iii): quadratic, cubic (Cardano) and quartic (Ferrari, with DLMF's resolvent cubic)
  formulas. Cube and square roots are replaced by arbitrary roots (`A ^ 3 = …`, `s ^ 2 = …`),
  so the statements are branch-free and cover every choice; DLMF's choice 1.11.20 of the square
  roots is a hypothesis.
* §1.11(iv): roots of `z^n = -1` and of `z^n = a + ib` (1.11.22–1.11.23).
* §1.11(v): the explicit Hurwitz determinants 1.11.25 and the Hurwitz criterion.

The depressed quartic's discriminant 1.11.17 uses TauCeti's `TauCeti.discr_resolventCubic`
(the quartic and TauCeti's resolvent cubic have the same discriminant).

# Second-order differential operators and eigenfunction expansions: definitions
(DLMF §1.18)

Hilbert spaces, `L²` spaces, orthonormal bases (`HilbertBasis`), bounded operators and their
adjoints, unbounded operators (`LinearPMap`) with their adjoints and self-adjointness are
Mathlib's. This file adds:

* `schrodingerOp q` (1.18.28), `hermiteOp` (1.18.41), `besselOp ν` (1.18.55) and the radial
  operator `radialSchrodingerOp ℓ V` (1.18.67), acting on functions `ℝ → ℂ`;
* the eigenfunctions of the examples: `sinEigenfunction`, `cosEigenfunction`,
  `expEigenfunction` (1.18.36–1.18.38) and the Hermite functions `hermiteFunction` (1.18.42),
  via Mathlib's `Polynomial.hermite`;
* for an unbounded operator `T : E →ₗ.[ℂ] E`: `IsSymmetricOp` (1.18.70),
  `IsEssentiallySelfAdjoint`, the resolvent set and the point, continuous and residual spectra
  (§1.18(ix)), the deficiency subspaces `deficiencySubspace T z` and indices;
* for the Weyl theory of `-d²/dx² + q`: `IsSchrodingerSolOn`, `AllSolutionsL2Left/Right`,
  `IsLimitCircleLeft/Right`, the `L²` solution space `l2SolutionSpace` and the boundary value
  `boundaryValueLeft` (1.18.71);
* `IsEigenfunctionTransform` (1.18.44–1.18.47, 1.18.60–1.18.63): a unitary map from `L²(X)`
  onto `L²(ν)`, `ν` the spectral measure on `σ = σ_c ∪ σ_p`, given on compactly supported
  continuous functions by `f̂(λ) = ⟨f, φ_λ⟩`; and `IsDiagonalizedBy` (`T ↔ λ`).

DLMF's inner product `⟨u, v⟩` is linear in `u`; Mathlib's `⟪u, v⟫` is linear in `v`, so
DLMF's `⟨u, v⟩` is Mathlib's `⟪v, u⟫`.

# Summability methods (DLMF §1.15): definitions

DLMF §1.15 defines summation methods for series and integrals, the Poisson and Fejér kernels
of Fourier series and Fourier integrals, the Abel and Cesàro means, and the Riemann–Liouville
fractional integrals and derivatives.

* Series (§1.15(i)): `seriesPartialSum` (1.15.1), the predicates `HasAbelSum` (1.15.2–1.15.3),
  `HasCesaroSum` (1.15.4–1.15.5), `HasCesaroSumOfOrder` (1.15.6–1.15.7) and `HasBorelSum`
  (1.15.8–1.15.9). The Abel and Borel predicates include the convergence of the power series
  for `0 < x < 1` (respectively of the exponential series for `t ≥ 0`), which DLMF leaves
  implicit; without it Lean's `tsum` would assign the junk value `0`.
* Fourier series (§1.15(iii)): the Poisson kernel `abelPoissonKernel` (1.15.12), the Fejér kernel
  `fejerKernel` (1.15.15), the Fourier coefficients `F(n)` (1.15.19) are Mathlib's
  `fourierCoeffOn Real.two_pi_pos f n` (bridge `fourierCoeffOn_two_pi_eq`), the Abel mean
  `abelMean` (1.15.18), the partial sums `fourierPartialSum` (1.15.22), the Cesàro means
  `fourierCesaroMean` (1.15.21) and the analytic extension `fourierAnalyticExtension` (1.15.27).
* Integrals (§1.15(iv)–(v)): `HasAbelIntegral` (1.15.29–1.15.30), `HasCesaroIntegral`
  (1.15.31–1.15.32), the half-plane Poisson kernel `halfPlanePoissonKernel` (1.15.33), the Abel
  mean of a Fourier integral `fourierAbelMean` (1.15.36), the Cauchy integral
  `poissonCauchyIntegral` (1.15.39), the Fejér kernel on the line `fejerKernelLine` (1.15.41)
  and the Cesàro mean of a Fourier integral `fourierCesaroMeanIntegral` (1.15.44).
* Fractional calculus (§1.15(vi)–(vii)): `fractionalIntegral` (1.15.47), its variants with
  other limits `riemannLiouvilleIntegralFrom`, `riemannLiouvilleIntegralUpper` and
  `weylFractionalIntegral` (§1.15(vi)), and `fractionalDerivative` (1.15.51) with
  `n = ⌊ℜα⌋ + 1`.

The kernels are stated with DLMF's normalizations: the circle kernels have mean `1` over
`[0, 2π]`, the half-plane kernel has `(1/2π) ∫ P = 1`, the Fejér kernel on the line has integral
`1`. At `θ ∈ 2πℤ` the quotient formula 1.15.15 is `0/0`; Lean's `fejerKernel n θ` is `0` there,
not the limit value `n + 1` (a null set, irrelevant for the integrals of §1.15).

# Summability of Fourier series (DLMF §1.15(iii))

The Poisson kernel `P(r, θ)` (1.15.12), the Fejér kernel `K_n(θ)` (1.15.15), the Abel means
`A(r, θ)` (1.15.18) and the Cesàro means `σ_n(θ)` (1.15.21) of the Fourier series of a function
on `[0, 2π]` with coefficients `F(n) = fourierCoeffOn Real.two_pi_pos f n` (1.15.19).

Proved: the uniform decay of the kernels away from `θ ∈ 2πℤ` (1.15.14, 1.15.17). Admitted: the
series and integral identities of the kernels, the integral representations 1.15.20 and 1.15.23,
the convergence theorem 1.15.24 and the analytic extension 1.15.25–1.15.28. Throughout,
`0 < δ < π` as in DLMF.

# Fractional integrals and derivatives (DLMF §1.15(vi)–(vii))

The Riemann–Liouville fractional integral `fractionalIntegral` (1.15.47) and the fractional
derivative `fractionalDerivative` (1.15.51, with `n = ⌊ℜα⌋ + 1`) are defined in
`Summability/Basic.lean`. The statements are for `x ≥ 0` (DLMF erratum of version 1.0.1); we take
`x > 0` where derivatives in `x` occur and `f` continuous on `[0, ∞)`.

Proved: the power rule `I^α t^μ = Γ(μ+1)/Γ(μ+α+1) x^{μ+α}` (the termwise form of 1.15.50, by
Mathlib's Beta integral `Complex.Gamma_mul_Gamma_eq_betaIntegral`) and the agreement of
`fractionalIntegral` with the variant of §1.15(vi) with lower limit `0`. Admitted: the semigroup
law 1.15.48, the power-series formula 1.15.49–1.15.50, the independence of `n` in 1.15.51, the
rule 1.15.52, the law 1.15.53 and the remark `D^{1/2} D ≠ D^{3/2}`.

**Missing hypothesis (1.15.53).** DLMF states `D^α D^β = D^{α+β}` whenever none of `α`, `β`,
`α + β` is an integer, without a condition on `f`. This fails in general: for `f(x) = x^{β-1}`
(`ℜβ > 0`), `I^{n-β} f = (Γ(β)/Γ(n)) x^{n-1}` by the power rule, so `D^β f = 0` and
`D^α D^β f = 0`, while `D^{α+β} f = (Γ(β)/Γ(-α)) x^{-α-1} ≠ 0`; e.g. `α = 1/2`, `β = 1/3`. We
acquire 1.15.53 for power functions `x^μ` with `ℜμ > -1` and `ℜ(μ - β) > -1`
(`fractionalDerivative_fractionalDerivative_cpow`), where it holds by the power rule.

# Summability of integrals and of Fourier integrals (DLMF §1.15(iv)–(v))

The Abel and Cesàro summability of integrals over `(-∞, ∞)` (`HasAbelIntegral`,
`HasCesaroIntegral`, 1.15.29–1.15.32), and the Poisson and Fejér kernels of Fourier integrals
(1.15.33–1.15.46) with DLMF's Fourier transform 1.14.1.

Proved: the normalization 1.15.34 of the half-plane Poisson kernel (from Mathlib's
`integral_univ_inv_one_add_sq`), the Abel summability of an absolutely integrable function to its
integral (dominated convergence), and the formulas 1.15.40 and `Re Φ = h` of §1.15(v) by
computing real and imaginary parts under the integral. The other statements are admitted.

**Correction (§1.15(v), after 1.15.40).** DLMF says that `lim_{y→0+} ℑΦ(x + iy)` "is the Hilbert
transform of `f(x)` (§1.14(v))". With DLMF's own normalization 1.14.41 (denominator `t - x`) the
limit is `-ℋ(f)(x)`: by 1.15.40 and 1.14.42 the kernels are `(x - t)/((x - t)² + y²)` and
`(t - x)/((t - x)² + y²)`. Numerically, for `f(t) = 1/(1 + t²)` and `x = 0.6`,
`ℑΦ(x + 0.001i) = 0.4405` while `ℋf(x) = -x/(1 + x²) = -0.4412` (1.14.43). The corrected form is
acquired (`tendsto_im_poissonCauchyIntegral`).

# Summability of series: regularity and Tauberian theorems (DLMF §1.15(ii), §1.15(viii))

DLMF §1.15(ii) states that the Abel, Cesàro, general Cesàro and Borel methods of §1.15(i) are
regular: a convergent series is summable by each of them to its sum. Convergence of a series is
convergence of its partial sums (`seriesPartialSum`), not Mathlib's unconditional `HasSum`.

Proved: regularity of the Abel method (from Mathlib's Abel limit theorem
`Complex.tendsto_tsum_powerSeries_nhdsWithin_lt`) and of the (C,1) method (from Mathlib's
`Filter.Tendsto.cesaro_smul`). Admitted: regularity of the (C,α) and Borel methods, and the
Tauberian theorems 1.15.54–1.15.57 (Littlewood's theorem and the Hardy–Littlewood theorem).

# Integral transforms in DLMF normalization (DLMF §1.14): definitions

DLMF §1.14 defines the Fourier, Fourier cosine and sine, Laplace, Mellin, Hilbert and Stieltjes
transforms. This file gives the definitions in DLMF's normalization, for complex-valued functions
of a real variable.

* `fourierTransform f x = (2π)^{-1/2} ∫ f(t) e^{ixt} dt` (1.14.1). Mathlib's Fourier transform
  `𝓕 f w = ∫ e^{-2πitw} f(t) dt` uses the opposite sign and the frequency `w = -x/(2π)`; the bridge
  `fourierTransform_eq_fourier` proves `fourierTransform f x = (2π)^{-1/2} 𝓕 f (-x/(2π))`.
* `fourierCosTransform`, `fourierSinTransform` (1.14.9, 1.14.10), integrals over `(0, ∞)`.
* `fourierConvolution f g t = (2π)^{-1/2} ∫ f(t - s) g(s) ds` (1.14.5), DLMF's normalized
  convolution; Mathlib's `MeasureTheory.convolution` has no factor `(2π)^{-1/2}`.
* `laplaceTransform f s = ∫₀^∞ e^{-st} f(t) dt` (1.14.17), `IsOfExponentialGrowth` (1.14.18)
  and the Laplace convolution `laplaceConvolution f g t = ∫₀^t f(u) g(t - u) du` (1.14.30).
* The Mellin transform (1.14.32) is Mathlib's `mellin`, the same normalization; only the Mellin
  convolution `mellinConvolution f g x = ∫₀^∞ f(y) g(x/y) dy/y` (1.14.39) is new.
* `hilbertTransform f x = (1/π) P.V.∫ f(t)/(t - x) dt` (1.14.41), as the limit as `ε → 0⁺` of
  the integrals over `|t - x| > ε` (`limUnder`, junk value when the limit does not exist).
  Note DLMF's sign: `t - x` in the denominator, so that the Fourier multiplier is `-i sign x` in
  DLMF's Fourier normalization (1.14.46).
* `stieltjesTransform f s = ∫₀^∞ f(t)/(s + t) dt` (1.14.47).

Lean totalization applies: an integral of a non-integrable function is `0`; all theorems carry
the integrability hypotheses that DLMF leaves implicit.

# Fourier, Fourier cosine and Fourier sine transforms (DLMF §1.14(i)–(ii))

The statements of DLMF §1.14(i)–(ii) for DLMF's Fourier transform
`𝓕(f)(x) = (2π)^{-1/2} ∫ f(t) e^{ixt} dt` (`fourierTransform`, 1.14.1) and the cosine and sine
transforms on `(0, ∞)`.

Proved here from Mathlib through the bridge `fourierTransform_eq_fourier`
(`𝓕(f)(x) = (2π)^{-1/2} 𝓕_Mathlib f(-x/(2π))`): continuity and the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma
(§1.14(i)), the bound 1.14.2, the inversion formula 1.14.4 when `F = 𝓕(f)` is integrable, the
convolution theorem (§1.14(i), after 1.14.5) and the uniqueness theorem. The integral
Fourier transform agrees almost everywhere with Mathlib's unitary `L²` transform, yielding
Parseval's formula 1.14.7_5, its bilinear form 1.14.7, convolution inversion 1.14.6 and the
norm identity 1.14.8. Even and odd extensions give the cosine and sine pairings
1.14.13–1.14.16. The bounded-variation inversion theorem 1.14.3, the principal-value form
of 1.14.4 and the half-line inversion theorems 1.14.11–1.14.12 remain admitted.

Hypotheses DLMF leaves implicit are explicit: integrability for each transform, and the one-sided
limits `f(u±)` in 1.14.3 are given as hypotheses (they exist for functions of bounded variation).

# The Laplace transform (DLMF §1.14(iii))

Statements of DLMF §1.14(iii) for `laplaceTransform f s = ∫₀^∞ e^{-st} f(t) dt` (1.14.17).

DLMF assumes throughout that `f` is piecewise continuous on `[0, ∞)` and of exponential growth
(1.14.18) with exponent `α`, and `ℜs > α`. Here "piecewise continuous" is replaced by the weaker
`LocallyIntegrableOn f (Ici 0)` wherever that suffices (stronger than DLMF), and the exponential
growth is the predicate `IsOfExponentialGrowth f α`.

Proved: absolute convergence, analyticity and decay for `ℜs > α` (§1.14(iii), 1.14.19),
the translation rules 1.14.21–1.14.22, and differentiation of every order (1.14.23).
Analyticity uses the project’s dominated-holomorphy theorem, and differentiation uses Mathlib’s
`hasDerivAt_integral_of_dominated_loc_of_deriv_le`. Admitted: inversion 1.14.20, integration
1.14.24, derivatives with jumps 1.14.28, and uniqueness. The convolution theorem 1.14.31
is proved from Mathlib’s `MeasureTheory.integral_convolution` by extension by zero.
The periodic and antiperiodic rules 1.14.25–1.14.26 and the derivative rules 1.14.27 and
1.14.29 are proved by splitting the half-line integral and by Mathlib’s improper-integral
fundamental theorem `integral_Ioi_of_hasDerivAt_of_tendsto`.

# DLMF §1.14 results already in Mathlib and TauCeti

Checked pointers (`dlmf_upstream`) for DLMF §1.14, deliberately not duplicate local theorems.

**Normalizations.** Mathlib's Fourier transform is `𝓕 f w = ∫ e^{-2πi⟨v,w⟩} f(v) dv`; DLMF's

# Distributional methods: definitions (DLMF §2.6)

Definitions for DLMF §2.6 (namespace `DLMF.AsymptoticApproximations`).

DLMF assigns distributions (continuous linear functionals on the space `𝒯` of rapidly
decreasing functions) to the functions `t^{-s-α}` and to the remainders `f_n` of an
asymptotic expansion. We record the *values* of these functionals as explicit integrals,
`φ ↦ ⟨·, φ⟩`, for an arbitrary function `φ : ℝ → ℂ`: the formulas only use `φ` and its
derivatives on `[0, ∞)`, and they are applied in DLMF both to Schwartz functions and to the
functions `φ_ε(t) = e^{-εt}/(t+z)` of 2.6.22, which are not Schwartz functions on `ℝ`.
Continuity of these functionals on the Schwartz space is not asserted by the definitions.
All integrals use Lean's totalization (the integral of a non-integrable function is `0`), so
every statement using them carries integrability hypotheses or conclusions where needed.

* `stieltjesTransform f z = ∫₀^∞ f(t)/(t+z) dt` (2.6.8) and its generalization
  `generalizedStieltjesTransform ρ f z` (2.6.32).
* `functionPairing f φ = ∫₀^∞ f φ` (2.6.11, 2.6.12).
* `powPairing α s φ = (α)_s⁻¹ ∫₀^∞ t^{-α} φ^{(s)}(t) dt` (2.6.13), `0 < α < 1`.
* `logPowPairing s φ = -(1/s!) ∫₀^∞ ln t φ^{(s+1)}(t) dt` (2.6.14), the case `α = 1`.
* `tPowPairing λ φ`: the distribution `t^λ` for real `λ`, as selected by 2.6.12–2.6.14.
* `diracDerivPairing s φ = (-1)^s φ^{(s)}(0)` (2.6.19).
* `repeatedTailIntegral n f t` (2.6.15) and `remainderPairing n f φ` (2.6.16).
* `riemannLiouvilleIntegral μ f x` (2.6.33) and `halfLineConvolution f g x` (2.6.34).
* `kPlusPairing n f φ = ⟨Dⁿ f, φ⟩` for the elements `Dⁿ f` of `K⁺` (2.6.37).

* 2.3.2: the Laplace transform of a function smooth at the origin has the expansion

  `DLMF.AsymptoticApproximations.Integrals.Watson` and Taylor's theorem.

  bound for the lower derivatives and the iterated Laplace derivative identity.

  integration by parts gives exact remainders. In the improper case convergence at
  two frequencies forces the boundary terms to vanish.

Smoothness "in a neighbourhood of the origin" is smoothness on some `[0, r]`, `r > 0` (only
`t ≥ 0` enters the Laplace transform), with one-sided derivatives `iteratedDerivWithin`.

# The method of stationary phase (DLMF §2.3(iv))

* 2.3.20: the analogue of Watson's lemma for `∫₀^∞ e^{ixt} q(t) dt`;
* 2.3.19, 2.3.21–2.3.23: `∫ₐᵇ e^{ixp(t)} q(t) dt` with the stationary point (if any) at `a`,
  with the functions `Pₛ = stationaryPhaseP p q s` of 2.3.21.

"Infinitely differentiable expansions" (DLMF) are expansions whose termwise derivatives of every
order are expansions of the derivatives; the derivative of `t^ν` of order `k` is
`ν(ν-1)⋯(ν-k+1) t^{ν-k}` (`descPochhammer`). Integrals over infinite ranges, and integrals that
DLMF requires to converge "uniformly for all sufficiently large `x`", are limits of integrals
over `[c, T]` as `T → ∞`, uniformly in `x ≥ x₀`. When two endpoint series appear (2.3.23), each
is interpreted separately (§2.1(iii)): the remainder after `N` terms of the first and `M` terms
of the second is `O(x^{-(N+λ)/μ}) + O(x^{-M-1})`.

Restriction: in 2.3.23 with `p(b)` finite, `b` is finite here; in case (d) (`p(b) = ∞`) the
range is `(a, ∞)`.

# The Mellin-transform example of DLMF §2.5(i): `∫₀^∞ J_ν²(xt)/(1 + t) dt`

For `ν > -½` and `x > 0` let `I(x) = ∫₀^∞ J_ν²(xt)/(1 + t) dt` (2.5.8), a Mellin convolution
with `f(t) = 1/(1 + t)` and `h(t) = J_ν²(t)`. With `A = besselSqMellinKernel ν`,
`aₙ = A(n)` and `bₙ = -A'(n)` (`Mellin.Basic`):

* 2.5.9: `𝓜f(1 - z) = π/sin(πz)` (proved);
* 2.5.10: `𝓜h(z) = A(z) π/sin(πz)`, here in the equivalent form
  `2^{z-1}Γ(ν + z/2)Γ(1 - z)/(Γ²(1 - z/2)Γ(1 + ν - z/2))`, valid also at `z = 0`, where the
  printed form is `0 · ∞` (the DLMF form is derived for `sin(πz) ≠ 0`);
* 2.5.11–2.5.13: residues at the double poles `z = n`;
* 2.5.14: `|Γ(x + iy)| ∼ √(2π) e^{-π|y|/2} |y|^{x-1/2}` (pointwise forms proved from 5.11.9);
* 2.5.15–2.5.16: the expansion of `I(x)` as `x → ∞`; `aₛ = bₛ = 0` for even `s ≥ 2` (proved).

**Erratum (signs in 2.5.11, 2.5.15, 2.5.16).** The residue of
`x^{-z} 𝓜f(1 - z) 𝓜h(z) = x^{-z} A(z) π²/sin²(πz)` at `z = n` is
`d/dz[x^{-z} A(z)]_{z=n} = -(aₙ ln x + bₙ) x^{-n}`, not `+(aₙ ln x + bₙ) x^{-n}` as printed in
2.5.11. Shifting the contour to the right (2.5.35) then gives
`I(x) = +∑_{s=1}^{2n} (aₛ ln x + bₛ) x^{-s} + O(x^{-2n-1+ε})`, and in 2.5.16 `cₛ = a_{2s+1}`,
`dₛ = b_{2s+1}`. Numerical check (`ν = 0`, `x = 20`): `I(x) = 0.089945`, while
`(a₁ ln x + b₁)/x = (ln 20 + 3 ln 2 + γ)/(20π) = 0.089961`; the printed sign gives `-0.089961`.
The sum in 2.5.15 is taken over `1 ≤ s ≤ 2n` here: the term `s = 0` of DLMF lies outside the
strip crossed by the contour (and `b₀ = -A'(0)` is not zero in general; it is `-1/(2ν)` for
`ν > 0`).

# Mellin transform methods (DLMF §2.5(i)–(ii))

The Mellin transform 2.5.1 is Mathlib's `mellin`, the inversion integral 2.5.2 along
`ℜz = c` is `mellinInv c` (`(2πi)⁻¹ ∫_{c-i∞}^{c+i∞} x^{-z} F(z) dz = mellinInv c F x`), and the
inversion theorem is `mellinInv_mellin_eq` (see `MathlibCoverage`). Residues are
`DLMF.AlgebraicAnalytic.residueAt` (§1.10(iii)), the circle integral `(2πi)⁻¹ ∮ F` around a small
circle.

* 2.5.6–2.5.7, 2.5.34–2.5.36: shifting the line of integration past finitely many poles, and

* §2.5(ii): the truncations `f₁, f₂, h₁, h₂` (2.5.21–2.5.24), the domains of convergence of

In the convolution theorems the transforms are required to converge absolutely on the line of
integration; then the double integral converges absolutely (Tonelli).
The convolution theorem reuses the logarithmic-coordinate convolution API in
`DLMFMathlib.Analysis.MellinConvolution`, together with Mathlib’s `mellin_comp_inv`.

# Bailey chains (AAR Chapter 12)

Rogers–Ramanujan identities, Bailey's lemma, and Watson's transformation are absent from
Mathlib. All three are proved here from the `q`-Pfaff–Saalschütz sum (`DLMF.QSeries.Saalschutz`).

* Bailey's lemma (`bailey_lemma`) reduces, after interchanging the double sum, to a shifted
  `q`-Pfaff–Saalschütz sum (`bailey_inner`); `bailey_relation` is its form at a fixed index with
  hypotheses only up to that index.
* The unit Bailey pair (`unit_pair`) is proved by an explicit telescoping certificate.
  Watson's transformation of a terminating very-well-poised `₈φ₇` into a balanced `₄φ₃`
  (`watson_transformation`) follows from two applications of Bailey's lemma to it; the values of
  `a` with `(aq;q)_{2n} = 0` that the hypotheses allow are reached by continuity in `a`.
* The limiting form of Bailey's lemma (`ρ₁, ρ₂ → ∞`, `bailey_limit_relation`) rests on the
  identity `∑_m [N m]_q q^{m(m-1)} A^m (Aq^m;q)_{N-m} = 1` (`sum_qBinom_limit`). Applied twice to
  the unit pair and with `n → ∞` (Tannery's theorem), it gives
  `∑ a^k q^{k²}/(q;q)_k = (aq;q)_∞⁻¹ ∑ a^{2k} q^{2k²} α_k` (`sum_unit_bailey`). At `a = 1` and
  `a = q` the right side is the Jacobi triple product at base `q⁵`, and regrouping
  `(q;q)_∞ = (q, q², q³, q⁴, q⁵; q⁵)_∞` (`qPochhammerInf_mod_five`) gives the Rogers–Ramanujan
  identities.

# Bernoulli and Euler numbers: arithmetic properties (DLMF §24.10)

DLMF §24.10(i): "two rational numbers are congruent if the modulus divides the numerator of
their difference"; this is `RatModEq M a b`. The von Staudt–Clausen theorem 24.10.1 is Mathlib's
`Bernoulli.vonStaudt_clausen` (pointer in `DLMF.BernoulliEuler.MathlibCoverage`); the second
assertion of 24.10.1 (the denominator of `B₂ₙ` is the product of the primes `p` with
`p - 1 ∣ 2n`) is `bernoulli_two_mul_den_eq_prod`.

## Corrections

* Kummer's congruence 24.10.3 fails if `m = 1` or `n = 1` (e.g. `p = 3`, `m = 1`, `n = 3`:
  `B₁/1 = -1/2 ≢ 0 = B₃/3 (mod 3)`); acquired for `m, n ≥ 2`. 24.10.4 needs no such condition
  (its factor `1 - p⁰` vanishes for `m = 1`).
* 24.10.5 also holds for `n = 1` (`E₁ = Eₚ = 0`), but not for `n = 0`; acquired as printed
  (`n ≥ 2`).

All congruences were checked in exact arithmetic for primes `p ≤ 13` and the index ranges
`m, n < 60` (24.10.3–24.10.4), `n < 200` (24.10.2), `n < 150` (24.10.8–24.10.9), `M < 12`,
`|b| ≤ 7` (24.10.7).

# Asymptotic approximations of Bernoulli and Euler numbers and polynomials (DLMF §24.11)

DLMF's `Bₙ`, `Bₙ(x)`, `Eₙ`, `Eₙ(x)` are Mathlib's `bernoulli` (with `B₁ = -1/2`),
`Polynomial.bernoulli`, and the project's `eulerNumber`, `Polynomial.euler`
(`DLMFMathlib.NumberTheory.EulerPolynomials`); at complex arguments they are
`bernoulliPolyB n x` and `eulerPolyE n x` (`DLMF.BernoulliEuler.Basic`).

* (24.11.1)–(24.11.4): the asymptotic equivalences of `(-1)ⁿ⁺¹ B₂ₙ` and `(-1)ⁿ E₂ₙ`, stated as
  `Asymptotics.IsEquivalent` along `n → ∞` in `ℝ`, all proved: (24.11.1) from
  `ζ(2n) = (-1)ⁿ⁺¹ (2π)²ⁿ B₂ₙ/(2 (2n)!)` and `ζ(x) → 1` as `x → ∞` (`LSeries.tendsto_atTop`),
  (24.11.3) in the same way from Dirichlet's `β(2n+1)`
  (`hasSum_sin_pi_div_two_div_pow_eulerNumber`), and (24.11.2), (24.11.4) from these and
  Stirling's formula.
* (24.11.5), (24.11.6): the normalized polynomials converge to `cos`/`sin` uniformly on compact
  subsets of `ℂ`; DLMF's single limit with a parity case split is stated as two limits, along the
  even and along the odd indices. All proved: with `cᵢ = (2π)ⁱ Bᵢ/i!`,
  `(2π)ⁿ Bₙ(x)/n! = ∑ᵢ cᵢ (2πx)ⁿ⁻ⁱ/(n-i)!`, and `ζ(2k) = 1 + O(4⁻ᵏ)` gives `cᵢ = dᵢ + O(2⁻ⁱ)`
  with `dᵢ` the coefficients that reproduce `±2 cos`/`±2 sin` exactly; the Euler limits follow
  from `Eₙ(x) = 2ⁿ⁺¹ (Bₙ₊₁(x/2 + 1/2) - Bₙ₊₁(x/2))/(n+1)`. DLMF's sign exponent

# Generalizations of Bernoulli and Euler polynomials (DLMF §24.16)

## Definitions (genuine, by finite formulas)

* `norlundPolynomial n : ℚ[X]`: the Nörlund polynomial `B_n^{(x)}` of 24.16.9 as a polynomial in
  the order `x`. If `g(t) = t/(eᵗ - 1) - 1` (Mathlib's `bernoulliPowerSeries`, minus `1`), then
  `(1 + g)^x = ∑ⱼ (x choose j) gʲ` and only `j ≤ n` contribute to the coefficient of `tⁿ`; so
  `B_n^{(x)} = n! ∑_{j ≤ n} [tⁿ] gʲ · x(x-1)⋯(x-j+1)/j!` (`descPochhammer`). This is the
  formal-power-series meaning of `(t/(eᵗ-1))^x`, the branch equal to `1` at `t = 0`.
* `bernoulliNumberOrder ℓ n = B_n^{(ℓ)}` (24.16.3) and `bernoulliOrder ℓ n : ℚ[X]`, the
  polynomial `B_n^{(ℓ)}(x) = ∑ₖ (n choose k) B_k^{(ℓ)} x^{n-k}` (the coefficient form of
  24.16.1, the factor `e^{xt}` contributing `x^{n-k}/(n-k)!`).
* `eulerNumberOrder ℓ n = E_n^{(ℓ)}` and `eulerOrder ℓ n` for 24.16.2, in the same way from
  `2/(eᵗ + 1) = ∑ Eₙ(0) tⁿ/n!`.
* `bernoulliSecondKind n = bₙ = ∫₀¹ (x choose n) dx` (24.16.5), written through the coefficients
  of `descPochhammer`: `bₙ = (1/n!) ∑ₖ [xᵏ] x(x-1)⋯(x-n+1) / (k+1)`.
* `degenerateBernoulli n : ℚ[X]`, the degenerate Bernoulli number `βₙ(λ)` (24.16.7) as a
  polynomial in `λ`: `((1 + λt)^{1/λ} - 1)/t = ∑ₖ (1-λ)(1-2λ)⋯(1-kλ) tᵏ/(k+1)!` has constant
  term `1`, and `βₙ(λ)/n!` is the `n`-th coefficient of its inverse (`PowerSeries.invOfUnit`).
* `bernoulliChar χ n = B_{n,χ}` (24.16.10) for a Dirichlet character `χ` modulo `f`, defined by
  the classical closed form `B_{n,χ} = f^{n-1} ∑_{a=1}^{f} χ(a) Bₙ(a/f)`; the generating function
  24.16.10 is a theorem. DLMF requires `χ` primitive (with `f` its conductor); the definition and
  the generating function make sense for every `χ` modulo `f ≥ 1`. `bernoulliCharPoly` is
  24.16.11.

## Generating functions and branches

DLMF's generating functions are stated as `HasSum` in `ℂ` for `t ≠ 0` (at `t = 0` the Lean
quotients are totalized). For the Nörlund polynomials of complex order (24.16.9) DLMF's power
`(t/(eᵗ-1))^x` is the branch analytic in `|t| < 2π` and equal to `1` at `0`; the principal power
`cpow` agrees with it only while `t/(eᵗ-1)` has not crossed the negative axis. Numerically the
principal argument stays below `π` for `|t| < 4.8`; we state 24.16.9 for complex `x` and
`0 < ‖t‖ < π`, and for real `x` and real `0 < |t| < 2π` (where `t/(eᵗ-1) > 0`). The degenerate
Bernoulli generating function 24.16.7 ("for sufficiently small `|t|`") is stated for `λ ≠ 0`
eventually in the punctured neighbourhood of `0`, with the principal power `(1 + λt)^{1/λ}`.

## Status

The generating functions 24.16.1, 24.16.2 and 24.16.10 are proved by summing the Cauchy
products of the absolutely convergent series of `t/(eᵗ-1)`, `2/(eᵗ+1)` and `e^{xt}`;
`natDegree_norlundPolynomial` is proved. The formal identity `t β' = β - tβ - β²` for
`β = t/(eᵗ-1)` gives the Nörlund recurrence
`a B_{n+1}^{(a+1)}(x) = (a-n-1) B_{n+1}^{(a)}(x) + (n+1)(x-a) B_n^{(a)}(x)`, hence
`B_n^{(n+1)}(x) = (x-1)⋯(x-n)`; with `∫₀¹ B_n^{(a+1)} = B_n^{(a)}` this proves 24.16.6, and with
the differential equation of `(ln(1+t)/t)^ℓ` it proves 24.16.4. 24.16.5 is proved by integrating
the binomial series `(1+t)^x = ∑ (x choose n) tⁿ` over `0 ≤ x ≤ 1`. 24.16.7 is proved for
`|t| < 1/(4(1+|λ|))` from the binomial series of `(1 + λt)^{1/λ}`, a geometric bound on the
coefficients of the formal inverse and the Cauchy product. The generating function 24.16.9 is
proved from a holomorphic logarithm `L` of `t/(eᵗ-1)` on `|t| < 2π` (a primitive of the
logarithmic derivative): the Taylor coefficients of `e^{xL}` are polynomials in `x` that agree
with `B_n^{(ℓ)}` at `x = ℓ ∈ ℕ`. The identity 24.16.8 is proved for real `0 < λ < 1/4` by writing
`(1+λt)^{1/λ} = eᵘ`, `u = ln(1+λt)/λ`, expanding `t/(eᵘ-1)` with 24.2.1, 24.16.5 and the
Stirling generating function 26.8.8 (`DLMF.Combinatorics.Stirling`), rearranging the absolutely
convergent double series and comparing coefficients with 24.16.7; agreement for infinitely many
`λ` gives the identity in `ℚ[λ]`. The file has no admissions.

# Zeros of Bernoulli and Euler polynomials (DLMF §24.12)

DLMF's `Bₙ(x)` and `Eₙ(x)` on the real line are Mathlib's `bernoulliFun n` and the project's
`eulerFun n` (`DLMFMathlib.NumberTheory.EulerPolynomials`).

## Definitions

* `bernoulliRealZerosGE n`: the real zeros of `Bₙ` in `[1/2, ∞)`, in increasing order and
  counted with multiplicity (they are simple by §24.12(iv)); `bernoulliRealZero n j` is DLMF's
  `x_j^{(n)}` (1-based, `j = 1, 2, …`). Beyond the last zero the totalized value is `0`.
  `bernoulliRealZeroCount n` is DLMF's `R(n)`, the number of real zeros (with multiplicity).
* `eulerRealZerosGE n`, `eulerRealZero n j` (DLMF's `y_j^{(n)}`): the same for `Eₙ`.

## Conventions

* The limits "as `n → ∞` with `m` fixed" for even (odd) `n` are taken along `n = 2k`
  (`n = 2k + 1`), `k → ∞`. The zero `x_{2m}^{(n)}` exists for large `n`, so the totalized value
  does not matter in these limits.
* "No multiple zeros" (§24.12(iv)) is `Polynomial.Separable` over `ℚ`, i.e. no repeated roots in
  an algebraic closure (in particular in `ℂ`). The statement for `Bₙ` is proved for every
  `n ≥ 0` (`B₀ = 1` is a unit), which includes DLMF's `n = 1, 2, …`.
* §24.12(iii) (complex zeros, irreducibility) consists of bibliographic pointers only.
* The numerical tables of zeros referred to elsewhere in the chapter are out of scope.

## Status

The zero counts in `[0, 1]` (§24.12(i)) are proved by Rolle's theorem from the derivative and
shift relations together with the Fourier series of `B₂ₘ` (Mathlib); `R(n) = n` for `n ≤ 5` is
proved from the explicit polynomials. The limits 24.12.4, 24.12.5 and 24.12.8 are proved from the
uniform limits 24.11.5–24.11.6 by a zero-counting (Hurwitz-type) argument, and so is the
corrected 24.12.11. The bounds 24.12.2, 24.12.9, 24.12.10 and the equivalence 24.12.3 are
proved from the Fourier series of `B₂ₖ` and `E₂ₘ₋₁` with explicit tail bounds (sign changes
locate the zero; `n = 2, 4` for 24.12.2 and `n = 5` for 24.12.10, where `y₂` is the double zero
`(1 + √5)/2`, from the explicit polynomials). The count 24.12.6 and the separability statements
of §24.12(iv) remain admitted. 24.12.11 as printed is
false: for odd `n` the limit of `y_{2m}^{(n)}` is `2m - 1/2`, not `m - 1/2`; the corrected
statement `y_m^{(n)} → m - 1/2` is proved (with a proved counterexample to the printed form).

# Bessel functions: definitions

Mathlib provides the first-kind Bessel function. The second-kind and modified functions
are defined here with their original integer-order limit conventions. Series, derivative
and differential-equation properties are developed in `DLMF.Bessel.RegularizedSeries`
and `DLMF.Bessel.Modified`.

# Bessel's integral (DLMF 10.9.1–10.9.2)

On the unit circle `t = e^{iθ}` the generating function becomes the Fourier series
`e^{iz sin θ} = ∑ₘ Jₘ(z) e^{imθ}` (Jacobi–Anger), whose coefficients are summable in absolute
value. Integrating term by term against `e^{-inθ}` over a period gives
`Jₙ(z) = (2π)⁻¹ ∫₀^{2π} e^{i(z sin θ - nθ)} dθ`, and folding the period at `θ = π` gives
Bessel's integral `Jₙ(z) = π⁻¹ ∫₀^π cos(z sin θ - nθ) dθ`.

# Absolute convergence of the Bessel generating function

Regroup the product of two exponential series by the difference of their indices.
Mathlib's regularized hypergeometric parameter shift supplies the negative integer orders.

# Gaussian and Laplace integrals of Bessel functions

Beals–Wong (9.8.3), with complex order, power, and Gaussian scale of positive real part.
The complex Gamma integral and absolute summation of Kummer's series extend the
Gamma-weighted regularized `₀F₁` argument of `DLMF.Confluent.IntegralRepresentations`.
The substitution `u = t²` gives the Bessel formula. Keeping Kummer's function
regularized also retains exceptional orders.
The Laplace transform reuses the existing full-half-plane Kummer Laplace theorem and
uses the continued Gauss function, even when the argument leaves the series disk.
`DLMF.Bessel.LaplaceTransform` supplies the conventional quadratic Gauss form
without the Kummer representation's order exclusions.

# Integral representations of `K_ν` (DLMF 10.32.9, 10.32.10)

For every complex order `ν` and `Re z > 0`,

`K_ν(z) = ½ ∫_ℝ e^{-z cosh t + νt} dt = ∫₀^∞ e^{-z cosh t} cosh(νt) dt` (DLMF 10.32.9),

and for `|ph z| < π/4`,

`K_ν(z) = ½ (z/2)^ν ∫₀^∞ e^{-t - z²/(4t)} t^{-ν-1} dt` (DLMF 10.32.10).

The proof does not use any Laplace-type representation of `K_ν`; this module sits below the
Tricomi integral representations (`DLMF.Confluent.IntegralRepresentations`), which may import it.

* The moments `Ψ_j(ν, z) = ∫ cosh^j t e^{-z cosh t + νt} dt` are holomorphic in `z` and `ν`, with
  `∂_z Ψ_j = -Ψ_{j+1}`; an integration by parts shows that `Φ = Ψ₀` solves the modified Bessel
  equation.
* For each solution `g`, the Wronskian combination `z (Φ g' - Φ' g)` is constant on the right
  half-plane; with `W{K_ν, I_ν} = 1/z` this gives `Φ = A(ν) K_ν - B(ν) I_ν`.
* The shift `t ↦ t - log(x/2)` and `v = e^t` turn `Φ` into Schläfli's form, whose limit as
  `x → 0⁺` gives `A(ν) = 2` for `Re ν > 0`; `A` is entire, hence `A ≡ 2`.
* The symmetry `Φ_{-ν} = Φ_ν`, `K_{-ν} = K_ν`, and the Wronskian of `I_{±ν}` give `B(ν) = 0` for
  `ν ∉ ℤ`; integer orders follow by continuity in `ν`.

# Laplace-type integrals for `K_ν` (DLMF 10.32.8)

Kummer's relation `U(ν+½, 2ν+1, 2z) = π^{-1/2} eᶻ (2z)^{-ν} K_ν(z)` (DLMF 13.6.10) and the
Laplace integral for `U` (DLMF 13.4.4) give, for `Re ν > -½` and `Re z > 0`,

`K_ν(z) = √π (2z)^ν e^{-z} / Γ(ν+½) ∫₀^∞ e^{-2zt} t^{ν-½} (1+t)^{ν-½} dt`,

and the substitution `u = 1 + 2t` turns this into DLMF 10.32.8,

`K_ν(z) = √π (z/2)^ν / Γ(ν+½) ∫₁^∞ e^{-zu} (u²-1)^{ν-½} du`.

# The Mellin transform of `K_ν` (DLMF 10.43.19)

For `|Re ν| < Re μ`,

`∫₀^∞ t^{μ-1} K_ν(t) dt = 2^{μ-2} Γ((μ-ν)/2) Γ((μ+ν)/2)` (DLMF 10.43.19),

with absolute convergence. The proof inserts Schläfli's form
`K_ν(x) = ½ (x/2)^ν ∫₀^∞ e^{-t - x²/(4t)} t^{-ν-1} dt` (`besselK_ofReal_eq_integral_schlafli`),
interchanges the order of integration (Tonelli, with the real Gaussian moments of Mathlib
bounding the absolute integrand) and evaluates the inner Gaussian moment
`∫₀^∞ x^{s-1} e^{-b x²} dx = ½ b^{-s/2} Γ(s/2)` and the outer Euler integral.

The result is also given in the language of Mathlib's `mellin` (`besselK_mellinConvergent`,
`mellin_besselK`), so that `mellin_comp_rpow` and `mellin_comp_mul_left` apply to
functions such as `K_ν(c t^p)`.

# The regularized Laplace–Bessel transform

Beals–Wong §9.8 in the conventional quadratic Gauss form. The proof starts with
Kummer's Laplace transform and the quadratic transformation, then lowers the
regularized denominator parameter by contiguous relations. This retains the
exceptional orders without cancellation of singular Gamma factors.

# Bessel functions of large order

All results come from the series `Γ(ν+1) ₀F̃₁(;ν+1;v) = ∑ v^n / (n! (ν+1)_n)` by dominated
convergence (Tannery's theorem) as `ν → +∞` along the reals.

* `tendsto_Gamma_mul_regularized0F1_mul`: `Γ(ν+1) ₀F̃₁(;ν+1;ν w) → e^w`.
* `tendsto_Gamma_mul_besselJ_sqrt_mul` (Beals–Wong (9.1.16)):
  `Γ(ν+1) J_ν(√ν x) / (√ν x/2)^ν → e^{-x²/4}`, and the companion
  `tendsto_Gamma_mul_besselI_sqrt_mul` for `I_ν` with limit `e^{x²/4}`.
* `norm_besselJ_le`: `|J_ν(z)| ≤ |(z/2)^ν| e^{|z|²/4} / Γ(ν+1)` for real `ν ≥ 0`.
* `besselJ_isEquivalent_large_order` (DLMF 10.19.1): `J_ν(z) ∼ (ez/(2ν))^ν / √(2πν)` for fixed
  `z ≠ 0`, using Binet's form of Stirling's formula.

# Lommel's integral and Fourier–Bessel orthogonality (DLMF 10.22.5, 10.22.37)

The function `F(t) = t (β J_ν(αt) J_{ν-1}(βt) - α J_{ν-1}(αt) J_ν(βt))` has derivative
`(α² - β²) t J_ν(αt) J_ν(βt)`. For `re ν > -1` the leading terms of the two products cancel at
`t = 0`, so `F(t) = O(t^{2 re ν + 2})` and `F(0⁺) = 0`; the integrand is `O(t^{2 re ν + 1})` and
hence integrable. The fundamental theorem of calculus then gives Lommel's integral on `[0, 1]`,
and orthogonality of `t ↦ J_ν(j t)` over distinct positive zeros `j` of `J_ν`. The normalization
`∫₀¹ t J_ν(jt)² dt = J_{ν+1}(j)²/2` uses the primitive
`t²(J_{ν+1}(jt)² + J_ν(jt)²)/2 - (ν/j) t J_ν(jt) J_{ν+1}(jt)`, whose `ν²` terms have cancelled so
that it vanishes at `0⁺` for every `re ν > -1`.

# Modified Bessel functions (AAR §4.12)

`I_ν` is the `₀F₁` series with argument `+z²/4`. `K_ν` is the second-kind combination of
`I_ν` and `I_{-ν}`.

# Neumann series of Bessel functions

A *Neumann series* is an expansion `∑ₖ aₖ J_{ν+nₖ}(z)` (or with `I`) in Bessel functions whose
orders increase by integers. Writing `J_{ν+n}(z) = (z/2)^ν (z/2)^n ₀F̃₁(;ν+n+1;-(z/2)²)`, such a
series is a double series in `(k, m)`. This file proves:

* `exists_norm_recip_Gamma_add_nat_le`: `|1/Γ(c+n)| ≤ C 2ⁿ/n!`, uniformly in `n`, for every `c`;
  hence `exists_norm_regularized0F1Coeff_le`, a bound on the `₀F̃₁` coefficients uniform in
  the integer shift of the order;
* `hasSum_neumann`: under `∑ₖ |aₖ| |w|^{eₖ} 2^{nₖ}/nₖ! < ∞` the double series is absolutely
  summable and the Neumann series is its sum (rearrangement theorem);
* `hasSum_neumannCoeff`: for `eₖ = 2k` the same sum is the power series `∑ⱼ bⱼ w^{2j}` whose
  coefficients `bⱼ = neumannCoeff` are finite antidiagonal convolutions;
* `hasSum_besselJ_neumann`, `hasSum_besselI_neumann`: the corresponding statements for
  `∑ₖ aₖ (z/2)^{pₖ} J_{ν+nₖ}(z)` and `I`, with `pₖ + nₖ = 2k`, and `differentiable_neumann`;
* coefficient identities: the partial-fraction sum `sum_antidiagonal_neg_one_pow_div_add`,
  Neumann's expansion of a power `(z/2)^λ = ∑ₖ (λ+2k)Γ(λ+k)/k! J_{λ+2k}(z)`
  (`hasSum_besselJ_neumann_power`), and the Lommel-type coefficients
  (`neumannCoeff_lommel`, `hasSum_besselJ_neumann_lommel`), obtained from the Bessel operator at
  coefficient level;
* growth bounds for the coefficients (`exists_norm_powerNeumannCoeff_le`,
  `summable_neumann_of_norm_le`) and small Pochhammer/binomial helpers;
* Neumann series with `eₖ = k` (orders of both parities): `hasSum_neumannLinCoeff`,
  `hasSum_besselJ_neumann_linear`, `hasSum_besselI_neumann_linear`, via the fibre-summation
  lemma `hasSum_sum_range_fiber`;
* two terminating hypergeometric identities in polynomial form, proved by WZ certificates and
  valid for all parameters: the very-well-poised `₄F₃(-1)` sum `sum_range_vwpTerm` and
  `sum_range_kumTerm`, which gives the power series of `₀F̃₁(;c;w²) e^{2w}`
  (`hasSum_regularized0F1_mul_exp`, the regularized DLMF 13.6.9).

# Graf's addition theorem (DLMF 10.23.7)

With `u - v cos α = w cos χ`, `v sin α = w sin χ` (DLMF 10.23.8) we have
`w e^{±iχ} = u - v e^{∓iα}`, so on the circle `t = e^{iθ}` the generating functions combine:
`e^{(w/2)(e^{iχ}t - e^{-iχ}/t)} = e^{(u/2)(t - 1/t)} e^{(v/2)(s - 1/s)}`, `s = -e^{-iα} t`.
Comparing Fourier coefficients (term-by-term integration against `e^{-inθ}`, with Bessel's
integral for the factor `e^{iu sin θ}`) gives `J_n(w) e^{inχ} = ∑_k J_{n+k}(u) J_k(v) e^{ikα}`
for every integer `n` and all complex `u`, `v`, `α` (no restriction `|v e^{±iα}| < |u|` is needed
at integer order of `J`).

# The product integral `J_μ J_ν` (DLMF 10.9.26)

For `ℜ(μ+ν) > -1`,
`J_μ(z) J_ν(z) = (2/π) ∫₀^{π/2} J_{μ+ν}(2z cos θ) cos((μ-ν)θ) dθ`.

## Method

* `integral_cos_cpow_mul_cos`: the cosine Beta integral DLMF 5.12.5 for complex parameters,
  `∫₀^{π/2} cos^{a-1} t cos(bt) dt = π Γ(a) 2^{-a} / (Γ((a+b+1)/2) Γ((a-b+1)/2))`, `ℜ a > 0`.
  The real case is `DLMF.Gamma.integral_cos_rpow_mul_cos`. It is extended to complex `b`
  (entire in `b`) and then to complex `a` (holomorphic on `ℜ a > 0`) by the identity theorem.
* Expanding `J_{μ+ν}(2z cos θ)` in its series and integrating termwise (dominated convergence)
  gives the product series DLMF 10.8.3 (`besselJ_mul_besselJ`).

# Regularized-series and differential properties of Bessel functions (AAR §§4.5–4.6)

The series

$$
J_ν(z)=\Bigl(\frac{z}{2}\Bigr)^ν\sum_{k=0}^∞\frac{(-1)^k}{k!\,Γ(ν+k+1)}\Bigl(\frac{z}{2}\Bigr)^{2k}
$$

is Mathlib's regularized `₀F₁(;ν+1;-z²/4)` multiplied by `(z/2)^ν`; it is Mathlib's
`Complex.besselJ`, used here directly, with `besselJ_eq_regularized` giving the series form. The
second-kind function `Y_ν` is the usual linear combination of `J_ν` and `J_{-ν}`.

# Schläfli's integral for `J_ν` (DLMF 10.9.6)

For complex `ν` and `ℜ z > 0`,
`J_ν(z) = π⁻¹ ∫₀^π cos(z sin θ - νθ) dθ - (sin νπ / π) ∫₀^∞ e^{-z sinh t - νt} dt`.

The integer case is Bessel's integral (`besselJ_int_eq_integral_cos`, DLMF 10.9.2).

## Method

With `c = z/2`, expand `e^{-c e^{-iθ}}` and `e^{c e^{-t}}` in powers of `c`. Termwise, Schläfli's
integral becomes `∑ₖ (-c)ᵏ/k! G(ν+k, c)`, where
`G(a, c) = (2π)⁻¹ ∫_{-π}^{π} e^{c e^{iθ} - iaθ} dθ - (sin πa/π) ∫₀^∞ e^{-c eᵗ - at} dt`
is Hankel's loop integral for `1/Γ` in the coordinate `u = e^w`. We show `G(a, c) = cᵃ/Γ(a+1)`
(`schlafli_gamma`):

* for `-1 < ℜ a < 0` and real `c > 0`, the circle part is `-2 sin πa ∫₀¹ u^{-a-1} e^{-cu} du`
  (termwise), the ray part is `∫₁^∞ u^{-a-1} e^{-cu} du` (substitution `u = eᵗ`), and Euler's
  integral and the reflection formula finish;
* both sides are entire in `a` and holomorphic in `c` on `ℜ c > 0`
  (`Complex.differentiableOn_integral_Ioi_of_locally_dominated`), so the identity theorem extends
  the formula.

The termwise sum is then the `₀F₁` series of `J_ν`.

## Main results

* `DLMF.Bessel.schlafli_gamma`: Hankel's formula for `1/Γ` in exponential coordinates.
* `DLMF.Bessel.besselJ_eq_schlafli`: Schläfli's integral (DLMF 10.9.6).
* `DLMF.Bessel.angular_sub_besselJ_eq_schlafli`: the difference form used for the Anger function.
* `DLMF.Bessel.integrableOn_schlafli`, `DLMF.Bessel.differentiable_schlafli_order`: integrability
  and holomorphy in the order of the radial integral.
* `DLMF.Bessel.tendsto_intervalIntegral_schlafliBoundary`: convergence of the radial integral as
  an improper integral for `ℜ μ > 0`, `ℜ w ≥ 0`, `w ≠ 0`, with continuity of its value.

# Bessel functions of the second kind and Hankel functions (Temme §§9.1–9.4, DLMF 10.2–10.6)

The series `J_ν(z) = (z/2)^ν ₀F₁(ν+1; -z²/4)` is jointly continuous in `(ν, z)` on `ℂ × slitPlane`
and entire in `ν`. Hence `D_ν(z) = J_ν(z) cos νπ - J_{-ν}(z)`, which vanishes at integer `ν`,
divided by `sin νπ` has a removable singularity at each integer. This shows that Weber's `Y_ν` at
integer order, defined in `besselY` as a limit, is the continuous extension, jointly in `(ν, z)`.
The recurrences, the derivative, the Bessel equation and the Wronskians then hold for every order.

# Sonine’s integral and Gamma-weighted integrals of regularized `₀F₁`

Termwise integration is justified by the absolute convergence of a regularized
`₁F₁` series whose first parameter is the real part of the Gamma weight.
Scaling and the substitution `u = t²` then give Sonine’s Bessel integral.

# Series in products of spherical Bessel functions (DLMF §§6.10, 10.51, 10.60)

The series `Cin(z) = ∑ aₙ jₙ(z/2)²` of DLMF 6.10.5 does not telescope termwise. It is reduced
here to three sums of squares of spherical Bessel functions, each of which does telescope:

* `sphProd_hasSum_sq`: `∑ (2n+1) jₙ(z)² = 1`;
* `sphProd_hasSum_alt_mul`: `∑ (-1)ⁿ (2n+1) jₙ(x) jₙ(y) = j₀(x+y)` (a case of the addition
  theorem DLMF 10.60.2); along the line `x + y = const` the derivative of the `n`-th term is a
  difference `Eₙ - Eₙ₊₁` of antisymmetric products;
* `sphProd_hasSum_alt_sq`: `∑ (-1)ⁿ (2n+1) jₙ(z)² = j₀(2z)`.

Also provided: the unified derivative `(2n+1) jₙ' = n jₙ₋₁ - (n+1) jₙ₊₁` (DLMF 10.51.2),
the Euler form `z jₙ'(z) = n jₙ(z) - z jₙ₊₁(z)`, the values `jₙ(0)`, and summable bounds for
spherical Bessel functions weighted by geometrically growing coefficients.

# Tools for series in spherical Bessel functions (DLMF §§6.10, 7.6, 10.51)

Series such as `C(z) = z ∑ₙ j_{2n}(πz²/2)` (DLMF 7.6.10) or `Si(z) = z ∑ₙ j_n(z/2)²`
(DLMF 6.10.4) share one mechanism: by the recurrences of DLMF 10.51.1–10.51.2 the
derivative of the `n`-th term is a difference `gₙ - gₙ₊₁`, so the differentiated series
telescopes to `g₀`, which is the derivative of the left-hand side.

This file provides
* `sphSeries_hasSum_of_hasDerivAt`: the telescoping principle for entire terms that are
  bounded on balls by a summable sequence (termwise differentiation through
  `hasSum_deriv_of_summable_norm`);
* norm bounds and summability for the spherical Bessel functions `sphericalJ`, `sphericalI`;
* the derivative and three-term recurrences of DLMF 10.51.1–10.51.2 for `sphericalJ`, valid for
  all complex arguments (no division by `z`);
* the elementary values `z j₀(z) = sin z` and `j₀(z) - z j₁(z) = cos z`.

# Zeros of Bessel functions and the large-argument behaviour of `I_ν`

* `besselJ_im_eq_zero_of_eq_zero`: for real `ν > -1` every zero of `J_ν` is real (DLMF 10.21(i)).
  With `g = ₀F̃₁(ν+1; ·)` and `A = -α²/4`, the function `t ↦ t^{2ν+2}(B g(At²) g'(Bt²) -
  A g'(At²) g(Bt²))` has derivative `2(B-A) t^{2ν+1} g(At²) g(Bt²)` (a Lommel identity), so for
  `B = Ā` and `g(A) = 0` the positive integral `∫₀¹ t^{2ν+1} |g(At²)|² dt` forces `A = Ā`. The
  case `A > 0` is excluded since `I_ν` is positive.
* `besselI_sub_exp_isBigO`, `besselI_isEquivalent`: `I_ν(x) = eˣ/√(2πx) + O(eˣ x^{-3/2})`
  (DLMF 10.40.1, leading term), from `I_ν(x) = c(x) 𝐌(ν+½, 2ν+1, 2x)` and DLMF 13.7.1.
* `IsRealBesselSolution`: real solutions of Bessel's equation (real cylinder functions). Through
  the Liouville normal form `u = √x y`, `u'' + (1 - (ν²-¼)/x²) u = 0`, Sturm comparison
  (`DLMFMathlib.Analysis.ODE.SturmComparison`) gives Beals–Wong Thm 9.2.1: infinitely many positive
  zeros (`infinite_zeros`), a zero in every `(a, a+π)` for `|ν| < ½` (`exists_zero_Ioo`), and
  gaps larger than `π` for `|ν| > ½` (`pi_lt_sub`); with the corollaries for `J_ν`.
* `besselJ_succ_ne_zero_of_eq_zero`, `existsUnique_besselJ_succ_zero_between`,
  `existsUnique_besselJ_zero_between`: the positive zeros of `J_ν` and `J_{ν+1}` interlace
  strictly (DLMF 10.21.3).

# Integral representations of `Y_ν` and of `K_ν = H_ν - Y_ν` (DLMF 10.9.5, 11.5.2)

For `re z > 0` let
`L_ν(z) = 2(z/2)^ν/(√π Γ(ν+½)) ∫₀^∞ e^{-zt} (1+t²)^{ν-½} dt` (`besselYLaplace`).

* `struveK_eq_integral` (DLMF 11.5.2): `K_ν(z) = H_ν(z) - Y_ν(z) = L_ν(z)` for **every** `ν`
  and `re z > 0`.
* `besselY_eq_integral` (DLMF 10.9.5): for `re ν > -½` and `re z > 0`,
  `Y_ν(z) = 2(z/2)^ν/(√π Γ(ν+½)) (∫₀¹ (1-t²)^{ν-½} sin(zt) dt - ∫₀^∞ e^{-zt} (1+t²)^{ν-½} dt)`.
* `besselJ_eq_poisson_cos`: Poisson's integral (DLMF 10.9.4) for complex `z` with `re z > 0`.
* `hankelH1_eq_integral_Ioi_one`: `H^{(1)}_ν(z)` through `∫₁^∞ e^{izu} (u²-1)^{ν-½} du`
  (DLMF 10.27.8 with 10.32.8) in the open first quadrant.

Proof. For `re ν > ½` and `z` in the open first quadrant, `H_ν - i J_ν` (Poisson integrals) and
`H^{(1)}_ν` (via `K_ν(-iz)` and DLMF 10.32.8) express `H_ν - Y_ν` through
`∫₀¹ (1-t²)^{ν-½} e^{izt} dt` and `∫₁^∞ (t²-1)^{ν-½} e^{izt} dt`. Cauchy's theorem on the squares
`[0,R]²` for `(-i(s-1))^{ν-½} (s+1)^{ν-½} e^{izs}` (`contour_identity`) rotates these onto the
imaginary axis, giving `L_ν(z)`. The identity theorem extends to `re z > 0`, and the lowering
relations `K_ν' = K_{ν-1} - (ν/z)K_ν`, `L_ν' = L_{ν-1} - (ν/z)L_ν` (the latter by differentiating
under the integral and integrating by parts) extend to all `ν` by downward induction.

# Schläfli's integral for `Y_ν` (DLMF 10.9.7)

For complex `ν` and `re z > 0`,
`Y_ν(z) = π⁻¹ ∫₀^π sin(z sin θ - νθ) dθ - π⁻¹ ∫₀^∞ (e^{νt} + e^{-νt} cos νπ) e^{-z sinh t} dt`.

At noninteger order this is `Y_ν = (J_ν cos νπ - J_{-ν}) / sin νπ` with Schläfli's integral for
`J_{±ν}` (`besselJ_eq_schlafli`, DLMF 10.9.6) and the reflection `θ ↦ π - θ` of the angular
integral; both sides are continuous in `ν`, which covers the integer orders.

# Monotonicity of the first zero of `J_ν` (DLMF 10.21(iv); Watson §15.6)

With `B_ν(z) = ν J_ν(z) - z J_{ν+1}(z) = z J_ν'(z)`, Bessel's equation reads
`B_ν' = (ν²/z - z) J_ν`,
so `W = J_ν B_μ - B_ν J_μ` satisfies `W' = (μ² - ν²)/z · J_ν J_μ`.

For real `0 ≤ ν < μ`, suppose `j_{μ,1} ≤ j_{ν,1}`. Then `W` is strictly increasing on
`(0, j_{μ,1}]` and tends to `0` at `0⁺`, so `W(j_{μ,1}) = J_ν(j_{μ,1}) J_μ'(j_{μ,1}) j_{μ,1} > 0`.
This contradicts `J_μ > 0` on `(0, j_{μ,1})`. Hence the first positive zero
`sInf {x > 0 | J_ν(x) = 0}`
is strictly increasing in `ν ≥ 0`. The infimum is attained because `J_ν > 0` near `0⁺` and the
zero set is closed, using `DLMF.Bessel.besselJ_infinite_zeros_of_real` for nonemptiness.

# Bessel functions (AAR Chapter 4, §§4.5–4.15; DLMF Chapter 10)

`J_ν` is Mathlib's `Complex.besselJ`, used directly; `besselJ_eq_regularized` gives its
regularized `₀F₁` series form, and Mathlib supplies parity at integer order (DLMF 10.11.1),
analyticity, entireness at integer order and the value at `0`. This cluster defines `Y_ν`,
`I_ν`, `K_ν` and the Hankel functions. It proves differential equations, recurrences,
Wronskians, half-integer values, Poisson's, Sonine's, Bessel's and Lommel's integrals, the
generating function, Hankel's large-argument expansions and the existence of infinitely many real
zeros.

The integer-order values of `Y` and `K` are parameter limits (`Filter.limUnder`). These limits
exist at every nonzero argument, are jointly continuous in order and argument
(`continuousAt_besselY`, `continuousAt_besselK`), and satisfy the recurrences and differential
equations for all orders. `WeberSeries` gives `Y_{-n} = (-1)ⁿ Y_n`, `Y_n` as an order derivative
of `J_ν`, the logarithmic series of `Y_n` (DLMF 10.8.1–10.8.2), the general solution
`A J_ν + B Y_ν` of Bessel's equation, the product formula 10.8.3 and the Jacobi–Anger cosine and
sine series. The values at zero supplied by the totalized definitions must not be
interpreted as finite limits of the classical singular functions.

The remaining admitted results are Gegenbauer's addition theorem (DLMF 10.23.8) and Nicholson's
integral (10.9.30). Their
stated domains agree with DLMF; in particular, no radius ordering is needed in 10.23.8 for `J`.

# Leading-order asymptotics of the canonical integrals: DLMF §36.11

* 36.11.1–36.11.2: the stationary-phase approximation of `Ψ_K(x)` far from the origin, away
  from the bifurcation set. DLMF does not say along which path `x → ∞`; we state it along the
  scaling rays of §36.6, `x(k) = (x₁k^{γ₁}, …, x_Kk^{γ_K})` (`cuspoidScaledCoords`) with
  `k → ∞`, for `x ∉` bifurcation set: on this ray `Ψ_K(x(k)) = k^{1/(K+2)} ∫ exp(ikΦ_K(τ; x)) dτ`,
  and 36.11.2 is the stationary-phase theorem for the large parameter `k`. Each term of the sum is
  of exact order `k^{1/(K+2) - 1/2}`, so DLMF's factors `1 + o(1)` amount to an `o` of that order.
* 36.11.3–36.11.8: asymptotics along symmetry lines, stated with `Asymptotics.IsLittleO`.

**Corrections (36.11.7, 36.11.8).** DLMF states both formulas for `z → ±∞`. They hold for
`z → +∞` only. By 36.2.24, `Ψ^{(U)}(0, 0, -z) = conj Ψ^{(U)}(0, 0, z)`, and conjugating the printed
formulas gives, for `z → -∞`,
`Ψ^{(E)}(0, 0, z) = (π/z)(i - √3 exp(4iz³/27) + o(1))` and
`Ψ^{(H)}(0, 0, z) = (2π/z)(-1 - (i/√3) exp(iz³/27) + o(1))`,
that is `(π/|z|)(i sign z + √3 e^{4iz³/27})` and `(2π/|z|)(1 - i sign z e^{iz³/27}/√3)`. Direct
quadrature confirms this: `Ψ^{(E)}(0, 0, -6) = 0.75621 - 1.01820i` against the printed
`-0.75656 - 0.02351i` and the corrected `0.75656 - 1.02369i`; `Ψ^{(H)}(0, 0, -12) =
0.80126 + 0.11760i` against the printed `-0.24548 + 0.11846i` and the corrected
`0.80172 + 0.11846i`. The `z → -∞` statements below are the corrected forms, derived from the
`z → +∞` statements and 36.2.24.

**36.11.6.** DLMF's `z → +∞` remainder `o(1)` is weaker than the size `|z|^{-1/3}` of the leading
term; we state the stronger `o(|z|^{-1/3})` (stronger than DLMF), which numerical quadrature
supports (relative error `3·10⁻⁵` at `z = 20` and `9·10⁻⁷` at `z = 60`).

Other numerical checks: 36.11.2 for `K = 1, 2, 3` at points with one to three real critical
points, 36.11.3–36.11.5 and 36.11.6 (`z → -∞`) at moderate arguments; relative errors decrease as
the argument grows.

**Proofs.** 36.11.3 for `y → +∞` (`cuspoidIntegral_two_zero_atTop`) is proved by the scaling
`t = u/√y` and dominated convergence to a complex Gaussian integral. 36.11.6 for `z → +∞`
(`cuspoidIntegral_three_z_atTop`) is proved by splitting `Ψ₃(0, 0, z) = 2 Re ∫_0^∞`, the
scaling `r = u/z^{1/3}`, dominated convergence to `∫_0^∞ e^{iπ/10} exp(i(ue^{iπ/10})³) du`, and
rotation of that ray to the angle `π/6` (the `θ`-derivative of the ray integral vanishes), where
it equals `e^{iπ/6} Γ(4/3)`.

# Integrals with coalescing saddles: definitions (DLMF Chapter 36)

This file defines the canonical integrals, catastrophe sets and scaling data of
DLMF Chapter 36 (namespace `DLMF.CoalescingSaddles`). Auxiliary moments, series
coefficients and zero models are in `DLMF.CoalescingSaddles.Basic.AuxiliaryData`.

## Potentials (DLMF 36.2.1–36.2.3)

* `cuspoidPotential K t x = t^(K+2) + ∑ₘ xₘ t^m` (36.2.1), for complex `t` and real
  parameters `x : Fin K → ℝ`; the coefficient of `t^(m+1)` is `x m`, so DLMF's `x₁, x₂, …`
  are `x 0, x 1, …`. `K = 1, 2, 3` are the fold, cusp and swallowtail.
* `ellipticUmbilicPotential s t x y z` (36.2.2), `hyperbolicUmbilicPotential s t x y z`
  (36.2.3), for complex `s, t` and real `x, y, z`.

## Canonical integrals (DLMF 36.2.4, 36.2.5, 36.2.10, 36.2.11)

The integrals `∫ exp(iΦ)` of DLMF over `ℝ` or `ℝ²` are oscillatory and not absolutely
convergent. Following the DLMF remark in §36.2(i) ("the convergence … can be confirmed by
rotating the integration paths in the complex plane"), they are defined here as absolutely
convergent Bochner integrals over rotated contours; the agreement with the improper real
integrals of DLMF is stated separately (`DLMF.CoalescingSaddles.CanonicalIntegrals`).

* Cuspoids: with `n = K + 2` and `θ = π/(2n)`, the contour is `r ↦ r·d(r)` for `r ∈ ℝ`, where
  `d(r) = e^{iθ}` for `r ≥ 0` and, for `r < 0`, `d(r) = e^{iθ}` if `K` is even (a straight line)
  and `e^{-iθ}` if `K` is odd (a V through `0`). On both rays `(r d(r))ⁿ = i|r|ⁿ`, so
  `|exp(iΦ_K)| = exp(-|r|ⁿ + O(|r|^{n-1}))`. `cuspoidIntegral K x = ∫ d(r) exp(iΦ_K(r d(r); x)) dr`.
* Hyperbolic umbilic: the product of two cubic V-contours (`K = 1`) in `s` and in `t`.
* Elliptic umbilic: with `a = s + it`, `b = s - it` the cubic part is `(a³ + b³)/2`; the real
  `(s, t)`-plane is replaced by the 2-cycle `∑ ε_{jk} ρ_j × ρ_k` of products of the rays
  `ρ_j = e^{i(π/6 + 2πj/3)}·[0, ∞)` in the `a`- and `b`-planes, with the integer matrix
  `ε = [[-1,0,1],[0,1,-1],[1,-1,0]]` (`ellipticUmbilicCycle`) and Jacobian `ds dt = (i/2) da db`.
  This choice was checked numerically against 36.2.6, 36.2.7, 36.2.18, 36.2.20, 36.2.24–36.2.26
  and 36.2.28 at sample points (agreement to 12 digits).
* Diffraction catastrophes `Ψ(x; k)` (36.2.10, 36.2.11) use the same contours with phase `kΦ`;
  DLMF requires `k > 0`.

## Critical points, bifurcation sets and Stokes sets (§§36.4, 36.5)

Derivatives are complex derivatives of the polynomial potentials (`deriv`, `iteratedDeriv`), and
real critical points are real arguments at which they vanish. Stokes sets are formalized by the
exponential dominance condition 36.5.1 together with a connecting path on which `Re Φ` is constant
(DLMF's steepest-descent path).

## Scaling exponents (§36.6)

`cuspoidSingularityIndex` (`β_K`), `cuspoidCoordinateIndex` (`γ_{mK}`), `cuspoidVolumeIndex`
(`γ_K`), and the umbilic exponents.

# Bifurcation sets (DLMF §36.4)

Statements acquired from the NIST DLMF (version 1.2.8), checked 2026-10-26.

The critical points (36.4.1, 36.4.2) and bifurcation sets (36.4.3, 36.4.4) are defined in
`DLMF.CoalescingSaddles.Basic` with complex derivatives of the polynomial potentials. Here the
explicit descriptions 36.4.5–36.4.13 are proved: the fold, cusp and swallowtail bifurcation sets,
the swallowtail self-intersection line and ribs, the elliptic umbilic astroid and ribs, and the
hyperbolic umbilic bifurcation set and rib. Two statements are adjusted: the self-intersection line
36.4.8 has `z < 0` (DLMF: `z ≤ 0`; the origin is only a limit point), and the hyperbolic umbilic
parametrization 36.4.12 is stated for `z ≠ 0` (the slice `z = 0` consists of two half-lines that
the parametrization does not produce). The cusp lines are formalized as `cuspoidCuspLines` and
`umbilicCuspLines` (Basic). The bounds `j_max ≤ K + 1` and `j_max ≤ 4` on the
number of real critical points are proved by mapping the critical points injectively into the
roots of a nonzero complex polynomial (`q2s_finite_ncard_le_of_poly`).

The derivatives are computed through `s36a_hasDerivAt_poly`: the derivative of
`∑_{i ≤ N} cᵢ uⁱ` is `∑_{i < N} (i+1) c_{i+1} uⁱ`.

# Differential equations for the canonical integrals: DLMF §36.10

The canonical integrals are defined (`DLMF.CoalescingSaddles.Basic`) as absolutely convergent
integrals over rotated contours, on which the integrand and all its polynomial moments have
Gaussian decay. This file proves

* differentiation under the integral sign: `∂Ψ_K/∂x_m` is `i` times the moment of order `m`
  (`hasDerivAt_cuspoidMoment_update`, `iteratedDeriv_cuspoidIntegral_update`), so that
  `∂ⁿΨ_K/∂x_mⁿ = iⁿ ∫ t^{mn} exp(iΦ_K) dt`;
* integration by parts along the contour: `∫ (∂Φ_K/∂t) exp(iΦ_K) dt = 0`
  (`cuspoidMoment_ibp`), since the integrand is `-i d/dt exp(iΦ_K)` and `exp(iΦ_K)` vanishes at
  both ends of the contour.

From these, the operator equation 36.10.1, the ordinary differential equation 36.10.2 in `x₁`,
its special cases 36.10.3–36.10.5, and the relations 36.10.6–36.10.10 between partial derivatives
are proved. Of the umbilic equations 36.10.11–36.10.18, those for `Ψ^{(H)}` (36.10.15, 36.10.16,
36.10.18) are proved in the same way on the product of two cubic contours
(`hasDerivAt_hyperbolicUmbilicMoment_x`, Fubini and integration by parts in each variable); those
for `Ψ^{(E)}` (36.10.13, 36.10.14, 36.10.17) are proved on the 2-cycle of
`ellipticUmbilicIntegral` in the coordinates `a = s + it`, `b = s - it`, with weighted moments
`q2t_EM` and integration by parts along each ray (the boundary terms cancel over the cycle).

Partial derivatives are written with `Function.update`: `∂ⁿΨ_K/∂x_mⁿ` at `x` is
`iteratedDeriv n (fun s => cuspoidIntegral K (Function.update x m s)) (x m)`, where (as in
`DLMF.CoalescingSaddles.Basic`) the Lean index `m : Fin K` is DLMF's `x_{m+1}`. All
differentiability used in these statements is proved here (the canonical integrals are smooth
in each variable), so the Lean convention `deriv f = 0` at non-differentiable points never
enters.

The integrability lemmas for the rotated contour (`norm_cuspoidContour`, `cuspoidContour_pow`,
`s36a_norm_integrand_le`, …) are those of `DLMF.CoalescingSaddles.CanonicalIntegrals`.

# Integral identities for the canonical integrals: DLMF §36.9

The squared moduli of the canonical integrals as integrals of canonical integrals of lower
"dimension" (DLMF 36.9.1–36.9.9). Notation: `Ψ₁(x) = cuspoidIntegral 1 ![x]`,
`Ψ₂(x, y) = cuspoidIntegral 2 ![x, y]`, `Ψ₃(x, y, z) = cuspoidIntegral 3 ![x, y, z]`.

Where the integral of DLMF converges absolutely (36.9.1, 36.9.2, 36.9.4–36.9.8) the statement
includes the integrability of the integrand; 36.9.3 converges only conditionally (the integrand is
of size `u^{-1/2}`) and is stated as the limit of `∫_0^R` as `R → ∞`; 36.9.9 is stated as the
iterated integral of DLMF, with the inner `θ`-integral over `[0, 2π]` and the outer `u`-integral
as a limit of `∫_0^R` (the integrand `Ai(w)Bi(w̄)` grows like `exp(c u³)` in some directions, so
the double integral is not absolutely convergent).

Numerical checks (mpmath, rotated-contour quadrature for the canonical integrals): 36.9.1–36.9.8
agree to 6–15 digits at sample points. For 36.9.9 the inner `θ`-integral involves cancellation
from `10^{50}` and the partial `u`-integrals oscillate; the check was inconclusive (see the
ledger).

The diffraction catastrophes `Ψ(x; k)` (36.2.10, 36.2.11) are expressed through the canonical
