# Convergent series for the canonical integrals: DLMF §36.8

* 36.8.1–36.8.2: the power series of `Ψ_K(x)` in the parameters, with the coefficients
  `a_n(x)` of `exp(i ∑ xₘ tᵐ) = ∑ aₙ(x) tⁿ` (`cuspoidSeriesCoeff`) and the moments
  `∫ tⁿ exp(i t^{K+2}) dt` written with gamma functions;
* 36.8.3: the hyperbolic umbilic `Ψ^{(H)}` as a series in `z` with Airy coefficients;
* 36.8.4–36.8.6: the elliptic umbilic `Ψ^{(E)}` as a series in `z`, with the functions `f_n` and
  the polynomials `c_n, d_n` (`ellipticUmbilicSeriesF`, `umbilicSeriesC`, `umbilicSeriesD`).

The series are stated with `HasSum` (all of them converge absolutely, the canonical integrals
being entire in the parameters). DLMF starts three of the four series of 36.8.3 at `n = 2, 2, 1`;
the omitted terms vanish because `d₀ = 0` and `c₁ = 0` (`umbilicSeriesD_zero`,
`umbilicSeriesC_one`), so 36.8.3 is stated as one series from `n = 0`.

Numerical checks (mpmath, rotated-contour quadrature): 36.8.1 for `K = 1, …, 4`, 36.8.3 and
36.8.4 at sample points, agreement to 19 digits.

# Stokes sets (DLMF §36.5)

Statements acquired from the NIST DLMF (version 1.2.8), checked 2026-10-26.

The Stokes sets are defined in `DLMF.CoalescingSaddles.Basic` (`cuspoidStokesSet`,
`umbilicStokesSet` and their complex–complex variants) by the exponential dominance condition
36.5.1 together with a connecting path of constant `Re Φ`. This file proves the fold case
(§36.5(ii), `K = 1`, in the form of the dominance condition for complex `x`) and states the
parametrizations 36.5.2–36.5.21 of the cusp, swallowtail, elliptic umbilic and hyperbolic umbilic
Stokes sets. The cusp case 36.5.2 is proved (necessity by elimination from the critical-point
equations; sufficiency by an explicit level curve of `Re Φ₂` joining the real saddle to a complex
one); the others are admitted. All of them were checked numerically at sample points (the real
parts of `Φ` at the real and the complex critical point agree to working precision).

Notation: the swallowtail coordinates `(x, y, z)` are `(x 0, x 1, x 2)`; `σ = Real.sign z`.
The decimal values 36.5.5 (`B_±`) and `X₁, Y₁, X₂, Y₂` are excluded as numerical; where DLMF
uses `Y₁` or `X₂` as a threshold the statement asserts the existence of the threshold.

# Zeros of the canonical integrals: DLMF §36.7

DLMF §36.7 describes the zeros of the canonical integrals, mostly through approximate formulas
read off from the stationary-phase approximation and from numerical computation (Berry, Nye and
Wright 1979). The approximate loci 36.7.1, 36.7.2, 36.7.4–36.7.7 are definitions in
`DLMF.CoalescingSaddles.Basic.AuxiliaryData`; the words "approximately", "close to", "deep inside" carry no
error bound and are not formalized. This file proves the exact statements:

* the zeros of `Ψ₁` are those of `Ai(x/3^{1/3})` (§36.7(i), from 36.2.13);
* 36.7.3 has exactly one positive solution `ξ_n` for every `n` (DLMF: "the real solution");
* the exact part of 36.7.4, `3(π(2n - 1/2)/4)^{1/3} = 3(π/2)^{1/3}(n - 1/4)^{1/3}` (the decimal
  value `3.48734` is excluded as numerical);

and states (admitted) the two analytic claims with a precise meaning: all zeros of the Pearcey
integral have `y < 0` (§36.7(ii)), and the asymptotic form 36.7.8 of the zeros of `Ψ^{(E)}` in the
plane `z = 0`. Table 36.7.1 is excluded as numerical.

# Notation and basic definitions (DLMF §§26.1–26.2)

DLMF 26.1.1 introduces the rising and falling factorials `x^{(n)} = x(x+1)⋯(x+n-1)` and
`x_{(n)} = x(x-1)⋯(x-n+1)`; these are Mathlib's `ascPochhammer` and `descPochhammer`
(evaluated at `x`). The other §26.2 notions are Mathlib's: a permutation of a finite set is an
`Equiv.Perm`, its cycles are `Equiv.Perm.cycleFactorsFinset` (with the cycle type, fixed points
included, in `Equiv.Perm.partition`), a partition of a finite set `S` is a `Finpartition S`,
and a partition of an integer `n` is a `Nat.Partition n` (the partition function `p(n)` is
`DLMF.Partitions.partitionFunction`).

Lattice paths (§26.2) have no Mathlib counterpart and are defined here. A lattice path from
`(0, 0)` to `(m, n)` with steps in a finite set `steps ⊆ ℕ × ℕ` is the list of its steps, a list
of elements of `steps` whose sum is `(m, n)`. Every step used in DLMF (`(1,0)`, `(0,1)`,
`(1,1)`, `(2,0)`, `(0,2)`) is nonzero, so such a path has at most `m + n` steps and
`latticePaths steps m n` is a finite set (`mem_latticePaths`). A path "stays on or above the
line `y = x`" when every vertex (every partial sum) does (`StaysWeaklyAboveDiagonal`); since the
segments are straight, this is the same as the whole path staying there. A `k`-dimensional
lattice path from the origin to `(n₁, …, n_k)` with unit steps is the word of its step
directions, a list over `Fin k` containing `i` exactly `nᵢ` times (`latticePathsFin`).

# Bell numbers (DLMF §26.7)

DLMF's Bell number `B(n)` (the number of partitions of `{1, …, n}`) is Mathlib's `Nat.bell n`,
defined there by the recurrence 26.7.6 (`Nat.bell_succ`); no new definition is made. The
counting statement (Mathlib's TODO) is acquired here as `card_finpartition_eq_bell`.

**Source corrections (implicit conditions).** 26.7.3 (`B(n) = ∑_{k=1}^m kⁿ/k! ∑_{j=0}^{m-k}
(-1)^j/j!`, `m ≥ n`) and the first form of 26.7.4 (Dobiński, `B(n) = e⁻¹ ∑_{k=1}^∞ kⁿ/k!`)
fail for `n = 0` (e.g. `m = 2` gives `1/2`, Dobiński gives `1 - e⁻¹`): the omitted `k = 0`
term `0⁰/0! = 1` matters only there. Both are acquired for `n ≥ 1`, together with the `k = 0`
forms valid for all `n`. The floor form of 26.7.4 holds for all `n ≥ 0`.

# Lattice paths: binomial coefficients (DLMF §26.3)

DLMF's binomial coefficient `C(m, n)` for nonnegative integers is Mathlib's `Nat.choose m n`
(with `C(m, n) = 0` for `n > m`, 26.3.2). Most of §26.3 is in Mathlib; the pointers are in
`DLMF/Combinatorics/MathlibCoverage.lean`. Here are the DLMF forms that Mathlib states
differently, the lattice-path counts of §26.3(i), and the asymptotic form 26.3.12 (derived from
Mathlib's Stirling formula `Stirling.tendsto_stirlingSeq_sqrt_pi`).

In 26.3.8 the term `k = 0` for `m = n` is `C(-1, 0) = 1`; the identity is stated with the
generalized binomial coefficient `Ring.choose` on `ℤ`, so that this boundary case is covered.

# Catalan numbers (DLMF §26.5)

DLMF's Catalan number `C(n)` is Mathlib's `catalan n` (defined by the recurrence 26.5.3,
`catalan_succ`); no new definition is made. Mathlib proves `C(n) = C(2n, n)/(n+1)`
(`succ_mul_catalan_eq_centralBinom`), the formal generating-function identity
`PowerSeries.catalanSeries_sq_mul_X_add_one`, and counts Dyck words
(`DyckWord.card_dyckWord_semilength_eq_catalan`); a Dyck word of semilength `n` is a lattice
path from `(0, 0)` to `(n, n)` staying on or above `y = x` (up-step `(0, 1)`, down-step
`(1, 0)`), and the lattice-path count in DLMF's form is acquired here.

The forms `C(2n, n) - C(2n, n-1)` and `C(2n-1, n) - C(2n-1, n+1)` in 26.5.1 are stated for
`n ≥ 1` (for `n = 0` they need `C(0, -1) = 0`, resp. `C(-1, 0) - C(-1, 1)` with nonnegative
upper index, which DLMF's conventions do not cover).

# Integer partitions: compositions (DLMF §26.11)

Compositions are Mathlib's `Composition n` (ordered lists of positive integers summing to `n`;
the empty composition of `0` included). `c(n)` is `compositionCount n`, `c_m(n)` is
`compositionCountLength m n` and `c(∈ T, n)` (no part `1`) is `compositionCountNoOne n`.
Mathlib already has `composition_card : Fintype.card (Composition n) = 2 ^ (n - 1)`.
The Fibonacci numbers are Mathlib's `Nat.fib`; (26.11.5) and Binet's formula (26.11.7,
`Real.coe_fib_eq`) are recorded as upstream pointers in `MathlibCoverageB`.

# Other lattice path numbers (DLMF §26.6)

DLMF defines the Delannoy number `D(m, n)`, the Motzkin number `M(n)`, the Narayana number
`N(n, k)` and the Schröder number `r(n)` as numbers of lattice paths (§26.6(i)). Mathlib has the
large Schröder numbers `Nat.largeSchroder` (`1, 2, 6, 22, 90, …`), which are DLMF's `r(n)`; the
other three are defined here, by the recurrence 26.6.10 (Delannoy), by the recurrence 26.6.11
(Motzkin), and by the explicit formula 26.6.3 (Narayana, with `N(n, 0) = 0`). The path counts
in DLMF's definitions are acquired as theorems about `latticePaths`.

The generating functions §26.6(ii) are stated for real arguments in explicit disks of
convergence (`3 - 2√2` is the radius for the central Delannoy and the Schröder numbers, `1/3`
for the Motzkin numbers), and with "sufficiently small" bounds where DLMF gives none (26.6.5,

# Lattice paths: multinomial coefficients and set partitions (DLMF §26.4)

DLMF's multinomial coefficient `(n₁ + ⋯ + n_k; n₁, …, n_k)` is Mathlib's

# Multiset permutations (DLMF §26.16)

For `a : Fin m → ℕ`, the multiset `S = {1^{a_1}, …, m^{a_m}}` has the permutations
`𝔖_S` = words `w : Fin (a_1 + ⋯ + a_m) → Fin m` taking the value `j` exactly `a_j` times
(`multisetPermutations a`; values `0`-based). Inversion number and major index are the word
statistics `wordInversions`, `wordMajorIndex` of §26.14. The `q`-multinomial coefficient
(26.16.1) is `qMultinomial q a`, built from the project's Gaussian coefficients `qBinom`; the
product is taken over all `k`, the factor `k = m` being `[a_m, a_m]_q = 1`.

# Plane partitions (DLMF §26.12)

A plane partition is, following DLMF §26.12(i), a finite set `π ⊆ ℕ × ℕ × ℕ` of points with
positive coordinates such that `(r, s, t) ∈ π` implies `B(r, s, t) ⊆ π` (`IsPlanePartition`),
where `B(r, s, t) = [1, r] × [1, s] × [1, t]` (`planeBox`, (26.12.3)); `|π|` is `π.card`. The
array description (weakly decreasing rows and columns) is the equivalent form of §26.12(i),
acquired as `planePartitionCount_eq_card_arrays`. `pp(n)` is `planePartitionCount n`.

Symmetry classes (all inside a box): symmetric (`(h, j, k) ∈ π → (j, h, k) ∈ π`), cyclically
symmetric (`(h, j, k) ∈ π → (j, k, h) ∈ π`), totally symmetric, the complement
`π^c = {(h, j, k) ∈ B | (r-h+1, s-j+1, t-k+1) ∉ π}` (`planeComplement`), self-complementary
(`π = π^c`) and transpose complement (`π^c` equals the transpose of `π`).

Strict shifted and descending plane partitions are lists of rows (`List (List ℕ)`), row `i`
indented by `i` places (`IsStrictShiftedPP`, `IsDescendingPP`). A descending plane partition
"in `B(r, r, r)`" is one with all parts at most `r`.

Counts in boxes are stated as rational numbers (`ℚ`), as DLMF's products are.

Corrections and clarifications (verified by brute force):

* §26.12(i), transpose complement: DLMF says "equal to the reflection through the `(x, y)`-plane
  of its complement". The count (26.12.12) is that of plane partitions whose complement is their
  transpose `(h, j, k) ↦ (j, h, k)` (reflection in the plane `x = y`); with the literal
  reflection `k ↦ t + 1 - k` the counts differ (`r = 1`, `t = 1`: none versus one). The
  transpose reading is acquired.
* (26.12.24): the product must run over `1 ≤ h ≤ j ≤ r`, not `1 ≤ h < j ≤ r`. As printed, for
  `r = 2` the right side is `(1 - q⁴)/(1 - q³)`, not a polynomial, whereas the descending plane
  partitions with parts at most 2 are `∅` and `(2)`, with generating function `1 + q²`; at
  `q = 1` the printed product does not reproduce (26.12.19). The corrected product matches for
  `r ≤ 5`.
* 26.12.27 (decimal values of `ζ(3)`, `ζ'(-1)`) and Table 26.12.1 are numerical and not acquired.

# The staircase bijection for partitions with parts differing by at least `k`

A partition of `n` into exactly `m` parts, any two of which differ by at least `k` and all of
which are at least `s ≥ 1`, is a decreasing list `λ₁ > ⋯ > λ_m`; subtracting the staircase
`k (m - i) + s` from `λ_i` gives a partition of `n - (k C(m,2) + s m)` into at most `m` parts,
and conversely (`s26a_card_staircase`). Summed over `m` (`s26a_card_diff_min_eq_sum`) this is
DLMF (26.10.10) (`s = 1`) and the counting behind the Rogers–Ramanujan identities.

# Stirling numbers (DLMF §26.8)

DLMF's Stirling numbers of the first kind `s(n, k)` are **signed**: `(-1)^{n-k}` times the
number of permutations of `{1, …, n}` with exactly `k` cycles (DLMF 26.8(i)). Mathlib's
`Nat.stirlingFirst n k` is the unsigned (cycle-counting) number, so the DLMF function is
`signedStirlingFirst n k = (-1)^{n-k} * Nat.stirlingFirst n k : ℤ` (defined here). DLMF's
`S(n, k)` (second kind) is Mathlib's `Nat.stirlingSecond n k` itself; no new definition is
made for it. Both are defined for all `n, k : ℕ` and vanish for `k > n`.

The key bridge is `coeff_descPochhammer`: the falling factorial `x(x-1)⋯(x-n+1)` (Mathlib's
`descPochhammer`) has the coefficients `s(n, k)`. DLMF writes it as the rising factorial
`(x-n+1)_n` (`ascPochhammer` evaluated at `x - n + 1`). The inverse expansion 26.8.10 is
derived from Mathlib's `Nat.pow_eq_sum_stirlingSecond_mul_descFactorial` by polynomial
identity (agreement at every natural number). The lean-codes module
`Pochhammer.PochhammerTransform` has the same expansions in the rising-factorial basis.

**Source corrections (implicit conditions).**
* 26.8.10 (`∑_{k=1}^n S(n,k)(x-k+1)_k = xⁿ`) fails for `n = 0` (empty sum `0 ≠ 1`); it is
  acquired for `1 ≤ n`, with the `k = 0` form valid for all `n` alongside.
* 26.8.29 (`∑_{k=1}^n (-1)^{n-k} s(n,k) = n!`) fails for `n = 0`; acquired for `1 ≤ n`.
* 26.8.31 as printed ("when `f` is analytic for all `x` and the series converges") is false:
  for `f(x) = sin(πx)` at `x = 0`, `k = 1` every `Δⁿf(0) = 0`, so the series converges to
  `0`, but `f'(0) = π`. It is acquired for polynomial `f` (where the series is finite), and
  the counterexample is recorded (`not_forall_stirling_deriv_eq_fwdDiff_series`).

# The twelvefold way (DLMF §26.17, Table 26.17.1)

Mappings `f : N → K` from a set `N` of `n` balls to a set `K` of `k` boxes are
`f : Fin n → Fin k`, restricted to all maps, injective maps or surjective maps
(`MapRestriction`). When the balls (resp. boxes) are unlabeled, maps are identified up to a
permutation of `N` (resp. of `K`): `f ∼ τ ∘ f ∘ σ` (`twelvefoldRel`). `twelvefoldCount balls
boxes r n k` is the number of equivalence classes, `Nat.card` of the quotient. The twelve
entries of Table 26.17.1 are the twelve theorems below, all tagged `26.17.T1`.

Conventions and qualifications:

* `(k-n+1)_n` (Pochhammer's symbol) is `(ascPochhammer ℤ n).eval (k - n + 1)`, which is `0` for
  `n > k`.
* `C(n-1, n-k)` (unlabeled balls, labeled boxes, onto) is stated for `1 ≤ k ≤ n`; for `k > n`
  there is no onto map, and `n = k = 0` gives `1`.
* `S(n,1) + ⋯ + S(n,k)` (labeled balls, unlabeled boxes, unrestricted) is stated for `n ≥ 1`: for
  `n = 0` there is one (empty) map while the sum is `0`; the sum from `j = 0` is correct for all
  `n`.
* `p_k(n) - p_{k-1}(n)` (unlabeled balls and boxes, onto) needs `k ≥ 1`.
* `S(n, k)` is Mathlib's `Nat.stirlingSecond`; `p_k(n)` is `partitionCountAtMostParts`.

# Kummer `M` and Tricomi `U`: remaining basic properties (DLMF §13.2)

Olver's regularized function `𝐌(a,b,z)` is Mathlib's `regularizedHGFun {a} {b}`.
The series `kummerM` is entire in `z` at regular denominator parameters; `kummerU`
uses the connection formula 13.2.42 and parameter limits at integer `b`.
The Kummer transformation includes integer parameters by parameter continuity.
The integer-denominator logarithmic expansion and its small-argument consequences follow
from termwise differentiation of the regularized series. Complex powers use the principal branch
on the slit plane. Numerically satisfactory pairs (13.2.24–13.2.26) are recorded as Wronskian
identities on the indicated argument sectors.

The connection formula 13.2.41 is proved for every `b`, in regularized form, as
`regularizedHGFun_eq_kummerU_connection`, from 13.2.42, Kummer's transformation 13.2.39 and the
reflection formula, then by continuity in `b`. The Wronskians 13.2.24, 13.2.25, 13.2.35, 13.2.37
and 13.2.38 that follow from it are in `DLMF.Confluent.ConnectionWronskians`.

# Wronskians from the connection formula 13.2.41

Write `F(w) = e^w U(b-a, b, -w)` for the second solution `e^z U(b-a,b,z e^{±πi})` on the
principal branch. On either side of the real axis, the regularized connection formula
`regularizedHGFun_eq_kummerU_connection` (DLMF 13.2.41) reads `𝐌 = c₁ U + c₂ F` near `z`, so
`W{𝐌, F} = c₁ W{U, F}` and, when `1/Γ(a) ≠ 0`, `W{U, F} = -W{𝐌, U}/c₂`. Continuity in `a`
covers the poles of `Γ(a)`. The statements were moved here from `DLMF.Confluent.BasicProperties`
unchanged, since the derivative of `U` is proved in `DLMF.Confluent.Recurrence`. Hypotheses that the
proofs do not need are kept with underscore names.

# Analytic continuation of Kummer's function in its parameters (DLMF §13.2(i))

Mathlib's regularized function `𝐌(a,b,z) = regularizedHGFun {a} {b} z = M(a,b,z)/Γ(b)` is
entire in `a`, in `b` and in `z`. We prove that it is entire along any entire curve in the
parameter plane, and use the identity principle to remove every parameter hypothesis from the
contiguous relations of §13.3, from the derivative formula 13.3.15 and from Kummer's

# Continued fractions (DLMF §§13.5, 13.17)

Partial numerators follow DLMF 13.5.2, 13.5.4, 13.17.2, and 13.17.4.
Convergence is acquired on a convenient real domain, matching the Chapter 15
restriction of meromorphic continued fractions.

Kummer's fraction 13.5.1 is proved for complex parameters
(`kummerM_continued_fraction_tendsto`) by Pincherle's theorem in the form
`GenContFract.cfConv_tendsto_of_ratio`: the backward solution
`M(a+m, b+2m, z)`, `M(a+m+1, b+2m+1, z)` comes from two contiguous relations
(`kumCF_contig_I`, `kumCF_contig_II`), it tends to `e^{z/2}`

# Coulomb wave functions (Temme §7.3.2; DLMF §33.2)

The regular Coulomb wave function is
`F_ℓ(η,ρ) = C_ℓ(η) ρ^{ℓ+1} e^{-iρ} M(ℓ + 1 - iη, 2ℓ + 2, 2iρ)` (DLMF 33.2.4) with the
normalization `C_ℓ(η)` of DLMF 33.2.5. The unnormalized function `coulombWave` is entire in `ρ`
for `ℓ ∈ ℕ`.

## Main results

* `conj_kummerM`: Kummer's function commutes with complex conjugation.
* `hasDerivAt_coulombWave`, `hasDerivAt_coulombWaveDeriv`, `deriv_deriv_coulombWave`: the Coulomb
  wave equation `w'' + (1 - 2η/ρ - ℓ(ℓ+1)/ρ²) w = 0` (DLMF 33.2.1), from Kummer's equation.
* `coulombWave_eq_conj_form`: the lower-sign form of 33.2.4, by Kummer's transformation.
* `conj_coulombWave`, `ofReal_coulombF`: `F_ℓ(η,ρ)` is real for real `η`, `ρ`.

The irregular functions `H_ℓ^±` (DLMF 33.2.8) and their asymptotic expansions (DLMF 33.11.1) are
in `DLMF.Confluent.CoulombAsymptotics`. The irregular function `G_ℓ`, the relation

`F_ℓ ~ sin θ_ℓ`, `G_ℓ ~ cos θ_ℓ` (33.10.1) are in `DLMF.Confluent.CoulombIrregular`.

# Irregular Coulomb functions and their asymptotics (Temme §7.3.2; DLMF 33.2.8, 33.11.1)

The outgoing and incoming Coulomb functions are
`H^±_ℓ(η,ρ) = e^{±iθ_ℓ} (∓2iρ)^{ℓ+1±iη} U(ℓ+1±iη, 2ℓ+2, ∓2iρ)` (DLMF 33.2.8) with the phase
`θ_ℓ = ρ - η ln(2ρ) - ℓπ/2 + σ_ℓ(η)`, `σ_ℓ(η) = ph Γ(ℓ+1+iη)` (DLMF 33.2.9–33.2.10). We use the
principal phase for `σ_ℓ`; DLMF's continuous branch differs by a multiple of `2π`, which does not
change `e^{±iθ_ℓ}` and hence does not change `H^±_ℓ`.

The argument `∓2iρ` lies on the imaginary axis, where Tricomi's expansion holds by the rotated
sectors of `DLMF.Confluent.TricomiRotated`. This gives the asymptotic expansion DLMF 33.11.1.

## Main results

* `hasAsymptoticExpansion_cpow_mul_kummerU_rotSector`: `z^a U(a,b,z) ~ ∑ cₖ z^{-k}`.
* `hasAsymptoticExpansion_coulombHPlus`, `hasAsymptoticExpansion_coulombHMinus`:
  `e^{∓iθ_ℓ} H^±_ℓ(η,ρ) ~ ∑ (a)_k (b)_k / (k! (±2iρ)^k)` with `a = ±iη - ℓ`, `b = ±iη + ℓ + 1`.

# The irregular Coulomb function and the Wronskian (DLMF 33.2.11–33.2.12, 33.10.1–33.10.2)

For `ρ > 0`, the logarithmic part of the phase `θ_ℓ` cancels against the power in DLMF 33.2.8.
This gives `H^+_ℓ = A^+ ρ^{ℓ+1} e^{iρ} U(ℓ+1+iη, 2ℓ+2, -2iρ)` with a constant `A^+`
(`coulombHPlus_eq`). Tricomi's function commutes with conjugation on the slit plane, so
`H^-_ℓ = conj H^+_ℓ`. The connection formula 13.2.41 at `z = 2iρ` then gives
`F_ℓ = (H^+_ℓ - H^-_ℓ)/(2i)`. The irregular function is defined by DLMF 33.2.11 as
`G_ℓ = Re H^+_ℓ`, so that `H^±_ℓ = G_ℓ ± i F_ℓ`.

The Wronskian `W{H^+_ℓ, F_ℓ}` reduces to `W{𝐌, U}` at `-2iρ`
(`wronskian_regularizedHGFun_kummerU_all`), whose constant evaluates to `1`.

## Main results

* `conj_kummerU`: `conj U(a,b,z) = U(conj a, conj b, conj z)` on the slit plane.
* `coulombHMinus_eq_conj`, `coulombF_eq_sub_div`, `coulombF_eq_im`.
* `coulombG`, `coulombH_eq_G_add_I_mul_F`: DLMF 33.2.11.
* `coulomb_wronskian`, `coulomb_wronskian_HPlus`, `coulomb_wronskian_HMinus`: DLMF 33.2.12.
* `tendsto_coulombHPlus_sub_exp`, `tendsto_coulombF_sub_sin_and_coulombG_sub_cos`:

# Exponential, sine and cosine integrals (Temme §7.3.5; DLMF Chapter 6, §§8.19–8.20)

The generalized exponential integral is `E_p(z) = z^{p-1} Γ(1-p, z)` (DLMF 8.19.1), defined
through the project's Tricomi-based `upperIncGamma`. Its integral representation, recurrence,
derivative and asymptotic expansion follow from the corresponding properties of `U`.
For `p = 1` the classical function `E₁` is related to the entire function `Ein` and Euler's
constant, which gives its power series. The sine and cosine integrals `Si`, `Ci` are defined
on the real line together with their power series.

## Main results

* `genExpIntE_eq_exp_mul_kummerU`: `E_p(z) = e^{-z} U(1, 2-p, z)`.
* `genExpIntE_eq_integral`: `E_p(x) = ∫₁^∞ e^{-xt} t^{-p} dt` for `x > 0`.
* `genExpIntE_add_one`, `hasDerivAt_genExpIntE`: recurrence and derivative.
* `hasAsymptoticExpansion_genExpIntE`: `E_p(x) ~ e^{-x}/x ∑ (-1)^k (p)_k x^{-k}`.
* `genExpIntE_one_eq_Ein`, `genExpIntE_one_eq_tsum`: `E₁(x) = Ein(x) - log x - γ` and
  its power series.
* `Real.hasSum_sinInt`, `Real.tendsto_sinInt_atTop`: the series of `Si` and `Si(∞) = π/2`.
* `Real.cosInt_eq_tsum`, `Real.hasDerivAt_cosInt`: the series and derivative of `Ci`.

The limit `Ci(x) → 0` (DLMF 6.2.14) and the Laplace-type representations of the auxiliary

# Auxiliary Fresnel functions and their asymptotics (Temme §7.3; DLMF 7.2.10, 7.5.10, 7.12.2)

The auxiliary functions `f, g` of DLMF 7.2.10–7.2.11 satisfy
`g(x) + i f(x) = (1+i)/2 · e^{ζ²} erfc ζ` with `ζ = √π (1-i) x / 2` (DLMF 7.5.10), and hence

# Incomplete Gamma functions (Temme §7.3.7; DLMF §§8.2–8.11)

The project defines the upper incomplete Gamma function through Tricomi's function,
`upperIncGamma a z = e^{-z} U(1-a, 1-a, z)` (DLMF 13.6.6), and the lower one through Kummer's
function, `lowerIncGamma a z = z^a / a · M(a, a+1, -z)` (DLMF 13.6.5). This file

asymptotic expansion of `Γ(a,x)` from Tricomi's expansion.

# Integrals (DLMF §§13.10, 13.23)

Gauss functions in the transforms use cut-plane continuation. The former series-only
statements were false when their transformed argument left the unit disk.

The general regularized Kummer Laplace transform is proved by termwise integration
when `‖k‖ < Re z` and then by holomorphic continuation throughout the full
convergence half-plane, retaining all denominator parameters, including Gamma poles.
The self-transform specializes it using the binomial identity.
Mathlib's summable-integral-norm theorem justifies the exchange, using a regularized
Gauss series to sum the absolute Gamma moments. The Whittaker M closed transform
then follows with an explicit principal-logarithm calculation in the right half-plane.
Tricomi's Mellin transform follows from its Laplace representation and Mathlib's
Fubini theorem. Absolute convergence of the double kernel reduces to the Tau Ceti
contributors' second Beta integrability theorem; the local proved Gamma and Beta
integral formulas evaluate the exchanged integrals.

The boundary Mellin transform uses a summable Gamma-moment majorant from the
proved Gamma-ratio asymptotics. Regularized Gauss summation, including singular
denominator parameters, evaluates the resulting series; the regularized Whittaker
M transform follows by combining positive-real powers and exponential factors.

The Hankel-type transforms 13.10.14–13.10.15 and 13.23.10–13.23.11 use a power bound for the
kernel `t^{ν/2} J_ν(2√(xt))`, its termwise Laplace transform
`x^{ν/2} s^{-ν-1} e^{-x/s}`, Fubini against the Tricomi Laplace or the Euler integral, and the
substitutions `s ↦ 1/s` and `s = 1/(1+v)`. The cosine transforms 13.10.12 and 13.23.8 use the
Gaussian Fourier integral in the same way. In the Euler cases the result is extended to all
parameters by the identity theorem: the integrals are holomorphic in a parameter by the locally
uniform decay bound of `DLMF.Confluent.KummerDecay`, and `U` is entire in its first parameter.
The Stieltjes transform 13.4.6 is proved here as well.

Indefinite integrals are stated as derivative identities. Laplace, Mellin, and
Bessel transforms use real half-lines. Hankel-loop formulas 13.10.8–13.10.9 and
13.23.6–13.23.7, and the inversion pair 13.23.13–13.23.14, are deferred.

# Decay of Kummer's function on the negative real axis (DLMF 13.2.23, 13.7.2)

On the negative real axis the regularized Kummer function decays algebraically:
`𝐌(a,b,-t) ~ ∑ₛ (a)ₛ (a-b+1)ₛ / (s! Γ(b-a)) · t^{-a-s}` as `t → +∞`, for all complex `a, b`.
This is the ray `ph z = π` of DLMF 13.7.2 (where the exponentially small companion series is
dropped) and its leading term is DLMF 13.2.23 on that ray. The proof is Kummer's transformation
13.2.39, `𝐌(a,b,-t) = e^{-t} 𝐌(b-a,b,t)`, combined with the positive-axis expansion 13.7.1
(`hasAsymptoticExpansion_regularizedConfluent`).

Consequences proved here:

* `isBigO_regularizedHGFun_neg`: `𝐌(a,b,-t) = O(t^{-Re a})`;
* `exists_norm_regularizedHGFun_neg_le`: `‖𝐌(a,b,-t)‖ ≤ C (1+t)^{-Re a}` for all `t ≥ 0`;
* `exists_eventually_norm_regularizedHGFun_neg_le`: the same bound, with exponent loss `ε > 0`,
  locally uniformly in both parameters. The base case is Euler's integral 13.4.1 in its
  convergence region, compared with a fixed real-parameter Euler integral; the bound spreads
  to all parameters through the contiguous relations 13.3.4 and 13.3.20 (`n = 1`), which keep
  the decay exponent.

The locally uniform bound is what holomorphy of parametric integrals of `𝐌(a,b,-t)` in the
parameters requires.

# Kummer's and Tricomi's functions for large negative `a`

Following Beals–Wong §13.2, the substitution `u(s) = s^{c-1/2} e^{-s²/(8κ)} 𝐌(c/2 - κ, c, s²/(4κ))`
turns Kummer's equation into the perturbed oscillator `u'' + u = g u` with
`g = ((c-1)² - 1/4)/s² + s²/(16κ²)` (`hasDerivAt_largeAU'`). As `κ → +∞` its data at a fixed
point converge, by a Tannery argument (`tendsto_regularizedConfluent_sub_div`), to those of
`u₀(s) = 2^{c-1} √s J_{c-1}(s)`, which solves the same equation with `g₀ = ((c-1)² - 1/4)/s²`.
The Volterra estimate `ODE.norm_sub_oscFree_le'` on `[s₀, S]`, with `s₀` large and then `κ`
large, gives `u_κ(S) - u₀(S) → 0` along `S = 2√(κx)` (`tendsto_largeAU_sub_largeAU0`), and the
Bessel asymptotics 10.7.8 give the cosine form.

## Main results

* `tendsto_regularizedConfluent_atBot`: the Erdélyi–Schmidt–Fejér asymptotics
  (Beals–Wong (8.1.12)) `√π ((c/2 - a)x)^{c/2-1/4} e^{-x/2} 𝐌(a, c, x)
  - cos(2√((c/2 - a)x) - cπ/2 + π/4) → 0` as `a → -∞`, for every real `c`.
* `tendsto_regularizedConfluent_atBot_besselJ`: the Bessel form (a weak form of DLMF 13.8.9).
* `tendsto_kummerU_atBot`: Beals–Wong (8.2.10) for non-integer `c` (compare DLMF 13.8.10).
* `laguerrePolyL_fejer`: Fejér's formula for Laguerre polynomials (Szegő (8.22.4)).

All error terms here are `o(1)`; the sharper `O(|a|^{-1/2})` rates of Beals–Wong and DLMF
(13.8.9, 13.8.10, 18.15.14) are proved in `DLMF.Confluent.LargeASharp`.

# Sharp rates for Kummer's and Tricomi's functions with large negative `a`

This file sharpens the `o(1)` results of `DLMF.Confluent.LargeA` to the error orders of
Beals–Wong (13.2.7)–(13.2.8) and DLMF 13.8.9 and 18.15.14.

The route keeps the Liouville form `u_κ(s) = s^{c-1/2} e^{-s²/(8κ)} 𝐌(c/2 - κ, c, s²/(4κ))` of
`LargeA`, which solves `u'' + u = g_κ u` with `g_κ = ((c-1)² - 1/4)/s² + s²/(16κ²)`, and the
Bessel limit `u₀(s) = 2^{c-1} √s J_{c-1}(s)`, which solves `u₀'' + u₀ = g₀ u₀` with
`g₀ = ((c-1)² - 1/4)/s²`. Two quantitative ingredients replace the limits of `LargeA`:

* a **quantitative Tannery estimate** `𝐌(d - κ, b, w/κ) = ₀F̃₁(;b;-w) + O(κ⁻¹)`
  (`isBigO_regularizedConfluent_sub_div`), which gives the data of `u_κ` at `s = 1` to
  within `O(κ⁻¹)`;
* a **comparison estimate** on `[s₀, S]` (`norm_largeAU_sub_largeAU0_le_sharp`): the
  difference `w = u_κ - u₀` solves `w'' + w = g₀ w + (s²/(16κ²)) u_κ`, so the Volterra equation
  and Gronwall's inequality bound `‖w(S)‖` by the data difference plus
  `sup ‖u_κ‖ · S³/(16κ²)`, times `exp (∫|g₀|)`. Only the *difference* `g_κ - g₀` enters, so the
  `1/s²` term costs a fixed factor `exp(|(c-1)² - 1/4|/s₀)` rather than an error.

Along `S = 2√(κx)` this gives `u_κ(S) - u₀(S) = O(κ^{-1/2})`.

## Main results

* `largeAU_sub_largeAU0_isBigO`: `u_κ(2√(κx)) - u₀(2√(κx)) = O(κ^{-1/2})`.
* `regularizedConfluent_atBot_besselJ_isBigO` (DLMF 13.8.9): with `S = √(2x(c - 2a))`,
  `((c/2 - a)x)^{(c-1)/2} e^{-x/2} 𝐌(a, c, x) - J_{c-1}(S) = O(S^{-1/2} |a|^{-1/2})`.
* `regularizedConfluent_atBot_cos_isBigO` (Beals–Wong (13.2.8)): the cosine form with error
  `O(|a|^{-1/2})`.
* `kummerU_atBot_isBigO` (DLMF 13.8.10): for non-integer `c`,
  `x^{(c-1)/2} e^{-x/2} U(a, c, x)/Γ(c/2 - a + 1/2) - (cos(aπ) J_{c-1}(S) - sin(aπ) Y_{c-1}(S))
  = O(S^{-1/2} |a|^{-1/2})`, from the connection formula 13.2.42, two instances of 13.8.9 and
  `J_{-ν} = cos(νπ) J_ν - sin(νπ) Y_ν`.
* `laguerrePolyL_fejer_isBigO` (DLMF 18.15.14 with `M = 1`): Fejér's formula with error
  `O(n^{-1/2})`.

In 13.8.9 and 13.8.10 DLMF writes the error as `env J_{c-1}(S) O(|a|^{-1/2})` and
`env Y_{c-1}(S) O(|a|^{-1/2})`; since the envelopes are `≍ S^{-1/2}` as `S → ∞`, the statements
here use `S^{-1/2} |a|^{-1/2}`.

# The analytic part of the integer-parameter Tricomi expansion

The logarithmic expansion separates into `log z` times a regularized Kummer function and
an ordinary power series. Parameter differentiation proves convergence of that series;
its analyticity at zero then supplies the small-argument remainder estimates.

# Parabolic cylinder functions (Temme §7.3.3; DLMF Chapter 12)

Weber's function `U(a,z)` is the solution of `w'' = (z²/4 + a) w` that is recessive as
`z → +∞`. We define it, following DLMF 12.4.1, through the even and odd Kummer solutions
`u₁(a,z) = e^{-z²/4} M(a/2 + 1/4, 1/2, z²/2)` and `u₂(a,z) = z e^{-z²/4} M(a/2 + 3/4, 3/2, z²/2)`
with the initial values 12.2.6 and 12.2.7. This makes `U(a, ·)` entire for every `a`.

# Tricomi's Laplace transform with unrestricted first parameter

Fubini and the half-line Euler integral evaluate the transform for `Re a > 0`.
Tricomi's contiguous relation then lowers `a` by natural steps, preserving both
endpoint convergence inequalities. The regularized Gauss contiguous relation
satisfies the same recursion even when its denominator parameter is singular.

# Tricomi's function along rotated rays (Temme §7.2; DLMF 13.4.4, 13.7.3)

For `re a > 0` and `|α| < π/2`, rotating the ray of integration in Tricomi's Laplace integral
gives

`U(a,b,z) = 1/Γ(a) · e^{iα} ∫₀^∞ e^{-z r e^{iα}} (r e^{iα})^{a-1} (1 + r e^{iα})^{b-a-1} dr`

on the half-plane `re (z e^{iα}) > 0` (`kummerU_eq_tricomiRotated`). The rotation uses
`Complex.integral_Ioi_eq_exp_mul_integral_Ioi_rotate` on the common half-plane and extends by
analytic continuation. Watson's lemma in a sector then gives Tricomi's expansion as `z → ∞` in
every rotated sector `δ |z| ≤ re (z e^{iα})` (`hasAsymptoticExpansion_kummerU_rotSector`).
These sectors cover `|arg z| ≤ π - ε`, including the imaginary axis needed for the Coulomb
and Fresnel functions.

# Zero counts of Tricomi's `U` by Sturm comparison

Tools for the real zero counts of DLMF §13.9(ii). For real parameters `a`, `b` and `x > 0`,
`U(a,b,x)` is real (`kzt_U_real`) and satisfies the self-adjoint form
`(x^b e^{-x} y')' - a x^{b-1} e^{-x} y = 0` of Kummer's equation on `(0, ∞)` (`kzt_U_isSol`).

The comparison theory is that of `DLMF/Legendre/ZeroTools.lean` (prefix `lzt_`), transplanted
from `(-1, 1)` to `(0, ∞)` with a general positive weight `p`: for two solutions `y`, `u` of
`(p y')' + q y = 0` with coefficients `qy < qu`, the weighted Wronskian `W = p (u'y - uy')` is
strictly monotone wherever `u y > 0`. This gives

* the classical Sturm comparison between consecutive zeros (`kzt_between`);
* comparisons at the ends, where a sign of `W` forces `y/u` to diverge as soon as
  `p u² = O(x)` at `0` (`kzt_lower_left`) or `p u² = O(1)` at `∞` (`kzt_upper_right`,
  `kzt_lower_right`), and on the whole half-line (`kzt_lower_whole`);
* lower and upper zero counts from exactly known comparison functions (`kzt_lower_count`,
  `kzt_upper_count`).

The comparison functions are the polynomial cases `U(-n,b,x) = (-1)ⁿ n! L_n^{(b-1)}(x)`
(DLMF 13.6.19), whose zeros are those of the Laguerre polynomial (`laguerrePolyL_zeros_pos`,
DLMF 18.16(iv)). Zeros of `U(a,b,·)`, `a ∉ -ℕ`, are simple by the Wronskian 13.2.34
(`kzt_U_simple`), and `U(a,b,x) ~ x^{-a}` at `∞` (`kzt_U_asymp`, DLMF 13.2.6). The result is the
count `⌈-a⌉` of positive zeros of `U(a,b,·)` for `a < 0` nonintegral and `b ≥ 1`
(`kzt_U_posZeros_count`), which gives DLMF 13.9.14 by Kummer's transformation.

All helper names carry the prefix `kzt_`.

# Catalan's constant (Duverney Remark 2.9, Exercise 2.12)

Catalan's constant `G = ∑ (-1)^k/(2k+1)² = β(2)` is not in Mathlib. With `λ(2) = (3/4) ζ(2) = π²/8`
from `DLMF.Constants.Dirichlet`, splitting the odd squares by residue mod 4 gives
`∑ 1/(4k+1)² = (π²/8 + G)/2` and `∑ 1/(4k+3)² = (π²/8 - G)/2`, hence, by the trigamma series,
`ψ'(1/4) = π² + 8G` and `ψ'(3/4) = π² - 8G`.

* `DLMF.Constants.BBP`: the Bailey–Borwein–Plouffe formula for `π`, BBP-type series for `ln 2`,

# Convergence and branch conventions for the DLMF Chapters 6–8 acquisition

Improper integrals assert limits of finite integrals. Logarithmic coordinates
retain continuation across cuts. Continued fractions assert convergence of
finite truncations, rather than an equality to a totalized infinite expression.

# Checked pointers from DLMF items to upstream declarations

Mathlib's `@[dlmf REF]` attribute can only be attached where a declaration is made. For a
DLMF item already formalized upstream (in Mathlib or TauCeti) without such a tag, the command

  dlmf_upstream 8.17.E3 Complex.betaIntegral_eq_Gamma_mul_div "special case: 0 < re a, re b"

records a pointer instead of a duplicate local theorem. The DLMF reference is parsed by the
same parser as `@[dlmf]`, and the declaration must exist, so a renamed upstream declaration
breaks the build rather than leaving a dead pointer. The optional string states how the
upstream statement relates to the DLMF one (see `DLMFIndex.md`: exact, stronger, special case,
different convention, partial), followed by free text.

The pointers are kept in the environment extension `upstreamExt` and harvested, together with
the `@[dlmf]` tags, by `scripts/DumpDLMF.lean`.

# Zero enumerations by modulus and one-zero-per-disc criteria

DLMF lists the complex zeros of a special function in a sector "arranged in order of increasing
absolute value". The project encodes this by `DLMF.orderedZero f S k`, an `epsilon`-choice of a
zero `z ∈ S` of `f` with exactly `k - 1` zeros of `f` in `S` of smaller modulus. This file gives
the combinatorics behind that encoding and the bridge from Rouché's theorem
(`TauCeti.rouche`, Tau Ceti) to it.

Write `Z = {z ∈ S | f z = 0}` and assume that every bounded part of `Z` is finite (true for an
entire function that is not identically zero, `zcnt_finite_zeros_lt`). Then:

* `zcnt_orderedZero_spec_iff`: the enumeration is well defined for every `k ≥ 1` if and only if
  the zeros in `S` have pairwise distinct moduli and there are infinitely many of them;
* `zcnt_orderedZero_strictMonoOn`: the enumeration is then strictly increasing in modulus;
* `zcnt_eq_orderedZero`: every zero in `S` is enumerated;
* `zcnt_injOn_infinite_of_discs`: "exactly one zero in each disc `D_k`, the discs lie in disjoint
  annuli of increasing radius, and every zero lies in some `D_k`" gives distinct moduli and
  infinitely many zeros;
* `zcnt_existsUnique_of_count_eq_one`, `zcnt_existsUnique_zero_of_rouche`: a zero count `1`
  (with multiplicity) on a disc, for instance transferred by Rouché's theorem from a model, gives
  exactly one zero in the disc.

# Coulomb functions `f`, `h`, `s`, `c`: large `|r|` (DLMF §33.21)

DLMF §33.21(i) describes how the limiting forms of `f`, `h`, `s`, `c` as `r → ±∞` follow from
the connection formulas of §33.16 and the limiting forms of `F_ℓ`, `G_ℓ` (33.10.1), of the
Whittaker functions `ζ_ℓ`, `ξ_ℓ` (33.21.1–33.21.2, acquired here) and of the Bessel functions
(§§10.7(ii), 10.30(ii)). §33.21(ii) cites Curtis (1964a, §6) for asymptotic expansions. Checked
numerically (mpmath, 40 digits, `ν = 2.3`, `ℓ = 1`, `|r|` up to 300); the convergence of `ξ_ℓ`
requires the principal branch `ph(e^{iπ} 2r/ν) = π` built into `coulombXi`.

# Coulomb functions in the variables `r`, `ε`: definitions (DLMF §§33.14–33.20)

DLMF §33.14 reparametrizes the Coulomb wave equation as
`w'' + (ε + 2/r - ℓ(ℓ+1)/r²) w = 0` (33.14.1) with `r = -ηρ`, `ε = 1/η²`, and defines the
regular solution `f(ε,ℓ;r)`, the irregular solution `h(ε,ℓ;r)` and their energy-normalized forms
`s(ε,ℓ;r)`, `c(ε,ℓ;r)`. All of them are real functions of real `ε`, `r` and `ℓ ∈ ℕ`
(except `s`, `c`, which become imaginary when `A(ε,ℓ) < 0`).

## Definitions and conventions

* `coulombKappa ε r`: the quantity `κ` of 33.14.6, with the upper sign `κ = i ε^{-1/2}` for
  `ε > 0` (DLMF: the sign is immaterial). For `ε < 0` the sign follows the sign of `r`
  (`r = 0` takes the `r < 0` branch). At `ε = 0` it is the junk value `0`.
* `coulombfKummer κ ℓ r`: the complex expression `(2r)^{ℓ+1} e^{-r/κ} M(ℓ+1-κ,2ℓ+2,2r/κ)/(2ℓ+1)!`
  of 33.14.5 as a function of `κ`.
* `coulombf ε ℓ r`: for `ε ≠ 0` the real part of `coulombfKummer (coulombKappa ε r) ℓ r`
  (the expression is real, `DLMF.Coulomb.ofReal_coulombf`); for `ε = 0` the confluent limit
  `(2r)^{ℓ+1} ₀F̃₁(;2ℓ+2;-2r)`, which DLMF 33.20.1–33.20.2 identifies with Bessel functions and
  which is the value of the power series 33.19.1 at `ε = 0`.
* `coulombSFactor ε r`: `S(ε,r)` of 33.14.8.
* `coulombhFormula ε ℓ r`: the complex right-hand side of 33.14.7, with Whittaker's functions
  written through Kummer's `M` and Tricomi's `U`
  (`W_{κ,ℓ+1/2}(z) = e^{-z/2} z^{ℓ+1} U(ℓ+1-κ,2ℓ+2,z)`, `M_{κ,ℓ+1/2}` likewise).
* `coulombh ε ℓ r`: the real part of `coulombhFormula`, except at `ε = 0` and at the poles of
  `Γ(ℓ+1-κ)` (`ε = -1/n²`, `n ≥ ℓ+1`, `r > 0`, where 33.14.7 is a removable `∞ · 0`), where it
  is the limit in `ε` along punctured neighbourhoods (DLMF: `h` is analytic in `ε ≠ 0`, and its
  value at `ε = 0` is the limit 33.20.1–33.20.2). Existence of these limits is a theorem.
* `coulombAProd ε ℓ = ∏_{k=0}^{ℓ} (1 + εk²)` (33.14.11), `coulombBFactor ε ℓ` (33.14.10).
* `coulombs`, `coulombc`: complex valued, `s = (B/2)^{1/2} f`, `c = (2B)^{-1/2} h` with principal
  powers (33.14.9), so that they are imaginary when `B < 0`, as DLMF states.
* `turningPointR ε ℓ` (33.14.3) and `hydrogenRadial n ℓ r` (`φ_{n,ℓ}`, 33.14.14).
* `coulombZeta`, `coulombXi`, `coulombKNorm`: `ζ_ℓ(ν,r)`, `ξ_ℓ(ν,r)` of 33.16.9 and `K(ν,ℓ)` of
  33.16.16. The argument `e^{iπ} 2r/ν` of `ξ` is the negative real `-(2r/ν)`, on which the
  principal branch takes `ph = π`.
* `coulombAlpha`, `coulombGammaCoeff`, `coulombBetaCoeff`, `coulombDeltaCoeff`: the coefficients
  `α_k`, `γ_k`, `β_k`, `δ_k` of 33.19.2–33.19.7; `coulombCkp`: `C_{k,p}` of 33.20.6.

# The regular Coulomb function `f(ε,ℓ;r)` as an entire function (DLMF 33.14.1, 33.19.1)

For every real `ε` the function `f(ε,ℓ;·)` is the restriction to `ℝ` of the real part of an
entire function `q2e_Phi ε ℓ` (the Kummer form 33.14.5 with `κ = coulombKappa ε 1` for `ε ≠ 0`,
the confluent form `(2z)^{ℓ+1} ₀F̃₁(;2ℓ+2;-2z)` for `ε = 0`). This entire function satisfies
the Coulomb equation 33.14.1 (from the Coulomb wave equation 33.2.1 by the substitution
`ρ = -iz/κ`, `η = -iκ`, resp. from the `₀F₁` equation), and its Taylor coefficients satisfy the
recurrence 33.19.2, which gives the power series 33.19.1.

## Main results

* `q2e_coulombf_eq_re`: `f(ε,ℓ;r) = Re q2e_Phi ε ℓ r`.
* `q2e_Phi_ode`: the equation 33.14.1 for `q2e_Phi ε ℓ` at `z ≠ 0`.
* `q2e_hasSum_of_ode`: an entire solution `z^{ℓ+1} ψ(z)` of 33.14.1 with `ψ(0) = α₀` has the
  power series `∑ α_k z^{k+ℓ+1}`.
* `q2e_Phi_hasSum`: the complex power series 33.19.1.
* `q2e_alpha_raise`, `q2e_alpha_lower`: ladder relations between the coefficients `α_k` for
  consecutive `ℓ`; `q2e_Phi_raise`, `q2e_Phi_three_term`: the recurrences 33.17.3 and 33.17.1
  for `q2e_Phi`, proved by comparing Taylor coefficients.

## Source correction: DLMF 33.19.3

Checked numerically (mpmath, 40 digits; `ε ∈ {0.3, 2.5, -0.13, -0.6}`, `ℓ ≤ 3`, both signs of

# Coulomb functions: asymptotic expansions (DLMF §§33.11–33.12)

* §33.11, large `ρ`: the expansion 33.11.1 of `H^±_ℓ` is `hasAsymptoticExpansion_coulombHPlus`
  and `hasAsymptoticExpansion_coulombHMinus` in `DLMF.Confluent.CoulombAsymptotics`. Here the
  equivalent amplitude–phase form 33.11.2–33.11.9: the amplitudes `f, g, f̂, ĝ` are
  `largeRhoF`, `largeRhoG`, `largeRhoFHat`, `largeRhoGHat` (defined by 33.11.2–33.11.3), their
  expansions use the terms `largeRhoTerm` (33.11.8–33.11.9), and the expansions 33.11.5–33.11.6
  are stated in Poincaré form: the remainder after the terms `k ≤ K` is `O(ρ^{-K-1})`.
* §33.12, large `η`: the transition-region expansions 33.12.2–33.12.3 (uniform for bounded
  `x = (2η-ρ)/(2η)^{1/3}`; three terms are given, so the remainder is `O(μ^{-4})`), the values
  at the turning point 33.12.6–33.12.7 (remainder `o` of the last printed term), and the scaled
  equation 33.12.8.

**Source corrections.**
* DLMF 33.11.7 prints `g f̂ - f ĝ = 1`. With `f, g, f̂, ĝ` defined by 33.11.2–33.11.3 one has
  `f ĝ - g f̂ = G_ℓ F_ℓ' - G_ℓ' F_ℓ = 1` (the Wronskian 33.2.12); the printed sign is wrong.
  Already the leading terms show it: `f_0 ĝ_0 - g_0 f̂_0 = 1 - η/ρ → 1`. mpmath at `ℓ = 2`,
  `η = 0.7`, `ρ = 30`: `g f̂ - f ĝ = -1.0`. The corrected form is acquired.
* DLMF 33.12.3 prints the factor of `Ai'(x)` (`Bi'(x)`) as `(B_1 + A_1')/μ + ⋯` without the
  leading `1`. Differentiating the leading term of 33.12.2 (`dx/dρ = -(2η)^{-1/3}`) gives
  `F_0' ∼ -π^{1/2}(2η)^{-1/6} Ai'(x)`, so the factor is `1 + (B_1 + A_1')/μ + ⋯`. mpmath at
  `η = 20, 80, 320` and `x ∈ {-1.3, 0, 0.8}` confirms the corrected form with remainder
  `O((2η)^{-1/6} μ^{-4})`.

# The arithmetic-geometric mean and Landen's transformations (Temme §12.1.2, DLMF §19.8)

Following Temme's proof of Theorem 12.1, the integral
`agmIntegral a b = ∫₀^{π/2} (a² cos²θ + b² sin²θ)^{-1/2} dθ` equals
`∫₀^∞ ((t²+a²)(t²+b²))^{-1/2} dt` (substitution `t = b tan θ`), and the substitution
`u = (t - ab/t)/2` shows that this is invariant under `(a, b) ↦ ((a+b)/2, √(ab))`. Along
Mathlib's AGM iteration `NNReal.agmSequences` the integral is therefore constant and squeezed
between `(π/2)/aₙ` and `(π/2)/bₙ`, which gives Gauss's theorem `agmIntegral a b = π/(2 M(a,b))`.
The same invariance with homogeneity gives the descending and ascending Landen
transformations of `K`.

# Complete elliptic integrals (Temme §12.1, DLMF §§19.2–19.7)

With the parameter `m = k²`,
`K(m) = ∫₀^{π/2} (1 - m sin²θ)^{-1/2} dθ` and `E(m) = ∫₀^{π/2} (1 - m sin²θ)^{1/2} dθ`.
The integrals are differentiated under the integral sign; one integration by parts,
`(1-m) ∫₀^{π/2} (1 - m sin²θ)^{-3/2} dθ = E(m)`, gives the derivatives (DLMF 19.4.1–19.4.2).
Legendre's relation (19.7.1) follows because its left side has zero derivative on `(0, 1)` and
tends to `π/2` as `m → 0⁺`: `E(m) - K(m) = O(m)` while `K(1-m) = O(m^{-1/2})`. Euler's integral
gives the hypergeometric forms (19.5.1–19.5.2).

# Incomplete elliptic integrals and Jacobi's elliptic functions (Temme §§12.2–12.3)

For a real parameter `m < 1` (`m = k²`), Legendre's incomplete integrals
`F(φ|m) = ∫₀^φ (1 - m sin²θ)^{-1/2} dθ` and `E(φ|m) = ∫₀^φ (1 - m sin²θ)^{1/2} dθ` are odd
and quasi-periodic, `F(φ + π|m) = F(φ|m) + 2K(m)`. Since `∂F/∂φ > 0` and `F(nπ|m) = 2nK(m)`,
`φ ↦ F(φ|m)` is an order isomorphism of `ℝ`; its inverse is Jacobi's amplitude `am(u|m)`
(Temme (12.21)–(12.22)), and `sn = sin ∘ am`, `cn = cos ∘ am`, `dn = (1 - m sn²)^{1/2}`. The
inverse function theorem gives `am' = dn` and the derivatives of DLMF 22.13.1–22.13.3.

# Identities for Jacobi's elliptic functions (Duverney Ch. 5; DLMF §§22.6, 22.8, 22.13)

For `m < 1`:
* `dn² - m cn² = 1 - m` and the first- and second-order equations of `sn`, `cn`, `dn`
  (DLMF 22.13.13–22.13.18, Duverney Ex. 5.12).
* The addition formulas for `sn`, `cn`, `dn` (DLMF 22.8.1–22.8.3, Duverney Ex. 5.14). Following
  Duverney, `Ψ(u) = N(u, w-u)/(1 - m sn²u sn²(w-u))` has zero derivative, so it equals `Ψ(0)`.
  The identity `N'D - ND' = 0` is a polynomial identity modulo `sn² + cn² = 1` and
  `m sn² + dn² = 1` at both points.
* The quarter-period shift `u ↦ u + K` and the values at `K/2` (Duverney Ex. 5.15).
* The simple pendulum: `y = 2 arcsin(√m sn(ωt + φ))` solves `y'' + ω² sin y = 0` and has period
  `4K/ω` (Duverney Thm 5.6, Temme §12.1.1).

# The algebraic form of `F`, `arcsn`, and special values (Duverney Ch. 5)

* The substitution `t = sin θ` (by the one-dimensional change of variables for set integrals,
  which handles the integrable singularity at `t = 1`) gives
  `∫₀ˣ dt/√((1-t²)(1-mt²)) = F(arcsin x|m)` for `0 ≤ x ≤ 1`, hence `K = ∫₀¹`. It also gives
  Jacobi's `arcsn = F ∘ arcsin` with `sn ∘ arcsn = id` and
  `arcsn' = ((1-x²)(1-mx²))^{-1/2}` (Duverney Thm 5.9).
* `K(1/2) = Γ(1/4)²/(4√π)`, by Gauss's second summation theorem and the reflection formula.
  With `K = π/(2M)` this gives Gauss's constant `Γ(1/4)² M(1, 1/√2) = 2π^{3/2}`, and with
  Legendre's relation the value of `E(1/2)` (Duverney (5.38), Ex. 5.9).
* `K(-1) = K(1/2)/√2` by homogeneity of the AGM, so the lemniscate integral is
  `∫₀¹ dt/√(1-t⁴) = Γ(1/4)²/(4√(2π))` (Duverney (5.10)–(5.13)).
* The perimeter of an ellipse is `4a E(e²) = 2πa F(-1/2, 1/2; 1; e²)` (Duverney (5.4), (5.6)).

# Jacobi's theta functions in DLMF normalization (Temme §12.3.2, DLMF §20.2)

Mathlib's `jacobiTheta₂ z τ = ∑ₙ exp(2πinz + πin²τ)` is `θ₃(πz|τ)`. We define `θ₁, …, θ₄` with
the DLMF argument convention (`q = e^{iπτ}`, period `π` in `z`) and derive their series,
periodicity, parity and the quasi-periodicity of `θ₃`, together with Jacobi's imaginary
transformation of `θ₃(0|τ)`, from Mathlib's results for `jacobiTheta₂`.

# Theta functions and the AGM: `K = (π/2) θ₃²` (Temme §12.3.2, DLMF 20.9.2)

For a real nome `0 < q < 1` let `θ₃(q) = ∑ q^{n²}` and `θ₄(q) = ∑ (-1)ⁿ q^{n²}`, the values at
`z = 0` of the DLMF theta functions with `q = e^{iπτ}` (`jacobiThetaThreeTau_zero_I_mul`). Splitting
`ℤ²` into the sublattice `a + b` even, parametrized by `(u+v, u-v)`, and its complement, on which
`(a,b) ↦ (b,a)` cancels the signed terms, gives the doubling identities
`θ₃(q)² + θ₄(q)² = 2θ₃(q²)²` and `θ₃(q) θ₄(q) = θ₄(q²)²`. Hence `(θ₃(q^{2ⁿ})², θ₄(q^{2ⁿ})²)` is an
AGM sequence. It tends to `(1, 1)`, so `M(θ₃², θ₄²) = 1`, and Gauss's theorem gives Jacobi's
`K(m) = (π/2) θ₃(q)²` with complementary modulus `k' = θ₄(q)²/θ₃(q)²`.

# The elliptic integral of the third kind (Temme (12.17), DLMF §19.2)

For `n < 1` and `m < 1` the integrand `(1 - n sin²θ)⁻¹ (1 - m sin²θ)^{-1/2}` is continuous, so
`Π(φ, n, m) = ∫₀^φ (1 - n sin²θ)⁻¹ (1 - m sin²θ)^{-1/2} dθ` needs no principal value; the argument
order is DLMF's, with characteristic `n = α²` and parameter `m = k²`. It is odd and
quasi-periodic, `Π(φ+π, n, m) = Π(φ, n, m) + 2Π(n, m)`, and `Π(φ, 0, m) = F(φ, m)`. At `m = 0` it
is elementary: with `c = √(1-n)`,
`Π(φ, n, 0) = (φ - arctan((1-c) sin φ cos φ/(cos²φ + c sin²φ)))/c`, which is `arctan(c tan φ)/c` on
`(-π/2, π/2)` but is smooth on all of `ℝ`. In particular `Π(n, 0) = π/(2√(1-n))`.

# Addition theorems for Legendre's integrals (DLMF §19.11)

The addition theorems are stated for real modulus `k` with `k² < 1` and real amplitudes, the
setting of DLMF's qualifications in §19.11(i). The Legendre integrals are the complex DLMF
integrals `incEllIntFk`, `incEllIntEk`, `incEllIntPik` (and `compEllIntKk`, `compEllIntEk`,
`compEllIntPik`) at real arguments; `R_C` is `symEllIntRC`.

**The amplitude `ψ`.** DLMF defines `ψ` by `sin ψ` (19.11.3) and lists `cos ψ` (19.11.4) as a
further property. For `θ, φ ∈ [0, π/2]` both formulas are needed to fix `ψ ∈ [0, π]` (the sine
alone does not distinguish `ψ` from `π - ψ`); the theorems take `ψ ∈ [0, π]` with both
`sin ψ` and `cos ψ` given, and `addition_sin_sq_add_cos_sq` shows that such a `ψ` exists.
Likewise for the duplication formulas, with (19.11.14) and the first formula of (19.11.15).

**Branches in (19.11.5), (19.11.10), (19.11.16).** DLMF warns that "care has to be taken with
the multivalued functions in (19.11.5)". With DLMF's principal `R_C` (Cauchy principal value
for a negative second argument) the formula (19.11.5) holds numerically (mpmath, 3000 random
samples) exactly when `α² < 1` and `α² (1 - cos θ cos φ cos ψ) < 1`, the region of (19.11.6_5);
it fails outside it. The theorems are stated on this region (with `θ, φ ∈ (0, π/2)`, so that
the cosecants are finite). The duplication formula (19.11.16) is the case `φ = θ`, with the
condition `α² (1 - cos²θ cos ψ) < 1`; (19.11.10) holds for all real `α² < 1`.
In (19.11.6_5) DLMF allows `α² = k²`, where `δ = 0` and the right side is a limit; the theorem
assumes `k² < α²`.

# Connection formulas for Legendre's integrals (DLMF §19.7)

Statements of DLMF 19.7.1–19.7.10. Legendre's relation (19.7.1) is proved for real `0 < k < 1`
from the existing real `DLMF.Elliptic.legendre_relation`. On the complex domain it follows by the
identity theorem on `Re k > 0`, by evenness in `k` for `Re k < 0`, and on the imaginary axis by a
one-sided limit from `Re k > 0` (dominated convergence across the cut of `K(k')` and `E(k')`).
19.7.2 is proved by the identity theorem from the real substitution `θ ↦ π/2 - θ`.
The modulus transformations 19.7.2–19.7.3 are stated for complex `k`; the transformations
19.7.4–19.7.7 for the real amplitudes on which DLMF states them (19.7.7 with complex `k`); the
parameter changes 19.7.8–19.7.10 for real data, with Cauchy principal values. Here
`k' = jacobiComodulusk k` (principal), `c = csc²φ` and `R_C = symEllIntRC`.

**Convention note.** DLMF prints the second and fourth formulas of 19.7.2,
`K(-ik'/k) = kK(k')` and `E(-ik'/k) = (1/k)E(k')`, without a condition; their left sides are even
in `k` (they depend on `k²` only) and the right sides odd, so they hold for `Re k > 0` (as in
19.7.3, which DLMF states for `Re k > 0`) and change sign for `Re k < 0`; checked numerically
with mpmath at `k = 0.6, 0.5 + 0.3i, 1.3 + 0.5i, 0.3 - 0.9i` (valid) and `k = -0.4 + 0.7i,
-1.3 + 0.5i, -0.3 - 2i` (sign reversed). They are acquired with `0 < Re k`.

# Derivatives and differential equations of Legendre's integrals (DLMF §19.4)

differentiated on the principal domain `{k ≠ 0, 1 - k² ∈ ℂ \ (-∞, 0]}`; the incomplete ones at

the existing `DLMF.Elliptic.Real.hasDerivAt_compEllIntKm`, `Real.hasDerivAt_compEllIntEm`,
`Real.hasDerivAt_compEllIntKm_sq` and `Real.hasDerivAt_compEllIntEm_sq` (tagged 19.4.E1–E2).

All of 19.4.1–19.4.9 are proved: the first relations of 19.4.1, 19.4.2 and 19.4.4–19.4.7 by
differentiation under the integral sign (`p19lR1_hasDerivAt_integral_cpow` for real paths,

follow from 19.4.8–19.4.9.

`incEllIntPik`, `compEllIntEk`, `compEllIntPik`, and `DLMF.JacobiElliptic.compEllIntKk`,
`cCompEllIntKk`), evaluated at real arguments; there they are real
(`incEllIntFk_eq_ofReal` etc.), and the inequalities are stated for their real parts.

  states for (19.9.1); for (19.9.13) DLMF leaves the range of `α²` implicit, and `α² < 1` is the

# Legendre's elliptic integrals: definitions (DLMF §§19.1–19.2)

DLMF 19.2 defines Legendre's integrals for complex amplitude `φ`, modulus `k` and
characteristic `α²` as integrals along the **line segment** from `0` to `φ`, with **principal**
square roots (DLMF §19.1):

* `incEllIntFk φ k = ∫₀^φ (1 - k² sin²θ)^{-1/2} dθ` (19.2.4),
* `incEllIntEk φ k = ∫₀^φ (1 - k² sin²θ)^{1/2} dθ` (19.2.5),
* `incEllIntDk φ k = ∫₀^φ sin²θ (1 - k² sin²θ)^{-1/2} dθ` (19.2.6),
* `incEllIntPik φ α² k = ∫₀^φ (1 - α² sin²θ)⁻¹ (1 - k² sin²θ)^{-1/2} dθ` (19.2.7), with the
  **Cauchy principal value** when `1 - α² sin²θ` vanishes at an interior point of the path;
* the complete integrals `K(k) = F(π/2, k)` (the existing `DLMF.JacobiElliptic.compEllIntKk`),
  `compEllIntEk`, `compEllIntDk`, `compEllIntPik` (19.2.8);
* Legendre's complementary integrals `cCompEllIntKk`, `cCompEllIntEk` (`K'`, `E'`, 19.2.8_1,
  19.2.8_2, 19.2.9), with the branch point at `k = 0` and principal branch `|ph k| ≤ π`;
* Bulirsch's integrals `bulirschCel`, `bulirschEl1`, `bulirschEl2`, `bulirschEl3`
  (19.2.11, 19.2.11_5, 19.2.12, 19.2.16).

## Design

* **Path integrals.** `ei19a_segmentIntegral f w = ∫₀¹ w f(t w) dt` is the integral of `f` along
  the segment `[0, w]`; for real `w` it is the interval integral `∫₀^w f`
  (`ei19a_segmentIntegral_ofReal`).
* **Principal values.** `ei19a_pvSegmentIntegral g f w` is the limit, as `ε → 0+`, of the segment
  integral of `f` over the part of the path where `‖g‖ ≥ ε`. For a simple zero of `g` this excises
  an asymptotically symmetric neighbourhood, so the limit is the Cauchy principal value
  (DLMF §1.4(v)); when `g` is bounded away from `0` on the path it is the ordinary integral
  (`ei19a_pvSegmentIntegral_eq`). `Π` and Bulirsch's `cel`, `el3` use it with
  `g = 1 - α² sin²θ`, resp. `g = cos²θ + p sin²θ`.
* **Branches.** Powers are Mathlib's principal `cpow` (argument in `(-π, π]`), which is DLMF's
  principal square root off the cut. Outside DLMF's domains (19.2(ii): `1 - sin²φ` and
  `1 - k² sin²φ` in `ℂ \ (-∞, 0]`, except that one of them may be `0`, and `1 - α² sin²φ ≠ 0`) the
  definitions are totalized: a non-integrable integrand gives `0`, a non-existent principal
  value gives `limUnder`'s junk value.
* **K and K'.** `K(k)` and the literal `K(k') = compEllIntKpk k` are the existing definitions of
  `DLMF.JacobiElliptic` (Chapter 22). The literal integral (19.2.8_1) is a function of `k²` and
  is discontinuous across the imaginary axis; DLMF's `K'` is its continuation from `k > 0` to
  `ℂ \ (-∞, 0]`, given explicitly by (19.2.9). `cCompEllIntKk`, `cCompEllIntEk` are defined by
  (19.2.9); on the imaginary axis they take the limit from `Re k > 0`, and on the cut
  `(-∞, 0)` (where 19.2.9 is silent) the limit from `Im k > 0`. Numerically (mpmath) the
  definition is continuous across the imaginary axis and satisfies Legendre's relation
  (19.7.1) at complex `k` with `Re k < 0`.
* **Bridges.** For real `φ` and real `k` with `k² ≤ 1` the complex integrals are the real
  `DLMF.Elliptic.Real.incEllIntFm/Em/Pim` (parameter `m = k²`) and the real
  `Carlson.Real.incEllIntFk/Ek/Pik` of `lean-codes`; the complete integrals are
  `Real.compEllIntKm/Em` and `Carlson.Real.compEllIntKk/Ek`.

Mathlib and the pinned TauCeti have no Legendre elliptic integrals of complex argument
(checked 2026-10-25); the companion library `lean-codes` (Carlson) has the real ones.

# Legendre's integrals: the statements of DLMF §19.2

The definitions of DLMF §19.2 are in `DLMF.EllipticIntegrals.Legendre`; this module states the
remaining content of §19.2:

* §19.2(i): the reduction of a general elliptic integrand `r(s, t)` to `ρ/s + σ` (19.2.1–19.2.3),
  as a field identity;
* §19.2(ii): `D = (F - E)/k²` (19.2.6), `D(k) = (K - E)/k²` (19.2.8), the parity and
  holomorphy of the principal `K`, `E` and `K'`, `E'` (prose), the integral forms of `K'`, `E'`
  (19.2.8_1, 19.2.8_2), the circular/hyperbolic alternation (prose) and the quasi-periodicity
  (19.2.10);
* §19.2(iii): Bulirsch's integrals as Legendre integrals (19.2.13–19.2.16);
* §19.2(iv): the function `R_C` (19.2.17–19.2.22), with ACQ19C's `symEllIntRC`.

Real amplitudes `φ` are used where DLMF's identities are path statements; the principal
domain `1 - k² ∈ ℂ \ (-∞, 0]` makes the integrand `(1 - k² sin²θ)^{∓1/2}` continuous for real `θ`.
The negative-real `R_C` formula is proved by evaluating the symmetrically truncated integral
with a logarithmic primitive. Mathlib's FTC lemmas for derivatives of constant sign provide
integrability on both sides, including the square-root singularity at the endpoint `x = 0`.

# Legendre's integrals as symmetric integrals: the substitution (DLMF §19.25(i))

Round-1 helpers (prefix `p19sR1_`). For real `0 < φ ≤ π/2` and `c = csc² φ`, the substitution
`t = csc² θ - c`, `θ ∈ (0, φ)`, maps `(0, φ)` onto `(0, ∞)` with `|dt/dθ| = 2 cos θ / sin³ θ`
(`p19sR1_integral_Ioi_eq_Ioo`). Under it
`√(t + c - 1) = cot θ`, `√(t + c - w) = √(1 - w sin² θ)/sin θ`, `√(t + c) = csc θ`
(principal branches, any complex `w`), so the defining integrals of `R_F`, `R_D`, `R_J` at
`(c - 1, c - k², c, c - α²)` become Legendre-type integrals over `(0, φ)` **for every complex
`k`** (no branch condition is needed at the level of the integrals).

# Reduction of general elliptic integrals (DLMF §19.14)

§19.14(i) gives examples of the reduction of elliptic integrals to Legendre's `F(φ, k)`
(`incEllIntFk`, at real arguments). In (19.14.1)–(19.14.3) DLMF assumes the integrand and
`cos φ` nonnegative; with `φ = arccos(…) ∈ [0, π/2]` this is the range of `x` stated in each

`0, a₁b₂, a₂b₁` (stated as a multiset equality), not all zero.

The special cases (19.14.7), (19.14.9), (19.14.10) are derived from (19.14.4)–(19.14.6) by
computing `U`; (19.14.8) (`x = ∞`) is the improper integral over `(y, ∞)`.

# Relations of elliptic integrals to other functions (DLMF §19.10)

DLMF §19.10(i) refers to §§20.9(i), 22.15(ii) and 23.6(iv) for the relations of Legendre's
integrals to theta, Jacobian and Weierstrass functions; those statements are acquired in the
chapters concerned (19.10.i.p1 is a cross-reference).

§19.10(ii) expresses the elementary inverse functions through `R_C` (19.10.1) and the
Gudermannian function through `R_C` (19.10.2). DLMF assumes `y > 0`; the formulas are real
formulas, with `R_C` evaluated at positive (or, for the endpoint cases, zero) real arguments.
DLMF does not state the ranges of `x` explicitly; we use the natural ones on which both sides
are defined and agree: `x > 0` for the logarithm, all real `x` for `arctan` and `arcsinh`,
`|x| < y` for `arctanh`, `|x| ≤ y` for `arcsin`, `0 ≤ x ≤ y` for `arccos` and `x ≥ y` for
`arccosh`. (For `x < 0` the `arccos` formula is false: its right side is even in `x`; for
example `arccos (-1/2) = 2π/3` while the right side is `π/3`.)

`R_C` is DLMF's `DLMF.EllipticIntegrals.symEllIntRC` (19.2.17). On positive arguments it is
`Carlson.TwoVariable.carlsonRC` of the companion library `lean-codes`, whose elementary values
(Carlson 1977, Exercise 6.9-16, formulas (6.9-15), (6.9-16)) are reused through homogeneity.

# Symmetric elliptic integrals: definitions (DLMF §§19.15–19.16)

DLMF's symmetric standard integrals, defined by DLMF's own integrals (19.16.1), (19.16.2),
(19.16.2_5), (19.16.5) and (19.2.17), and DLMF's multivariate hypergeometric `R`-function
`R_{-a}(𝐛; 𝐳)` of §19.16(ii):

* `symEllIntRF x y z = (1/2) ∫₀^∞ dt / s(t)` (19.16.1), `s(t) = √(t+x) √(t+y) √(t+z)` (19.16.4)
  with principal square roots (`symEllIntS`);
* `symEllIntRJ x y z p = (3/2) ∫₀^∞ dt / (s(t) (t + p))` (19.16.2), the **Cauchy principal value**
  (`cauchyPVIoi`) being taken when `p` is real and negative;
* `symEllIntRG x y z = (1/4) ∫₀^∞ s(t)⁻¹ (x/(t+x) + y/(t+y) + z/(t+z)) t dt` (19.16.2_5);
* `symEllIntRD x y z = R_J(x, y, z, z)` (19.16.5);
* `symEllIntRC x y = (1/2) ∫₀^∞ dt / (√(t+x) (t+y))` (19.2.17), with the Cauchy principal value
  when `y < 0`;
* `symEllIntR a b z = R_{-a}(𝐛; 𝐳)` (19.16.8): on the product slit plane it is Carlson's
  `R`-function `Carlson.carlsonR (-a) b z` of the companion library `lean-codes` (note DLMF's
  sign convention for the subscript: DLMF's `R_{-a}` is `carlsonR (-a)`); at the boundary
  (some `z_j = 0`, "without destroying convergence", §19.16(iii)) it is the limit from the
  slit domain.

**Domains.** DLMF 19.16(i): `x, y, z ∈ ℂ \ (-∞, 0]` except that one or more of them may be `0`
when the integral converges; for `R_F` and `R_J` at most one may vanish, for `R_G` any number,
for `R_D` the third argument is nonzero; `p ≠ 0`. These are the predicates `symEllIntArg` and
`symEllIntRFDomain`. Because the definitions are Lean integrals, values outside these domains
are totalized (a divergent integral is `0`). Square roots are principal, so the defining
integrands are those of DLMF on the whole complex domain.

**Bridges** to `lean-codes` (`Carlson.carlsonRF`, `Carlson.carlsonRG`,
`Carlson.TwoVariable.carlsonRC`, `Carlson.carlsonR`) on the slit plane are DLMF's
(19.16.14)–(19.16.18); the normalizations were checked numerically (mpmath `elliprf`, `elliprj`,
`elliprg`, `elliprc`; for `p < 0` mpmath's `elliprj` returns a complex number whose real part is
the principal value used here).

## §19.15 Advantages of symmetry (prose)

The `R`-function reveals the permutation symmetry hidden in Lauricella's `F_D` (19.15.p1).
Symmetry of `R_F`, `R_G`, `R_J` in `x, y, z` (`Carlson.carlsonRF_perm`, …, and
`symEllIntR_comp_perm`) replaces the five Legendre transformations (19.7.2), (19.7.4)–(19.7.7),
unifies Landen and Gauss transformations (§19.22) and the parameter changes of `Π` (19.21.12)
(19.15.p2); it permits the elementary-symmetric expansion (19.19.7) (19.15.p3) and the
reduction theorems of §19.29 (19.15.p4); symmetry in the semiaxes of ellipsoids is preserved
(19.15.p5). These are commentary; the mathematical content is in the cited formulas.

# Asymptotic approximations of the symmetric elliptic integrals (DLMF §19.27)

DLMF §19.27 gives approximations of `R_F`, `R_G`, `R_D`, `R_J` with real nonnegative
arguments when some arguments are much smaller than the others, with relative or absolute
`O`-terms (from Carlson and Gustafson, SIAM J. Math. Anal. 25 (1994), with explicit bounds).

## Reading of the `O`-terms

DLMF writes, e.g., `R_F(x, y, z) = (1/(2√z)) ln(8z/(a + g)) (1 + O(a/z))` as `a/z → 0`. All
formulas are homogeneous, so the limit is realized here by letting the **small arguments tend
to `0` jointly** (through DLMF's domain: real, nonnegative, at most one of `x, y, z` zero, `p > 0`)
with the **large arguments fixed** and positive; the `O`-term is then a Mathlib
`Asymptotics.IsBigO` along `𝓝[S] 0` (or `𝓝[>] 0`, `𝓝[≥] 0`). Uniformity in the fixed
arguments, which Carlson–Gustafson's explicit bounds also provide, is not asserted. Every
statement was checked numerically (mpmath, random directions of approach, 2026-10-25).

## Corrections

* **19.27.8.** DLMF: `R_D(x, y, z) = 3/√(xyz) - (6/(xy)) R_G(x, y, 0) (1 + O(z/g))`. The
  relative error of the bracket is of order `√(z/g)`, not `z/g`: numerically, for
  `x = 2, y = 3`, `(3/√(xyz) - R_D)/((6/(xy)) R_G(x, y, 0)) - 1 ≈ -1.2895 √(z/g)` for
  `z = 10⁻⁴, …, 10⁻¹⁰`. This agrees with Carlson–Gustafson (1994, (37)):
  `R_D = 3/√(xyz) - (6/(xy)) R_G(x, y, 0) + (6a√z/g³)(1 - (πθ/4)√(z/a))` with bounded `θ`. The
  statement below has `O(√(z/g))`.
* **19.27.12.** DLMF: `R_J(x, y, z, p) = (3/(2√(xyz))) (ln(4f/p) - 2)(1 + O(p/f))`. This fails
  unless `x = y = z`: for `(x, y, z) = (1, 2, 3)` the difference `R_J - (3/(2√(xyz)))(ln(4f/p) - 2)`
  tends to `-0.0381…`, not `0`, as `p → 0`. Carlson–Gustafson (1994, (42)) state
  `R_J = (3/(2√(xyz))) (ln(4f/p) - 2 + r)` with `-ln(f/H) < r < (3p/(2(f - p))) ln(f/p)`, where
  `H = 3/(x⁻¹ + y⁻¹ + z⁻¹)` is the harmonic mean (`r → 0` only when `f = H`). That bounded form
  (with non-strict inequalities, checked numerically on 400 random triples and `0 < p < f`) is
  acquired.

# Inequalities for the symmetric elliptic integrals (DLMF §19.24)

Inequalities for the complete integrals (§19.24(i)) and the incomplete integrals (§19.24(ii)).
All variables are real and positive (or nonnegative where DLMF says so); on such arguments the
symmetric integrals of `DLMF.EllipticIntegrals` are real, and the inequalities are stated for
their real parts (`symEllIntRF_ofReal_im` etc. record that the imaginary parts vanish).

* (19.24.1)–(19.24.4): bounds for `R_F(0, y, z)`, `R_G(0, y, z)`, `R_G(0, y², z²)` and
  `R_J(0, y, z, p)`; the condition `y ≤ z` in (19.24.1)–(19.24.2) only identifies the smaller
  variable (19.24.i.p1). `R_D(0, y, z)` is the case `p = z` of (19.24.4) (19.24.i.p2).
* (19.24.5)–(19.24.6): the AGM bounds `1/aₙ ≤ (2/π) R_F(0, a₀², g₀²) ≤ 1/gₙ`.
* (19.24.7): the perimeter of an ellipse `L(a, b) = 8 R_G(0, a², b²)` (`ellipsePerimeter` of
  §19.9(i)); the approximations of §19.9(i) then apply (19.24.i.p4).
* (19.24.8)–(19.24.9): strict product and sum bounds for `R_F(x, y, 0)`, `R_G(x, y, 0)` and
  Neuman's bounds for `R_G/R_F` through the first AGM step.
* (19.24.10)–(19.24.12): bounds for `R_F`, `R_J`, `R_G` by elementary means (special cases of
  Carlson (1966), Theorems 2 and 3; "all variables are positive", 19.24.ii.p1); the cases
  `R_C`, `R_D` are included (19.24.Px1.p1).
* (19.24.13)–(19.24.15): Neuman's bounds `R_a R_{-a} > 1`, `R_a + R_{-a} > 2`, their special
  case `R_F R_G > 1`, `R_F + R_G > 2`, and `R_C(x, (y+z)/2) ≤ R_F(x, y, z) ≤ R_C(x, √(yz))`.

The lower bound in (19.24.10) is proved from `lean-codes`' capacity bound
`Carlson.inv_dupMean_le_carlsonRF_sq` (Carlson 1966, Theorem 3). The AGM bounds in
(19.24.5) use the RF–AGM identity from §19.22 and Mathlib's `NNReal.agmSequences` bounds.
The upper bound in (19.24.10) uses monotonicity of Carlson's hypergeometric mean;
(19.24.13)–(19.24.14) use strict exponential Jensen inequalities for the real R-averages.
The `R_J` bounds use the five-node capacity inequality and order monotonicity; the `R_G`
bounds are Jensen bounds before and after Euler transformation. The `R_F`–`R_C` bounds in
(19.24.15) compare the real integral kernels using strict arithmetic–geometric mean
inequalities and `lean-codes`' `integral_lt_integral_of_ae_lt`. The complete `R_G` bounds
in (19.24.2) use `Carlson.carlsonRE_eq_compEllIntEk` and the bounds for `E(k)` from §19.9.

# Reduction of general elliptic integrals (DLMF §19.29)

DLMF §19.29 reduces integrals over a real interval `(y, x)` whose integrands contain the square
root of a quartic or cubic polynomial, written as a product of linear factors
`a_α + b_α t`, to the symmetric integrals `R_F`, `R_D`, `R_J`, `R_C` of
`DLMF.EllipticIntegrals.Symmetric`.

* §19.29(i): the notation (19.29.1)–(19.29.3), (19.29.5), (19.29.9) as definitions
  (`ellRedRoot`, `ellRedDet`, `ellRedS`, `ellRedU`, `ellRedUInf`, `ellRedUNegInf`,
  `ellRedU5Sq`, `ellRedS5`, `ellRedQ5Sq`); the algebraic identities of (19.29.5) and (19.29.9)
  are **proved** for arbitrary complex coefficients; the reduction theorems (19.29.4), (19.29.6),
  (19.29.7), (19.29.8) and the example (19.29.10) are stated for DLMF's complex coefficients.
  The real case of (19.29.4) with four positive linear factors is **proved** from Carlson's
  (9.8-12) in `lean-codes` (`Carlson.integral_quartic_eq_carlsonRF`).
* §19.29(ii): the integrals `I(𝐦)` (19.29.11), the unit vectors (19.29.12), the basic
  integrals (19.29.13), (19.29.14), the partial-fraction relation (19.29.15) and the
  recurrence (19.29.18) (**proved**, under explicit integrability hypotheses that DLMF leaves
  implicit), the cubic recurrence (19.29.16) and the reduction statement of 19.29.ii.p3.
* §19.29(iii): the examples (19.29.19)–(19.29.33). The case `0 < y` of (19.29.19) is
  **proved** from Carlson's Exercise 9.8-3 (`Carlson.integral_quadratic_mul_quadratic`).

## Conventions

**Convergence.** In §19.29(iii) DLMF assumes only that the quadratics are positive on the open
interval; an integrand can then still be non-integrable (a double zero at an endpoint, e.g.
`Q₁ = Q₂ = 1 - t²` on `(0, 1)`, or `t⁴` at `y = 0`). The theorems (19.29.19)–(19.29.21), (19.29.24),
(19.29.26), (19.29.27), (19.29.30) therefore carry an explicit integrability hypothesis
(`IntegrableOn … (Ioo y x)`), which is DLMF's implicit convergence assumption.

The coefficients `a_α`, `b_α` are complex, indexed by `Fin 5` (DLMF's `α = 1, …, 5` is Lean's
`0, …, 4`; the fifth factor occurs only in (19.29.8), (19.29.9)). Square roots are principal.
All integrals over `(y, x)` with `y < x` are Lebesgue integrals over `Ioo y x`; for a
non-integrable integrand the Lean value is `0`, so integrability is either implied by the
hypotheses or assumed explicitly. DLMF's condition that the segment with endpoints
`a_α + b_α y`, `a_α + b_α x` lie in `ℂ \ (-∞, 0)` is `∀ t ∈ [y, x], symEllIntArg (a_α + b_α t)`.

`R_J`, `R_D` and of `R_{-a}(𝐛; 𝐳)` (§19.20(i)–(v)). As DLMF says (19.20.i.p1), the variables
satisfy the constraints of §19.16(i) unless stated otherwise; we state them explicitly
(slit-plane membership, admissible zeros, real variables where DLMF uses real ones, e.g. for
Cauchy principal values). Homogeneity is stated for real `λ > 0` (for complex `λ` see
`symEllIntR_mul`). "`= ∞`" is formalized as non-integrability of the defining integrand,
"`→ +∞`" as `Tendsto … atTop` of the (real) value.

Decimal values of the lemniscate constants (19.20.2), (19.20.22) are excluded: numerical.

**Domain corrections.** The lemniscatic cases (19.20.3), (19.20.23) are stated for real positive
`x, y`; with complex arguments they fail without a branch condition (numerically, at
`x = -1 + 0.3i`, `y = 2 + i` the two sides differ by a factor `-i`).

# Where the zeros of `erf` and `erfc` can lie, DLMF §7.13(i)–(ii)

Elementary localization of the complex zeros of the error functions, used to reduce the zero
classifications of `DLMF/ErrorFunctions/Zeros.lean` to the modulus enumerations there.

* `zcnt_erf_conj`, `zcnt_erfc_conj`: `erf (z̄) = conj (erf z)`, by the identity theorem for the
  derivative (`HasDerivAt.conj_conj`).
* `zcnt_erfc_ne_zero_of_re_pos`: `erfc z ≠ 0` for `Re z > 0`, from the Cauchy integral
  `∫ e^{-t²}/(t - u) dt = π i w(u)` (DLMF 7.7.2) of the Faddeeva function at `u = iz`, whose
  imaginary part is a positive integral.
* `zcnt_norm_erfc_le_one`: `‖erfc z‖ ≤ 1` for `Re z ≥ 0`, `Re z² ≥ 0`, from the Laplace form
  `erfc z = π^{-1/2} e^{-z²} ∫₀^∞ e^{-zr - r²/4} dr`.
* `zcnt_erfc_zero_arg`: every zero of `erfc` satisfies `π/2 < |ph z| < 3π/4`.
* `zcnt_erf_ofReal_ne_zero`, `zcnt_erf_I_mul_ofReal_ne_zero`: `erf` has no zero on the real or
  imaginary axis other than `0`.
* Fresnel integrals: the symmetries `C(-z) = -C(z)`, `C(z̄) = conj C(z)`, `C(iz) = i C(z)` and
  `S(iz) = -i S(z)` (`zcnt_fresnelCosInt_neg` …); no zeros on the diagonal `ℝ(1+i)`
  (`C((1+i)x) = (1+i)x ∫₀¹ cosh(πt²x²) dt`); no real zeros (`zcnt_fresnelCosInt_ofReal_ne_zero`,
  `zcnt_fresnelSinInt_ofReal_ne_zero`): for `0 < x ≤ 1` the integrand is positive, and for `x ≥ 1`
  `C = 1/2 + f sin − g cos` with `‖f‖ + ‖g‖ < 1/2` from the Laplace integrals 7.7.10–11.
* `zcnt_octant_classification`: the eight-fold symmetry reduces a zero classification to the
  modulus enumeration in the octant `0 < ph z < π/4`.

# Zero localization by comparison with an exponential model

Asymptotic zeros of special functions (erf and Fresnel zeros, DLMF §7.13; large zeros of Kummer's
function, DLMF 13.9.9; Airy `Bi` zeros) are located by comparing the function on a small circle
with the model `A (exp (z - w) - 1)`, whose only zero in a disc of radius `ρ ≤ 1/2` about `w` is
the simple zero `w`. Rouché's theorem (`TauCeti.rouche`, Tau Ceti) then transfers existence and
the count, with multiplicity, to the function.

## Main results

* `DLMF.erfZ_count_eq_one_of_expModel`: exactly one zero, counted with multiplicity.
* `DLMF.erfZ_exists_zero_of_expModel`: a zero in the open disc.
* `DLMF.erfZ_existsUnique_zero_of_expModel`: exactly one zero in the open disc, and it is simple.

The single-point count lemma follows the private `TauCeti.count_eq_single` of
`TauCeti.Analysis.Complex.Conformal.LocalDegree`.

# The Gamma and Beta functions, after AAR Chapter 1, §1.1

Andrews–Askey–Roy (AAR), *Special Functions*, Chapter 1, §1.1 takes Gauss's product
as the definition of `Γ`. Mathlib instead defines `Complex.Gamma` / `Real.Gamma` by Euler's
integral on `{s | 0 < re s}` and meromorphic continuation. The two definitions agree:
Euler's limit formula is `Complex.GammaSeq_tendsto_Gamma` (and the real analogue), which
lives in `Mathlib.Analysis.SpecialFunctions.Gamma.Beta` together with the reflection
formula `Complex.Gamma_mul_Gamma_one_sub`.

## Correspondence with AAR §1.1

* **Definition 1.1.1** (Gauss product). Mathlib: `Complex.GammaSeq` and
  `Complex.GammaSeq_tendsto_Gamma` in `Gamma.Beta`.
* **Theorem 1.1.2** (Weierstrass product). Proved below as
  `Complex.one_div_Gamma_eq_tprod`.
* **Definition 1.1.3** (Beta integral). Mathlib: `Complex.betaIntegral`.
* **Theorem 1.1.4** (`B(x,y) = Γ(x)Γ(y)/Γ(x+y)`). Mathlib:
  `Complex.betaIntegral_eq_Gamma_mul_div` and
  `Complex.Gamma_mul_Gamma_eq_betaIntegral`.
* **Corollary 1.1.5** (Euler's integral). Mathlib: `Complex.Gamma_eq_integral`,
  `Real.Gamma_eq_integral`.
* Recurrence `Γ(x+1) = x Γ(x)` and `Γ(n+1) = n!`: `Complex.Gamma_add_one`,
  `Complex.Gamma_nat_eq_factorial`.

The statements below use Mathlib's convention that `Γ` vanishes at non-positive integers
and that `0⁻¹ = 0` in a field, so `1 / Γ` is an entire function
(`Complex.differentiable_one_div_Gamma`) and the Weierstrass formula holds at the poles
as well.

# Binet's formula for complex arguments (DLMF 5.11.1, 5.6.9)

Binet's function is taken in Stieltjes' form
`μ(z) = ∫₀^∞ P(t)/(z+t)² dt`, with the periodic weight `P(t) = ({t} - {t}²)/2 ∈ [0, 1/8]`.
This integral is holomorphic on the whole slit plane. On the positive reals it agrees with
the Laplace form `binetIntegral`: both differ from their unit shift by
`(x + 1/2) log(1 + 1/x) - 1` and tend to `0`. The identity theorem then gives

`Γ(z) = exp((z - 1/2) log z - z + (1/2) log 2π + μ(z))` for `z ∈ slitPlane`.

From `|z + t|² ≥ ((|z| + Re z)/(2|z|)) (|z| + t)²` follows Stieltjes' bound
`|μ(z)| ≤ 1/(6(|z| + Re z))`, in particular `|μ(z)| ≤ 1/(6|z|)` for `Re z ≥ 0`.

# The digamma series (AAR Theorem 1.2.5)

Andrews–Askey–Roy, Theorem 1.2.5:

* `Γ'(1) = -γ` is `Real.hasDerivAt_Gamma_one` / `Complex.digamma_one`;
* `ψ(x) = -γ + ∑_{k=0}^∞ (1/(k+1) - 1/(x+k))` for `x > 0`, proved below;
* log-convexity of `Γ` on `(0,∞)` is `Real.convexOn_log_Gamma`.

The series is obtained from Gauss's product `GammaSeq` by differentiating `log ∘ GammaSeq`
and passing to the limit, using convexity on `(0,∞)`.

# Gauss's multiplication formula for the digamma function (AAR Theorem 1.2.7)

Logarithmic differentiation of Gauss multiplication (AAR 1.5.2) yields, for `m > 0` and
`s > 0`,

$$
\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\psi\bigl(s+k/m\bigr)= m\,\psi(ms)-m\log m.
$$

This is the first identity of AAR Theorem 1.2.7 (in the form obtained from
`Γ(x+n) = (x)_n Γ(x)` by taking logarithmic derivatives, together with the multiplication
formula). Combined with reflection `ψ(1-x)-ψ(x)=π cot(πx)` one obtains Gauss's evaluation
of `ψ` at rational arguments; the case `ψ(1/2)` is recorded below.

# Gauss's multiplication formula (AAR Theorem 1.5.2)

Mathlib has Legendre's duplication formula `Gamma_mul_Gamma_add_half` (the case `m = 2`)
but not the general Gauss multiplication formula. Andrews–Askey–Roy, Theorem 1.5.2:

$$
\Gamma(mz)=(2\pi)^{(1-m)/2}\, m^{mz-1/2}\prod_{k=0}^{m-1}\Gamma\bigl(z+k/m\bigr).
$$

The real-positive case is obtained from the Bohr–Mollerup theorem, after evaluating the
constant via Euler's reflection formula and the sine product
`∏_{k=1}^{m-1} sin(π k / m) = m / 2^{m-1}`. The identity is then extended to all complex
arguments by analytic continuation of `1/Γ`.

# Derivatives of the reciprocal Gamma function

`1/Γ` is entire, while the digamma function `ψ = Γ'/Γ` has poles at `0, -1, -2, …`. Mathlib's
`Complex.digamma` takes the value `0` at those poles, so a product such as
`ψ(x) · (1/Γ(x))` evaluates to `0` there although its continuous extension is
`(-1)^{n+1} n!` at `x = -n`. Statements in which digamma occurs only through such products
are therefore best written with the entire functions `recipGammaDeriv n = (1/Γ)^{(n)}`:

* `(1/Γ)' = -ψ/Γ` (`recipGammaDeriv_one_eq`), with `(1/Γ)'(-n) = (-1)^n n!`;
* `(1/Γ)'' = (ψ² - ψ')/Γ` (`recipGammaDeriv_two_eq`), so that the entire function
  `((1/Γ)')² - (1/Γ)(1/Γ)''` extends `ψ'/Γ²` (`deriv_digamma_mul_recip_Gamma_sq`);
* `ψ(x+n)/Γ(x) = -(x)_n (1/Γ)'(x+n)` (`recip_Gamma_mul_digamma_add_nat`).

Results stated with `recipGammaDeriv` hold for all parameters; the digamma forms follow on the
complement of the poles.

# Bounds for `Γ` on vertical lines, uniform under shifts of the line

Contour shifts in Mellin–Barnes integrals move a vertical line `Re s = c` to `Re s = c ± N`
and need bounds for `Γ` that are uniform in `N`. Writing `s = x + iy`:

* `shiftB_norm_Gamma_le`: `|Γ(x+iy)| ≤ Γ(x)` for `x > 0`;
* `shiftB_norm_recip_Gamma_le`: `|1/Γ(x+iy)| ≤ e^{π|y|/2} / Γ(x)` for `x ≥ 1/2`, uniformly in
  `x` (from `|Γ(x)/Γ(x+iy)|² = ∏ (1 + y²/(x+k)²) ≤ cosh πy`, DLMF 5.8.3);
* `shiftB_norm_Gamma_le_of_le_half`: `|Γ(x+iy)| ≤ 2π e^{-π|y|/2} / (|sin πx| Γ(1-x))` for
  `x ≤ 1/2`, uniformly in `x` (reflection formula);
* `shiftB_norm_Gamma_sub_nat_le`: hence on the shifted lines `x = x₀ - N`,
  `|Γ(x₀ - N + iy)| ≤ 2π e^{-π|y|/2} / (|sin πx₀| Γ(1 - x₀ + N))`, uniformly in `N`;
* `shiftB_norm_recip_Gamma_add_nat_le`: on `x = x₀ + N` with `x₀ ≥ 1/2`,
  `|1/Γ(x₀ + N + iy)| ≤ e^{π|y|/2} / Γ(x₀ + N)`.

The factorial growth of `Γ(1 - x₀ + N)` and `Γ(x₀ + N)` makes the shifted-line integrals of
Mellin–Barnes integrands tend to `0`.

# Bounds for the Gamma function on vertical lines

From the product `|Γ(x)/Γ(x+iy)|² = ∏ₖ (1 + y²/(x+k)²)` (DLMF 5.8.3) and its exact values

* `exists_norm_Gamma_le`: `|Γ(x+iy)| ≤ C (1+|y|)^K e^{-π|y|/2}` for fixed `x > 0`;
* `exists_norm_recip_Gamma_le`: `|1/Γ(x+iy)| ≤ C (1+|y|)^K e^{π|y|/2}`, uniformly for `x` in a
  bounded interval.

These are the estimates needed for Mellin–Barnes integrals.
