# Expansions in series of eigenfunctions of Hill's equation (DLMF §28.30)

For a real continuous `π`-periodic potential `Q` of mean zero, let `λ̂_m` be the periodic and
antiperiodic eigenvalues in their natural order (`DLMF.Mathieu.hillEigenvalueHat`) and let
`w_m` be an orthonormal set of real `2π`-periodic eigenfunctions (28.30.1–28.30.2). Every
continuous `2π`-periodic `f` whose second derivative is square integrable on `[0, 2π]` has the
uniformly and absolutely convergent expansion `f = ∑ f_m w_m`,
`f_m = (2π)⁻¹ ∫₀^{2π} f w_m` (28.30.3–28.30.4).

The eigenfunctions are a choice (DLMF: "let `w_m(x)` … be the eigenfunctions, that is, an
orthonormal set of `2π`-periodic solutions"); the existence of such a family is stated
separately (`exists_hill_eigenfunctions`), and the expansion theorem is stated for every such
family. "Second derivative square integrable" is formalized as: `f` is differentiable with
derivative `f'`, and `f'(x) = f'(0) + ∫₀^x g` on `[0, 2π]` for some `g ∈ L²(0, 2π)`.

§28.30(ii) only points to Schäfke and Meixner et al. for analogues of §28.19; no statements.

# Hill's equation: Floquet theory and the discriminant (DLMF §28.29)

Statements of DLMF §28.29 for Hill's equation `w'' + (λ + Q(x)) w = 0` (definitions in
`DLMF.Mathieu.Hill.Basic`):

* §28.29(i): Mathieu's equation is the case `Q(x) = -2q cos 2x` (`isHillPotential_mathieu`).
* §28.29(ii): existence (`hill_exists_solution`, from `ODE.exists_linear_ode`) and uniqueness
  (`IsHillSolution.eq_of_initial`) of solutions with given initial data, the basic
  solutions, the shift relations 28.29.4–28.29.5, the
  characteristic equation 28.29.8–28.29.9, Floquet solutions 28.29.10, the exceptional cases
  `ν = 0, 1` (28.29.11–28.29.12), 28.29.13 and the symmetric case 28.29.14.
* §28.29(iii) (real `Q`): the discriminant, the periodic and antiperiodic eigenvalues
  28.29.16–28.29.18 and their asymptotics 28.29.19–28.29.22.

The basic solutions are definitions by choice (`hillWI`, `hillWII`); the existence theorem
`hill_exists_solution` for continuous `Q` is proved from the global existence theorem
`ODE.exists_linear_ode` (`DLMFMathlib.Analysis.ODE.P1oLinearGlobal`). The Floquet theory of
§28.29(ii) is proved in coordinates: the Wronskian of `w_I`, `w_II` is `1`
(`p1o_hill_wronskian`), a solution is determined by its data at `0`, and the shift by `π` acts
on the data by the monodromy matrix (`p1o_hill_data_pi`, `p1o_hill_multiplier_iff`), whose
characteristic polynomial is `ρ² - Δ(λ) ρ + 1` (`p1o_hill_two_step`).

# The equations of Whittaker–Hill and Ince (DLMF §28.31)

Statements of DLMF §28.31 for the definitions in `DLMF.Mathieu.Hill.Basic`: the reduction of
the Whittaker–Hill equation 28.31.1 to Ince's equation 28.31.3 (28.31.2), the Fourier-series
solutions and their coefficient recurrences (28.31.4–28.31.9), the Ince polynomials
`C_p^m`, `S_p^m` and their eigenvalues `a_p^m`, `b_p^m` (28.31.10–28.31.15), and the
paraboloidal wave functions `hc_p^m`, `hs_p^m` (28.31.16–28.31.24 and the asymptotic
behaviour). The limits 28.31.14–28.31.15 use the Mathieu functions `ce_m`, `se_m` and
eigenvalues `a_m`, `b_m` of `DLMF.Mathieu.Basic` (real `q`).

The admissible indices are `m ≤ p`, `m ≡ p (mod 2)` (and `m ≥ 1` for `S_p^m`, `hs_p^m`), as in
DLMF 28.31.10–28.31.11 (`m = 0, 1, …, n` with `p = 2n`, `2n + 1`, `2n + 2`).

**Correction (§28.31(iii), Asymptotic Behavior, second paragraph).** DLMF says that for
`ξ > 0` the functions `hc_p^m(z, -ξ)`, `hs_p^m(z, -ξ)` behave as multiples of
`exp(¼ξ cos 2z) (cos z)^{-p-2}` as `z → ½π ± i∞`, and all other periodic solutions as
multiples of `exp(-¼ξ cos 2z) (cos z)^p`. By the reflection formulas 28.31.19–28.31.20
(`z ↦ ½π - z`, under which `cos 2z ↦ -cos 2z` and `cos z ↦ sin z`) and the first paragraph,
the correct factors are `exp(¼ξ cos 2z) (sin z)^p` for `hc_p^m(z, -ξ)`, `hs_p^m(z, -ξ)`, and
`exp(-¼ξ cos 2z) (sin z)^{-p-2}` for the other periodic solutions. Numerically
(`ξ = 0.8`, `p = 2, 3, 4`, all `m`, `z = ½π + iy`, `y = 2, 3, 4`), the ratio
`hc_p^m(z, -ξ) / (exp(¼ξ cos 2z) (sin z)^p)` converges (e.g. `-0.416, -0.472, -0.480` for
`hc_2^0`) while the ratio with DLMF's factor `exp(¼ξ cos 2z) (cos z)^{-p-2}` grows like
`e^{(2p+2)y}`. The corrected form is acquired (`paraboloidal_asymptotic_neg`).

All other formulas of §28.31 were checked: 28.31.3 and the recurrences 28.31.6–28.31.9
symbolically (sympy), and 28.31.13 and the reflection formulas 28.31.19–28.31.20 numerically
(finite eigenproblems for `p ≤ 6`, `ξ = 0.8`).

# Integral equations (DLMF §28.10)

The integral equations 28.10.1–28.10.8 with elementary kernels (`q = h²`, real `h`, so
`q ≥ 0`; the notation `A^n_m`, `B^n_m` is that of §28.4) and 28.10.9–28.10.10 with the Bessel
kernel `J₀` (Mathlib's `Complex.besselJ 0`; `J₀(2√w)` is entire in `w`, so the branch of the
square root in 28.10.9 is immaterial — the principal one is used). All ten were checked
numerically (`h = 1.3`, `z = 0.4`, `n ≤ 2`). §28.10(iii) is bibliographic.

28.10.1–28.10.8 are proved by the kernel method: each kernel `K(z, t)` satisfies the PDE
`K_zz - 2q cos 2z K = K_tt - 2q cos 2t K`, so two integrations by parts show that the integral
`G(z)` solves Mathieu's equation with the eigenvalue of the integrand; parity and the value or
derivative at `z = 0` or `π/2` identify `G` as a multiple of `ce_n` or `se_n`, and the constant is a
quarter-period Fourier integral (`p1a2_quarter_*`) of §28.4.

# Asymptotic expansions for large `q` (DLMF §28.8)

With `h = √q → +∞` (real): the eigenvalue expansion 28.8.1 and the exponentially small gap
28.8.2; Sips' expansions 28.8.3–28.8.7 near `x = π/2` and Goldstein's expansions 28.8.8–28.8.12
away from `π/2`, both in terms of `D_m(ξ) = e^{-ξ²/4} He_m(ξ)` (`He_m` is Mathlib's
probabilists' Hermite polynomial `Polynomial.hermite m`).

DLMF gives the functions `U_m`, `V_m`, `Ĉ_m`, `Ŝ_m`, `σ_m`, `τ_{m+1}`, `P_m`, `Q_m` only through
their asymptotic series. Here the printed truncations are inserted and the resulting
approximation is stated with a relative error: `O(h⁻³)` for Sips' expansions at fixed `λ`
(the first omitted terms are of order `h⁻³`), and `O(h⁻¹)` for Goldstein's expansions at fixed
`μ ≥ 1` (a safe order: the printed `P_m`, `Q_m` are series in `1/(h cos² x)` with
`cos x ≍ μ h^{-1/4}`). Both were checked numerically (Fourier eigenvectors at 60 digits;
Sips: `h = 10, 20, 40`, `m ≤ 2`, `λ ∈ {0, 0.5, 1}`; Goldstein: `h = 6, 9, 12`, `m ≤ 2`,
`μ ∈ {1.5, 2.5}`). DLMF notes that Sips' results are derived formally.

The uniform approximations of Barrett and Dunster (§28.8(iv)) are described only in words in
DLMF and are not acquired.

# Modified Mathieu functions: definitions (DLMF §§28.20, 28.22–28.28)

This is the definitions file for the modified Mathieu functions of DLMF §§28.20–28.28.

* `IsModMathieuSolution a q w`: `w` is an entire solution of the modified Mathieu equation
  28.20.1 `w'' - (a - 2q cosh 2z) w = 0`.
* `modMathieuCe ν z q = Ce_ν(z, q)`, `modMathieuSe`, `modMathieuMe`, `modMathieuFe`,
  `modMathieuGe` (28.20.3–28.20.7): Mathieu functions at imaginary argument.
* `besselJExp μ h z`, `besselYExp μ h z`, `mathieuCylExp j μ h z`: the cylinder functions
  `𝒞^{(j)}_μ(h e^z)` of 28.23.1 (`J`, `Y`, `H^{(1)}`, `H^{(2)}`), **continued analytically in
  `z`** from the real axis: `(h e^z / 2)^μ` is read as `(h / 2)^μ e^{μ z}` with the principal
  power of `h / 2`. For `h > 0` and `|Im z| < π` they agree with the principal-branch Bessel
  functions at `h e^z`; elsewhere they are DLMF's continuations (DLMF continues `M^{(j)}_ν`
  analytically in `z`, §28.20(iii)).
* `mathieuCylCosh j μ h z`, `mathieuCylSinh j μ h z`: `𝒞^{(j)}_μ(2h cosh z)` and
  `𝒞^{(j)}_μ(2h sinh z)` continued from the positive real axis through the half-plane
  `Re z > 0`, written as `𝒞^{(j)}_μ(h e^{z'})` with `z' = z + log(1 ± e^{-2z})` (principal
  logarithm; `|e^{-2z}| < 1` there).
* `modMathieuM j ν z h = M^{(j)}_ν(z, h)` (§28.20(iii)), **defined by the absolutely convergent
  series 28.24.1 in cross-products of Bessel functions**,
  `c^ν_{2n}(h²) M^{(j)}_ν(z, h) = ∑_ℓ (-1)^ℓ c^ν_{2ℓ}(h²) J_{ℓ-n}(h e^{-z}) 𝒞^{(j)}_{ν+n+ℓ}(h e^z)`,
  for one index `n = modMathieuIndex ν h` with `c^ν_{2n}(h²) ≠ 0` (chosen by
  `Classical.choose`; the independence of `n` is the theorem 28.24.1). The coefficients are
  ACQ28B's `mathieuMeCoeff ν (h²)`, which for integer `ν` follow 28.12.11.
* `radialMathieuMc j n z h = Mc^{(j)}_n(z, h)`, `radialMathieuMs j n z h = Ms^{(j)}_n(z, h)`
  (28.20.15–28.20.16) and `modMathieuIe`, `modMathieuIo`, `modMathieuKe`, `modMathieuKo`
  (28.20.17–28.20.20).
* The joining factors `g_{e,m}`, `g_{o,m}`, `f_{e,m}`, `f_{o,m}` of 28.22.5–28.22.10, the
  coefficients `D^±_m` of 28.25.2–28.25.3, Goldstein's `Fc_m`, `Gc_m`, `Fs_m`, `Gs_m`
  (28.26.1–28.26.3), the kernels `w`, `R`, `φ` of §28.28, the path integrals along `𝓛_j`
  (28.28.6), the cross-products `D_0`, `D_1`, `Ds_k`, `Dc_k`, `Dsc_k` and the integrals
  `α`, `γ`, `α̂`, `β̂`, `γ̂` of §28.28(iii)–(iv).

## Design notes

* The integer-order functions of `DLMF.Mathieu.Basic` are defined for real `q` only; the
  radial functions take a complex `h` and use `q = h²`, so for integer order they are
  meaningful when `h²` is real (`h` real or purely imaginary, as in `Ie_n`, `Ke_n`).
* For the general order the definition by 28.24.1 avoids the asymptotic characterization of
  §28.20(iii) (stated as theorems). For integer `ν = n` the series reduces to
  28.24.2–28.24.5 (checked numerically); for `ν = -n` some coefficients vanish
  (e.g. `c^{-2}_0 = 0`), which is why the index `n` is chosen with `c^ν_{2n} ≠ 0`.
* `j ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4}`; other values of `j` give the junk value `0`.

## Correction to DLMF 28.23

DLMF states that 28.23.2–28.23.5 are valid "for all `z` when `j = 1`". For noninteger `ν` this
is false: the terms with `n → -∞` behave like `c^ν_{2n} J_{ν+2n}(2h cosh z)`, and since
`c^ν_{2n}/c^ν_{2n+2} ~ -q/(4n²)` (28.14.6) while `J_{μ-2}(w)/J_μ(w) ~ 4μ²/w²` as
`μ → -∞` through nonintegers, the ratio of consecutive terms tends to `1/cosh² z`
(resp. `1/sinh² z`). The series therefore converge only for `|cosh z| > 1`
(resp. `|sinh z| > 1`), for every `j`. Numerically, with `ν = 0.3`, `h = 1.2`, the series 28.23.2
with `j = 1` at `z = 0.2 + 1.2i` (`|cosh z| = 0.41`) has partial sums of size `10⁵` at
`|n| ≤ 10` and `10¹²` at `|n| ≤ 20`, and 28.23.4 diverges at `z = 0.3`. For integer `ν`
(28.23.6–28.23.13) the `j = 1` series do converge for all `z`. The statements below for
noninteger `ν` carry the hypothesis `|cosh z| > 1` (resp. `|sinh z| > 1`) for all `j`.

# Integral equations with the kernel `e^{2ihw}` (DLMF 28.28.2–28.28.3)

For `w = cosh z cos t cos α + sinh z sin t sin α` the kernel `e^{2ihw}` satisfies
`(∂_α² - 2q cos 2α) K = (∂_t² - 2q cos 2t) K`, `q = h²`, so `α ↦ ∫₀^{2π} e^{2ihw} f(t) dt` solves
Mathieu's equation whenever `f` is a `2π`-periodic solution (`p3m_isMathieuSolution_kernelW`).
For `f = ce_n` (`se_n`) the integral is even (odd) in `α`, hence a multiple of `ce_n(α)`
(`se_n(α)`); the multiplier is evaluated by the integral equations 28.10.1, 28.10.3, 28.10.6 and
28.10.7 at the point `iz`, and compared with `Mc^{(1)}_n`, `Ms^{(1)}_n` by the connection formulas
28.22.1–28.22.2 (`h > 0`), the parity in `h` (`h < 0`) and the values at `h = 0`.

* `p3m_integral_exp_mathieuCe`: DLMF 28.28.2.

# The Wronskian of `M^{(1)}_ν` and `M^{(2)}_ν` (toward DLMF 28.20.21)

The Wronskian `𝒲{M^{(1)}_ν, M^{(2)}_ν}` is constant in `z`. Along the real axis `x → +∞` the
cross-product series 28.24.1 is dominated by its term with `J_0(h e^{-x})`; the other terms are
bounded by `h e^{-x}` times the size of the cylinder functions at `h e^x`, which tend to `0`
(DLMF 10.7.8 and Hankel's expansion 10.17.5). The Wronskian of the dominant terms is
`J_0(h e^{-x})² 𝒲{J_μ(h e^x), Y_μ(h e^x)} = (2/π) J_0(h e^{-x})² → 2/π` (DLMF 10.5.2).

* `p3m_tendsto_besselJ`, `p3m_tendsto_besselY`: `J_λ(x), Y_λ(x) → 0` as `x → +∞`, real `λ`.
* `p3m_F_tail`, `p3m_wronskian_alg`, `p3m_assemble`: the tail estimates.
* `p3m_tendsto_WF`: the Wronskian of the shifted series tends to `(2/π) c_n²`.
* `p3m_wronskian_one_two`: `𝒲{M^{(1)}_ν, M^{(2)}_ν} = 2/π` (DLMF 28.20.21).

# Mathieu functions of noninteger order: definitions (DLMF §§28.12, 28.14)

DLMF §28.12 introduces, for `ν ∉ ℤ`, the eigenvalues `λ_ν(q)` (the values of `a` for which
Mathieu's equation 28.2.1 has a Floquet solution with respect to `ν`, continued analytically
from `λ_ν(0) = ν²`, 28.12.1), the Floquet solutions `me_ν(z, q)` normalized by 28.12.5, and
`ce_ν`, `se_ν` (28.12.12, 28.12.13). For integer order DLMF completes the definitions by
`λ_m = a_m` (`m ≥ 0`), `λ_m = b_{-m}` (`m < 0`) (28.12.3) and `me_n = √2 ce_n`,
`me_{-n} = -√2 i se_n` (28.12.11).

## Design (definitions by choice)

The Fourier series 28.14.1, `me_ν(z, q) = ∑_m c^ν_{2m}(q) e^{i(ν+2m)z}`, turns the Floquet
problem into the three-term recurrence 28.14.4 with the normalization 28.14.5
(`∑ (c^ν_{2m})² = 1`, which is 28.12.5). `IsMeCoeffSeq ν q a c` says that `c : ℤ → ℂ` is an
absolutely summable solution of 28.14.4 for the value `a` and satisfies 28.14.5.

DLMF defines `λ_ν(q)` for `q ≠ 0` "by analytic continuation" from `q = 0`, and fixes the sign
of the coefficients "by continuity" from 28.14.9 (`c^ν_0(0) = 1`). We make this precise
along the **straight segment** `t ↦ t q`, `t ∈ [0, 1]`:

* `IsMathieuLambdaPath ν q Λ c`: `Λ : ℝ → ℂ` and every `t ↦ c t m` are continuous on
  `[0, 1]`, `Λ 0 = ν²`, `c 0 0 = 1`, and for each `t ∈ [0, 1]` the sequence `c t` satisfies
  `IsMeCoeffSeq ν (t q) (Λ t)`.
* `MathieuNormalSegment ν q`: the endpoint `(Λ 1, c 1)` of such a path exists and is unique.
  For `ν ∉ ℤ` this holds when every point `t q` of the segment is a normal value with respect
  to `ν` in DLMF's sense (§28.12(i): the roots of 28.2.16 are simple), in particular for real
  `ν ∉ ℤ` and real `q` (all roots are then real and simple). It is the hypothesis of the
  theorems where DLMF assumes `q` normal; it is stronger than DLMF's pointwise normality.
* `mathieuLambdaData ν q`: that endpoint if `MathieuNormalSegment ν q`, and `(0, 0)` otherwise
  (junk value).

Then, for `ν ∉ ℤ`, `mathieuLambda ν q = λ_ν(q)` is the first component, the Fourier
coefficients `mathieuMeCoeff ν q m = c^ν_{2m}(q)` are the second, and
`mathieuMe ν z q = me_ν(z, q)` is the Fourier series 28.14.1 (a `tsum`; its convergence for
all complex `z` is the theorem 28.14.1).

For integer order the project's eigenvalues and eigenfunctions are defined for real `q` only
(`DLMF.Mathieu.mathieuA`, `mathieuB`, `mathieuCe`, `mathieuSe` in `DLMF.Mathieu.Basic`), so
`mathieuLambda m q` and `mathieuMe m z q` for `m ∈ ℤ` follow 28.12.3 and 28.12.11 when `q` is
real and are junk `0` for nonreal `q`. For integer `ν` the coefficients `mathieuMeCoeff` are
defined as the Fourier coefficients `π⁻¹ ∫₀^π me_ν(x, q) e^{-i(ν+2m)x} dx` of `me_ν`.

`mathieuCeNu`, `mathieuSeNu` are given by 28.12.12, 28.12.13 for every `ν`; DLMF uses them
for `ν ∉ ℤ` only (at integer `ν` they are not `ce_n`, `se_n`).

Argument order is DLMF's: `λ_ν(q)` is `mathieuLambda ν q`, `me_ν(z, q)` is
`mathieuMe ν z q`, `c^ν_{2m}(q)` is `mathieuMeCoeff ν q m` (index `m`, not `2m`).

# Fourier series of the Mathieu functions of noninteger order (DLMF §28.14)

`me_ν(z, q) = ∑_m c^ν_{2m}(q) e^{i(ν+2m)z}` (28.14.1), with the cosine and sine series of

# Mathieu functions of noninteger order: basic properties and Fourier series
(DLMF §§28.12, 28.14)

Statements of DLMF §28.12 (eigenvalues `λ_ν(q)`, Floquet solutions `me_ν(z, q)`, the functions
`ce_ν`, `se_ν`) and §28.14 (Fourier series and their coefficients `c^ν_{2m}(q)`), for the
definitions of `DLMF.Mathieu.Noninteger.Basic`.

Proved here from the definitions (no admissions):

* the values at `q = 0` (28.12.1, 28.12.4, 28.14.9): along the segment `[0, 0]` the only
  continuation is the constant one (a continuous path in the countable set `{(ν + 2m)²}` is
  constant, and the sign of `c_0` is fixed by continuity);
* the symmetries 28.12.2, 28.12.8, 28.12.9, 28.12.10, 28.12.14, 28.12.15, 28.14.7, 28.14.8,
  obtained by transporting continuation paths along the involutions
  `c_m ↦ c_{-m}` (`ν ↦ -ν`), `c_m ↦ (-1)^m c_m` (`q ↦ -q`) and complex conjugation;
* the pseudoperiodicity 28.12.6, the reality of `ce_ν`, `se_ν` for real `ν`, `q`, `z`, and
  the recurrence and normalization 28.14.4–28.14.5 at normal values;
* at normal values: the Floquet property of `me_ν(±z, q)` (§28.12(ii)), the normalization
  28.12.5 and the characteristic equation `cos πν = w_I(π; λ_ν(q), q)` (§28.12(i)). The key
  step (`p1b_summable_norm_mul_exp`) is that an absolutely summable solution of the
  recurrence 28.14.4 decays faster than every exponential, so `∑ c_m e^{i(ν+2m)z}` is entire
  and can be differentiated termwise (`p1b_isMathieuSolution_series`);
* the periodicity of all solutions for rational noninteger `ν` (§28.12(iii)), from the
  Floquet dichotomy of `DLMF.Mathieu.Properties`.

All statements are for `ν ∉ ℤ`, as in DLMF §28.12 ("we now restrict `ν̂ ≠ 0, 1`"); several of
them are false for integer `ν` with DLMF's completion 28.12.3, 28.12.11 (for example
`λ_1(-q) = a_1(-q) = b_1(q) ≠ λ_1(q)`).

**Stronger than DLMF (28.12.10).** DLMF warns that 28.12.10 "is not valid for cuts on the real
axis in the `q`-plane for special complex values of `ν`". With the straight-segment
continuation used here (`DLMF.Mathieu.MathieuNormalSegment`), conjugation maps continuation
paths to continuation paths, and 28.12.10 holds for every `ν ∉ ℤ` and every `q` (when `q` is
not normal along the segment both sides are junk values).

# Mathieu's equation as a separated Sturm–Liouville problem

For real `a`, `q` the basic solutions `w_I(x; a, q)`, `w_II(x; a, q)` restricted to `ℝ` are the
basic solutions `ODE.p2lY V false a`, `ODE.p2lY V true a` of `w'' = (V - a) w` with
`V(x) = 2q cos 2x`, and the spectra of Table 28.2.1 are the separated spectra
`ODE.p2lSpec V (π/2) odd0 oddK`. Sturm's oscillation theorem (`ODE.p2s_oscillation`) then
gives the zero counts of the eigenfunctions in `(0, π/2)` (DLMF §28.2(vi)) and the signs of the
basic solutions at `π/2` (used for 28.2.34–28.2.37).

# The expansions DLMF 28.6.21–28.6.26 of `ce_n`, `se_n` for small `n`

Explicit trial vectors (Rayleigh–Schrödinger perturbation series of the Fourier coefficients)
for `p3q_expand_AE0`, `p3q_expand_AE`, `p3q_expand_AO`, `p3q_expand_BO`, `p3q_expand_BE`:
`√2 ce₀`, `ce₁`, `se₁` to `O(q⁴)`, `ce₂`, `se₂` to `O(q³)` (DLMF 28.6.21–28.6.25), and the
general formula 28.6.26 (and its `se` analogue) at `m = 3, 4, 5`, where the boundary rows of the
recurrences enter.

# The expansion DLMF 28.6.26 of `ce_m`, `se_m` for `m ≥ 6`

A trial vector `T_j(m, q)` (`p3qHT`, `|j| ≤ 2`) rational in `m`, with every row of the generic
recurrence `((m + 2j)² - P) T_j + q (T_{j-1} + T_{j+1})` equal to `q³ p3qHS m q j`
(`p3q_h_row`). For `m ≥ 6` all four recurrences 28.4.5–28.4.8 agree with the generic one on
the rows that meet the support of `T`, so `p3q_expand_AE`, `p3q_expand_AO`, `p3q_expand_BO`,
`p3q_expand_BE` give DLMF 28.6.26 and its `se` analogue with remainder `O(q³)`
(`p3q_ce_ge6`, `p3q_se_ge6`). The cases `m = 3, 4, 5` are in `DLMF.Mathieu.P3qCeSe`.

# The expansion DLMF 28.6.14 of `a_m(q)`, `b_m(q)` for general `m`

For `m ≥ 7` the eigenvalues have the common expansion
`m² + q²/(2(m²-1)) + (5m²+7)q⁴/(32(m²-1)³(m²-4)) + (9m⁴+58m²+29)q⁶/(64(m²-1)⁵(m²-4)(m²-9))`
up to `O(q^{min(m,8)})`. We prove it with the eigenvalue estimate `p3q_eig_isBigO` of
`DLMF.Mathieu.P3qJacobi`, applied to a trial vector `v_i = T_{i-n}(m, q)` whose components
`p3qGT` are rational in `m` (obtained by Rayleigh–Schrödinger perturbation theory). The rows of
the recurrence applied to `T` are the explicit multiples `q^{8-|j|} p3qGS m q j` of `q`-powers
(`p3q_gen_row`). For `m ≥ 8` all four recurrences 28.4.5–28.4.8 agree with the generic
diagonal `(m + 2j)²` on the support of `T`, so the remainder is `O(q⁸)`
(`p3q_mathieuA_ge8`, `p3q_mathieuB_ge8`). At `m = 7` the boundary term `±q` of 28.4.6–28.4.7
meets the support and the remainder is `O(q⁷)` (`p3q_mathieuA_seven`, `p3q_mathieuB_seven`).

# Three-term recurrences of Mathieu type

The Fourier coefficients of the Mathieu functions satisfy the recurrences 28.4.5–28.4.8,
`d_i A_i + q (lo_i + A_{i+1}) = a A_i`, where `lo_0 = 0`, `lo_1 = β A_0`, `lo_i = A_{i-1}`
(`β = 2` for 28.4.5, `β = 1` otherwise). This file contains the elementary theory of such
recurrences used for the small-`q` behaviour (DLMF §28.6, §28.4(vi)):

* `p3q_pair`: the finite Green identity (symmetry of the recurrence with the weights
  `w₀ = β`, `w_i = 1`);
* `p3q_window`: a solution tending to `0` forces some `|a - d_i| ≤ 3|q|` (maximum principle);
* `p3q_decay`: geometric decay `|A_i| ≤ (3|q|)^{|i-n|} |A_n|` away from an isolated diagonal
  entry;
* `p3q_eig_isBigO`: the eigenvalue estimate `a(q) - p(q) = O(q^K)` from a trial vector with
  small residual.

# The eigenvalues `a_n(q)`, `b_n(q)` near `q = 0`

The Fourier coefficients of `ce_n`, `se_n` solve the recurrences 28.4.5–28.4.8, which are
instances of the recurrences of `DLMF.Mathieu.P3qJacobi` (`p3q_rec_AE`, `p3q_rec_AO`,
`p3q_rec_BO`, `p3q_rec_BE`). Their maximum principle puts every eigenvalue within `4|q|` of a
square `k²` of the right parity (`p3q_window_A`, `p3q_window_B`). Together with

* the interlacing `a_m(q) < a_{m+1}(q)`, `b_m(q) < b_{m+1}(q)` (Sturm oscillation:
  `p3q_mathieuA_lt_succ`, `p3q_mathieuB_lt_succ`), and
* for small `q`, a sign change of the boundary functions `w_I'(π/2)`, `w_I(π/2)`,
  `w_II'(π/2)`, `w_II(π/2)` between consecutive squares (`p3q_exists_spec_A`,
  `p3q_exists_spec_B`, from their explicit values at `q = 0`),

this identifies the window of `a_m(q)`: `|a_m(q) - m²| ≤ 4|q|` and `|b_m(q) - m²| ≤ 4|q|` for
small `q` (`p3q_mathieuA_near`, `p3q_mathieuB_near`). In particular `a_m`, `b_m` are continuous
at `q = 0`.

# Expansions of `ce_n(z, q)`, `se_n(z, q)` near `q = 0` from trial vectors

The Fourier coefficients `A_i` of `ce_n`, `se_n` solve one of the recurrences 28.4.5–28.4.8.
Given a trial vector `v` (`v_n = 1`, finitely supported) whose residuals in every row are
`O(q^K)`, the maximum principle of `DLMF.Mathieu.P3qJacobi` gives the uniform estimate
`|A_i/A_n - v_i| ≤ C|q|^K` together with the decay `|A_i/A_n| ≤ (3|q|)^{|i-n|}`
(`p3q_vec_bound`). The normalization 28.4.9–28.4.12 and the sign convention
`ce_n(0, q) > 0`, `se_n'(0, q) > 0` then fix `A_n = c(q) + O(q^K)` for any `c` with
`c(0) = 1` and `c² ∑ w_i v_i² = 1 + O(q^K)`, so that
`ce_n(z, q) = c(q) ∑ v_i cos((2i+δ)z) + O(q^K)` for every fixed `z ∈ ℂ` (`p3q_expand`, and the
class versions `p3q_expand_AE`, `p3q_expand_AE0`, `p3q_expand_AO`, `p3q_expand_BO`,
`p3q_expand_BE`).

# Second solutions `fe_n`, `ge_n` (DLMF §28.5)

`fe_n(z, q) = mathieuFe n z q` and `ge_n(z, q) = mathieuGe n z q` (real `q`) are defined in
`DLMF.Mathieu.Basic` as the odd solution for `a = a_n(q)` and the even solution for
`a = b_n(q)`, normalized by 28.5.5 with `fe_n'(0, q) > 0`, `ge_n(0, q) > 0` (equivalent to DLMF's
sign rule `C_n f_n → sin nz`, `S_n g_n → cos nz` as `q → 0`), together with the factors
`C_n(q) = mathieuFeC n q`, `S_n(q) = mathieuGeS n q` and the periodic parts
`f_n = mathieuFeF n z q`, `g_n = mathieuGeG n z q`.

**Correction (28.5.6, second relation).** With DLMF's own sign rule for `C_n`, `S_n`, the
relation is `C_{2m+1}(-q) = -S_{2m+1}(q)`, not `C_{2m+1}(-q) = S_{2m+1}(q)`: numerically
(direct integration of 28.2.1) `C_1(-1) = -0.95506…`, `S_1(1) = 0.95506…`,
`C_3(-1) = -0.0051465…`, `S_3(1) = 0.0051465…`; analytically, `ge_{2m+1}(π/2 - z, q)` is an odd
multiple `c fe_{2m+1}(z, -q)` plus a multiple of `ce_{2m+1}(z, -q)` with
`sign c = -sign ge'_{2m+1}(π/2, q) = (-1)^m`, which gives `C_{2m+1}(-q) S_{2m+1}(q) < 0`.

**Remark (`n = 0`).** For `n = 0` the normalization 28.5.5 makes `fe_0'(0, q) ≈ 2/|q|` blow up as
`q → 0` (numerically `fe_0'(0, 0.01) = 201.0…`), so 28.5.5 and `fe_0(z, 0) = z` (28.5.7) are not
connected by continuity; `mathieuFe 0 z 0 = z` by definition.

# Zeros of the Mathieu functions (DLMF §28.9)

For real `q`, each of `ce_{2n}`, `se_{2n+1}`, `ce_{2n+1}`, `se_{2n+2}` has exactly `n` zeros in
`0 < z < π/2`, depending continuously on `q`; as `q → ∞` they approach the zeros of
`He_{2n}(q^{1/4}(π - 2z))` (resp. `He_{2n+1}`). For `q > 0` there are also purely imaginary
zeros, and none in the strip `|ℜz| < π/2` off the two axes.

DLMF's further remark that the purely imaginary zeros "correspond uniquely" to those of
`J_m(2√q cos z)` and are "asymptotically equal as `q → 0` and `|ℑz| → ∞`" is too imprecise to
be stated faithfully and is not acquired; the existence of infinitely many purely imaginary
zeros is.

# Functions of matrix argument: definitions (DLMF Chapter 35)

This file holds the definitions of DLMF Chapter 35 (namespace `DLMF.MatrixArgument`).

## Notation of §35.1

* Matrices are `Matrix (Fin m) (Fin m) ℝ`. The space `𝓢` of real symmetric matrices is Tau
  Ceti's `selfAdjoint.submodule ℝ (Matrix (Fin m) (Fin m) ℝ)` (abbreviation `SymMatrix m`), and
  DLMF's `dX = ∏_{j ≤ k} dx_{j,k}` is Tau Ceti's `TauCeti.symmetricLebesgue m`, the push-forward
  of Lebesgue measure on the `m(m+1)/2` upper-triangular coordinates. With this normalization
  Tau Ceti proves `∫_Ω etr(-X) |X|^{a-(m+1)/2} dX = Γ_m(a)` (DLMF 35.3.1, real `a`).
* `Ω` is `posDefCone m`, and DLMF's matrix interval `S < X < T` is `matrixInterval S T`.
* `etr X = exp(tr X)` is `etr`; `|(X)_j|` is `leadingMinor X j`; the spectral norm `‖T‖` is
  `matrixSpectralNorm T`.
* The orthogonal group `O(m)` is Mathlib's `Matrix.orthogonalGroup (Fin m) ℝ`. It is compact
  (`instCompactSpaceOrthogonalGroup`), and its normalized Haar measure `dH` is
  `orthogonalHaar m`, the Haar measure giving the whole group mass `1`.
* Integrals with a convergence claim use `HasIntegralOn s f I`: `f` is integrable on `s` for
  `dX` and its integral is `I`, so the Lean convention that a non-integrable function has
  integral `0` never enters a statement.

## Partitions and zonal polynomials (§35.4)

* A partition `κ = (k₁, …, k_m)` is a nonincreasing vector `κ : Fin m → ℕ` (DLMF's definition,
  with at most `m` nonzero parts); `partitions m k` is the finite set of partitions of weight
  `|κ| = k`, and `partitionLength κ` is `ℓ(κ)`.
* `partitionalShiftedFactorial a κ = [a]_κ = ∏_j (a - (j-1)/2)_{k_j}` (35.4.1), over any field.
* `zonalPolynomialAtOne κ` is the right-hand side of 35.4.2, and `zonalPolynomial κ T` is the
  defining integral 35.4.3 over `O(m)`, for every real matrix `T`. This is DLMF's own definition
  (35.4.2–35.4.3), so it is honest; the properties of §35.4(ii) are theorems. The two factors
  `|T|^{k_m}` and `∏_{j<m} |(HTH⁻¹)_j|^{k_j - k_{j+1}}` of 35.4.3 are combined as
  `∏_{j=1}^{m} |(HTHᵀ)_j|^{k_j - k_{j+1}}` with `k_{m+1} = 0`, using `|HTHᵀ| = |T|`.
* DLMF's `Z_κ` is a function on `𝓢`. Where DLMF evaluates a function of matrix argument at a
  product such as `TX` with `X ∈ Ω`, meaning the function of the (real) eigenvalues of `TX`,
  the statements use the symmetric matrix `X^{1/2} T X^{1/2}` (`CFC.sqrt X * T * CFC.sqrt X`),
  which has the same eigenvalues.

* `besselA ν T` (35.5.1–35.5.2), `besselB ν T` (35.5.3), `kummerPsi a b T` (35.6.2),

# Functions of additive number theory (DLMF §27.13)

Waring's `g(k)` and `G(k)` (§27.13(iii)) are defined as infima of the admissible numbers of
`k`th powers (`waringSmallG`, `waringBigG`); `sInf ∅ = 0` is only a junk value, Hilbert's
theorem (`waring_hilbert`) shows that the sets are nonempty. `r_k(n)` (27.13.3) is
`sumSquaresCount k n`, the number of `(x₁, …, x_k) ∈ ℤ^k` with `x₁² + ⋯ + x_k² = n`. DLMF's
`ϑ(x) = 1 + 2∑ x^{m²}` (27.13.4) is `jacobiThetaSeries x`; it is Mathlib's `jacobiTheta τ` at
`x = e^{πiτ}` (`jacobiTheta_eq_jacobiThetaSeries`) and the project's `θ₃(0, q)`.

Goldbach's conjecture and the Hardy–Littlewood conjectures on `G(k)` are open: they are named
as propositions (`GoldbachConjecture`, `HardyLittlewoodWaringConjecture`) and not asserted.
Lagrange's four-square theorem is Mathlib's `Nat.sum_four_squares`.

# Asymptotic formulas: partial sums (DLMF §27.11)

DLMF's `∑_{n≤x}` is the sum over `1 ≤ n ≤ ⌊x⌋` (`Finset.Icc 1 ⌊x⌋₊`) and `∑_{p≤x}` the sum over
the primes `p ≤ ⌊x⌋` (`Nat.primesLE ⌊x⌋₊`). The error terms `O(g(x))` are
`Asymptotics.IsBigO atTop`; DLMF's "for all `x ≥ 1`" (resp. `x ≥ 2`) uniform bounds imply these
and conversely they follow from them when both sides are bounded on compact intervals, which is
the case here. Constants that DLMF only asserts to exist (`A` in 27.11.8, `B` in 27.11.9, `C` in
27.11.12) are existentially quantified. `γ` is `Real.eulerMascheroniConstant`.

Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions (§27.11 after 27.11.11) is Mathlib's
`Nat.infinite_setOfPred_prime_and_modEq` (`Nat.setOf_prime_and_eq_mod_infinite`).

# Dirichlet characters, quadratic characters, periodic functions (DLMF §§27.8–27.10)

DLMF defines a Dirichlet character mod `k` as a function on the positive integers with the
four properties 27.8.1–27.8.4 (`IsDirichletCharacterFn`). Mathlib's
`DirichletCharacter ℂ k` (a multiplicative character of `ZMod k`) is the same object:
`DirichletCharacter.isDirichletCharacterFn` shows that `n ↦ χ n` has the four properties.
Mathlib's `legendreSym p a` and `jacobiSym a P` (`J(a | P)`) are DLMF's `(a|p)` and `(a|P)`.

The exponentials `e^{2πimn/k}` of §27.10 are written `Complex.exp (2πi m n / k)`;
`ramanujanSum k n` is `c_k(n)` (27.10.4) and `gaussSumDLMF χ n` is `G(n, χ)` (27.10.9),
DLMF's sum over `m = 1, …, k`. Mathlib's `gaussSum χ ψ` sums over `ZMod k` with an additive
character `ψ`; `G(n, χ)` is `gaussSum χ (ZMod.stdAddChar.mulShift n)`.

# Euler products and Dirichlet series (DLMF §27.4)

The Dirichlet series `F(s) = ∑_{n≥1} f(n) n^{-s}` of DLMF 27.4.4 is Mathlib's `LSeries f s`
(a totalized `tsum`, the term at `n = 0` being `0`); convergence is asserted with
`LSeriesHasSum f s a`, which is `HasSum` of the terms `f(n)/n^s`, `n ≥ 1`. Mathlib's Euler
products (`EulerProduct.eulerProduct_hasProd`,
`EulerProduct.eulerProduct_completely_multiplicative_hasProd`, `riemannZeta_eulerProduct_hasProd`)

`LSeries_vonMangoldt_eq_deriv_riemannZeta_div` give 27.4.5 and 27.4.12. All half-plane
conditions are DLMF's.

# Divisor sums and Lambert series (DLMF §§27.6–27.7)

Divisor sums are written `∑ d ∈ n.divisors, …`; DLMF's `∑_{d²∣n}` is the sum over the divisors
`d` of `n` with `d² ∣ n`. DLMF 27.6.2 is stated by DLMF for `n > 1`; it holds for `n = 1` as
well and is proved for all `n ≥ 1`. Lambert series (27.7.1) are written with the index shifted
to `n + 1 ≥ 1`; for `|x| < 1` every series of §27.7 converges absolutely, and the identities

# Functions of multiplicative number theory (DLMF §§27.1–27.3)

DLMF §27.2 introduces the number-theoretic functions of Chapter 27 and §27.3 their
multiplicative properties. Most of them are Mathlib's:

* `ν(n)` is `ArithmeticFunction.cardDistinctFactors` (`ω`), `Ω` is `cardFactors`;
* `φ(n)` is `Nat.totient`, `d(n) = σ₀(n)` and `σ_k(n)` (natural `k`) are
  `ArithmeticFunction.sigma`;
* `μ`, `λ`, `Λ` are `ArithmeticFunction.moebius`, `ArithmeticFunction.liouville`,
  `ArithmeticFunction.vonMangoldt`;
* `π(n)` is `Nat.primeCounting`, the `n`th prime `p_n` is `Nat.nth Nat.Prime (n - 1)` (DLMF
  starts at `p₁ = 2`, Mathlib's `Nat.nth` at index `0`).

New here: the real-argument prime counting function `primePi x = π(⌊x⌋)` (DLMF 27.2.2, `x`
real), `nthPrime`, the power sums `φ_k(n)` of the reduced residues (`totientPowerSum`, 27.2.6),
the multiplicative divisor function `d_k(n)` (`divisorCountK`, the number of ordered
factorizations into `k` factors), the divisor function `σ_α(n)` for complex `α` (`sigmaC`,
27.2.10) and Jordan's function `J_k(n)` (`jordanTotient`, 27.2.11), together with the
definitions of multiplicative and completely multiplicative functions on the positive
integers (27.3.1, 27.3.9).

DLMF's functions live on the positive integers `n = 1, 2, …`; the Lean definitions are total
on `ℕ` and all statements carry `0 < n` (or `n ≠ 0`) where DLMF has `n ≥ 1`. Tables 27.2.1
and 27.2.2 (§27.2(ii)) are tabulated values and are not acquired (excluded: numerical).

**Correction (27.3, first sentence).** DLMF says that, except for `ν`, `Λ`, `p_n` and `π(x)`,
the functions of §27.2 are multiplicative. The power sums `φ_k` with `k ≥ 1` are not:
`φ₁(2)φ₁(3) = 1 · 3 ≠ 6 = φ₁(6)` (`totientPowerSum_one_not_multiplicative`). The remaining
functions (`⌊1/n⌋`, `φ = φ₀`, `d`, `d_k`, `σ_α`, `J_k`, `μ`, `λ`) are multiplicative.

**Correction (27.3.6).** For complex `α` the hypothesis `α ≠ 0` does not keep the denominators
`p^α - 1` away from zero (`p^α = 1` for `α = 2πi m / ln p`); the formula is stated under
`p^α ≠ 1` for every prime `p ∣ n`, which holds for every real `α ≠ 0`.

# Products of binomial series

`binomSeries a = ∑ (a)_n / n! Xⁿ` is the formal binomial series `(1 - X)^{-a}`. It satisfies
`(1 - X) G' = a G` and `G_a G_b = G_{a+b}` (Chu–Vandermonde). The product
`binomProductSeries a b u = G_a(uX) G_b(X/u)` satisfies a first-order differential equation,
which gives a three-term recurrence for its coefficients. The coefficients are therefore
identified with any sequence satisfying the same recurrence and initial values; this is used
for the Gegenbauer, Meixner–Pollaczek and Pollaczek polynomials. For `‖u z‖, ‖z / u‖ < 1`
the coefficient series sums to `(1 - u z)^{-a} (1 - z/u)^{-b}`.

# Gegenbauer polynomials and the formal series `G_λ(wX) G_λ(X/w)`

Let `G_λ = ∑ (λ)_n / n! Xⁿ` be the formal binomial series `(1 - X)^{-λ}`. The product
`G_λ(wX) G_λ(X/w)` is the formal Gegenbauer generating function at `x = (w + w⁻¹)/2`.
It satisfies the generating-function differential equation, whose coefficients give the
three-term recurrence. Comparing with `ultrasphPoly_recurrence` identifies its coefficients
with `C_n^{(λ)}((w + w⁻¹)/2)` for `Re λ > -1/2`. This gives the trigonometric sum
DLMF 18.5.11 (`ultrasphPoly_cos_sum`) and, with `|w| = 1` and binomial series, the
generating functions. The explicit sum DLMF 18.5.10 (`ultrasphPoly_finite_sum`) is proved
separately: its terms satisfy the same three-term recurrence. Comparing coefficients
with the Jacobi hypergeometric sum in `x²` then gives the quadratic transformations
DLMF 18.7.15–18.7.16; the Jacobi forms 18.7.13–18.7.14 follow by the Gegenbauer–Jacobi
relation, extended to `α = -1/2` by continuity in `α`. The multiplicativity `G_λ G_μ = G_{λ+μ}`
(Chu–Vandermonde, `poch_add_binomial_sum`) gives the convolution identities in `Series.lean`.

# Hermite polynomials of large degree at a fixed point

The Hermite function `u = e^{-x²/2} H_n` solves `u'' + (2n+1) u = x² u`. The Volterra
perturbation estimate `ODE.norm_sub_oscFree_le'` with `ω = √(2n+1)` and `g = x²` compares

explicitly. This gives the leading term of the large-`n` expansion at fixed `x`
(Beals–Wong, §13.1; Szegő, (8.22.8)) with an explicit error bound:

other declarations below still include admitted results.

The Hermite cosine and sine transforms 18.17.23 and 18.17.27 integrate by parts

# Bounds for individual Jacobi zero angles

Beals–Wong Theorem 5.5.1: if `α², β² ≤ 1/4` and `cos θ_k` are the zeros in
increasing angular order, then `(k-1+γ)π/(n+γ) ≤ θ_k ≤ kπ/(n+γ)`,
where `γ = (α+β+1)/2`. The angular Liouville transformation is proved specifically
for the Jacobi polynomial, and the existing Sturm comparison theorem controls the gaps.
A uniform improvement of the comparison coefficient gives strict inequalities unless
both squared parameters equal `1/4`.

# The formal Laguerre generating series

`laguerreSeries α x = ∑ L_n^{(α)}(x) tⁿ` (with `laguerreExtended`) is the unique formal
solution with constant term one of the generating-function equation
`(1 - t)² f' = ((α + 1)(1 - t) - x) f` (`LaguerreODE`). The equation is equivalent to the
three-term recurrence. Products of solutions solve the equation with parameters
`α + β + 1` and `x + y`, which gives the Laguerre addition theorem for `Re α, Re β > -1`.
Both sides of that theorem are entire in `α` and `β`, so the identity theorem removes the
restriction.

# The finite Legendre addition kernel

Derivative ladders and the differentiated Legendre equation prove the three-term
recurrence of the finite angular kernel. Identifying its first two values gives
Legendre's addition theorem, including vanishing sines and all boundary indices.
The proof uses the Mathlib contributors’ analytic differentiation, finite-sum,
and trigonometric APIs. The angle-free kernel permits complex coordinates
satisfying `s² = 1-x²` and `t² = 1-y²`.

# The singular integral of a Legendre polynomial

The quotient `(P_n(x)-P_n(t))/|x-t|` is interval integrable: on either side
of `t=x` it agrees with a continuous divided slope up to sign. The Mathlib
contributors’ `dslope` continuity and interval-integral congruence theorems
justify the split without changing the totalized diagonal value.

The degree recurrence reduces the integral to a signed Legendre integral.
The derivative ladders supply its primitive, and the resulting recurrence
has eigenvalue twice the finite harmonic sum (DLMF 18.17.44).

# Generating functions, connection formulas, and linearization

Statements from NIST DLMF Chapter 18, each tagged with its equation number by `@[dlmf]`.
Jacobi and Gegenbauer statements retain regularity hypotheses because the project's
hypergeometric definitions do not implement continuation in singular parameters.
The adjacent Jacobi generating function combines the local parameter-raising relation
with Mathlib’s shifted-series API and the proved Gegenbauer generating function.
The finite Gegenbauer proofs combine the local explicit sums and recurrence with
the Mathlib contributors’ finite-sum, factorial, binomial and polynomial APIs.

The Jacobi generating function 18.12.1 (`jacobi_generating_function`) follows from the
coefficient form of the Lagrange–Bürmann formula (`Complex.lagB_hasSum_iteratedDeriv`):
`P_n^{(α,β)}(x) = [tⁿ] F(t) φ(t)ⁿ` with `φ(t) = (1 + (x+1)t/2)(1 + (x-1)t/2)` and
`F(t) = (1 + (x+1)t/2)^α (1 + (x-1)t/2)^β` (by 18.5.8), the root of `t = z φ(t)` being
`w = 2z/(1 - xz + R)`, `R = (1 - 2xz + z²)^{1/2}`. This gives the identity for small `|z|`;
it extends to `|z| < 1` because the right side is holomorphic there
(`Complex.lagB_hasSum_of_differentiableOn`). The weighted form 18.12.3
(`jacobi_weighted_generating_function`) is proved for small `|z|` by summing an absolutely
convergent double series in two ways, and then on the star-shaped domain
`{|z| < 1, |2(x+1)z/(1+z)²| < 1}` by the identity theorem, the left side having radius of
convergence at least `1` by 18.12.1.

Brafman's generating function 18.12.2_5 (`jacobi_brafman_generating_function`) follows from
Bailey's product formula for Appell's `F₄` (`DLMF.Hypergeometric.appF4_bailey`): with
`U = (1 - R - z)/2`, `V = (1 - R + z)/2` one has `U(1 - V) = (x-1)z/2`, `V(1 - U) = (x+1)z/2`,
and the antidiagonal sums of `F₄((x-1)z/2, (x+1)z/2)` are the Jacobi terms by 18.5.8. The
bound `|U|², |V|² ≤ |z|` on the unit disc (`jacB_norm_sq_le`, from `Re(R conj(1 ∓ z)) > 0`
by a connectedness argument) makes the right side holomorphic there, so the hypotheses
`|U|, |V| < 1` of the statement are redundant.

# Sonine–Pólya bounds for the classical differential equations

Sonine's function `S = y² + (k/φ) y'²` for the self-adjoint form `(k y')' + φ y = 0` (see
`DLMFMathlib.Analysis.ODE.SoninePolya`) applied to the Jacobi, Hermite and Laguerre equations
(Szegő, §§7.2, 7.31–7.32; Beals–Wong, §3.5). Here `k` vanishes at the ends of the Jacobi and
Laguerre intervals, so `S` is written directly in terms of the equation in its usual form
and differentiated by hand. The results are stated for arbitrary solutions `y` with derivatives
`y'`, `y''`, so they apply to the classical polynomials once their differential equations are
supplied.

* `jacobi_ode_abs_le_max`: if `λ > 0` and `α + β + 1 > 0`, a solution of
  `(1 - x²) y'' + (β - α - (α + β + 2) x) y' + λ y = 0` satisfies
  `|y x| ≤ max |y (-1)| |y 1|` on `[-1, 1]`. This is the core of DLMF 18.14.1–2.
* `jacobi_ode_abs_le_right`: the one-sided form `|y x| ≤ |y 1|` when
  `β - α ≤ (α + β + 1) x` on `(-1, 1)` (the case `α + β + 1 ≤ 0 ≤ 2α + 1`).
* `jacobi_ode_sq_le_zero`, `jacobi_ode_sq_lt_zero`: for the symmetric equation with
  `2a + 1 ≤ 0` (Gegenbauer `λ ≤ 0`), `y x ² ≤ y 0 ² + y' 0 ² / λ`, strictly on `(0, 1]` when
  `2a + 1 < 0`; the core of DLMF 18.14.5–6.
* `hermite_ode_abs_le`: for `y'' - 2 x y' + λ y = 0`, `λ > 0`, and a critical point `b ≥ 0`,
  `|y| ≤ |y b|` on `[a, b]` with `0 ≤ a`: the relative maxima of `|H_n|` increase on `x ≥ 0`.
* `laguerre_ode_abs_le_right`, `laguerre_ode_abs_le_left`: for
  `x y'' + (α + 1 - x) y' + λ y = 0`, the relative maxima of `|y|` decrease on
  `[0, α + 1/2]` and increase on `[α + 1/2, ∞)`.

# Combinatorics and orthogonal polynomials (DLMF §32.14, §32.15)

§32.14: the Baik–Deift–Johansson theorem: the length `ℓ_N(π)` of the longest increasing
subsequence of a uniformly random permutation, centred by `2√N` and scaled by `N^{1/6}`,
converges in distribution to the Tracy–Widom distribution `F(s)` of 32.14.2, built from the
Hastings–McLeod solution of `PII` with `α = 0` (32.14.3–32.14.4). The random-matrix
interpretation of `F` (Gaussian Unitary Ensemble, §32.14 second paragraph) is not formalized.

§32.15: for the weight `exp(-ξ⁴/4 - zξ²)` of 32.15.1 the squared recurrence coefficients
`u_n = a_n²` (`freudRecurrenceSq`, Hankel-determinant form) satisfy the discrete equation
32.15.3 and, as functions of `z`, `PIV` with `α = -n/2`, `β = -n²/2`. Both were checked
numerically (moments by quadrature, `n ≤ 3`, residuals below `10⁻³⁹`).

All statements are admitted.

Mathlib's Picard–Lindelöf and local Lipschitz theorems apply to the autonomous

uniqueness of germs at every initial value, as used in Beals–Wong §15.3.

scaling reduction of sine-Gordon (32.13.7) and the travelling-wave reduction of Boussinesq
(32.13.9–32.13.10) are proved as PDE statements, with the principal branch of `(3t)^{-1/3}`
(`3t` in the slit plane), from the chain rule and `d/dt (3t)^{-1/3} = -((3t)^{-1/3})⁴`.

The ODE parts are proved: the sine-Gordon reduction `zv'' + v' = sin v` gives `PIII` with
`α = -β = 1/2`, `γ = δ = 0` for `w = exp(-iv)` (§32.13(ii)); the similarity reduction of KdV,
`W'' = -3W² + λz + C`, is solved by `W(z) = -2μ²w(μz - C/(2μ⁴))` with `w` a solution of `PI`
and `μ⁵ = -λ/2` (the "expressible in terms of `PI`" of §32.13(i), for `λ ≠ 0`); and the
Boussinesq travelling-wave equation 32.13.10 with `A ≠ 0` is solved by
`v(z) = λ²w(λz + μ) - (c² - 1)/12` with `w` a solution of `PI`, `λ⁵ = A` (§32.13(iii)). The
case `A = 0` (Weierstrass function) is not formalized.

# Special function solutions of the Painlevé equations (DLMF §32.10)

DLMF normalization (`DLMF.Painleve.Basic`). For each of `PII`–`PVI`, the Riccati equation of
§32.10 (the case `n = 0` of the parameter conditions 32.10.11, 32.10.15, 32.10.23, 32.10.28)
is proved to imply the Painlevé equation. The Airy solutions 32.10.4–32.10.6 of `PII` are
proved, bridging to the Beals–Wong construction of `DLMF.Painleve.Airy` (`airyPII`, with the
cube-root scale `k = -2^{-1/3}`, `k³ = -1/2`); existence for every `α = n + 1/2` (32.10.2) is
the Airy hierarchy `airyPIIHierarchy`. The `α = 5/2` member 32.10.7 and the Wronskian formula
32.10.8–32.10.9 are admitted. The Hermite solutions 32.10.20–32.10.21 and the error-function
solutions 32.10.16, 32.10.22 of `PIV` are proved. The Bessel, parabolic cylinder and
hypergeometric solutions of the Riccati equations (32.10.13–32.10.14, 32.10.18–32.10.19,
32.10.30–32.10.31) are proved from the linear ODEs of `J_ν`, `Y_ν`, `U`, `V` and `₂F₁`; the
Whittaker solution 32.10.26–32.10.27 and Picard's solution 32.10.32–32.10.34 are admitted
(the special-function solutions were verified numerically with mpmath, residuals about
`10⁻³⁰`).

**Source correction.** DLMF introduces the Riccati equation 32.10.29 of `PVI` with "If `n = 1`";
it is the case `n = 0` of 32.10.28, i.e. `a + b + c + d = 1` (verified symbolically: the
Riccati equation implies `PVI` exactly when `(1 - a - b - c)² = d² = 1 - 2δ`). The statement
`painleveVI_of_riccati` uses `δ = (1 - (1 - a - b - c)²)/2`.

The phrase "expressible in terms of special functions" (32.10.1 and the "iff" of 32.10.2,
32.10.11, 32.10.15–32.10.16, 32.10.23–32.10.24, 32.10.28) is not formalized; the existence

Beals–Wong (15.3.10)–(15.3.11) imply that `u = v/w` solves `PII(c)`
wherever `w` is nonzero. The proof is local differentiation and does not
assume or claim the global existence of entire `v` and `w`.

# Painlevé transcendents: DLMF Chapter 32 and Beals–Wong Chapter 15

The DLMF modules (`Basic`, `Basic.Solutions`, `Equations`, `BacklundDLMF`, `Hamiltonian`,
`Isomonodromy`, `RationalDLMF`, `ElementarySolutions`, `SpecialSolutions`, `RealAsymptotics`,
`Reductions`, `Combinatorics`) state DLMF Chapter 32 in its own normalization; see

`Poles`, `Tau`) follow Beals–Wong Chapter 15.

The parameter convention is `u'' = 2u³ + xu - c` for `PII(c)`.

This development proves local real existence and uniqueness, the Bäcklund reflection
and integer shifts, rational solutions for every integer parameter, and meromorphic
Airy-based solutions for every half-integer parameter. It also proves the Lax
compatibility calculation, the energy derivative, a tau-quotient converse, and simple
pole/residue restrictions for solutions already known to be meromorphic.

The rational classification converse and uniqueness, global meromorphic continuation
of arbitrary solutions, Stokes/isomonodromy theory, and the real connection formulas
of Beals–Wong §15.8 are not yet formalized. The Airy scale satisfies `k³ = -1/2`;
this corrects the substitution printed on page 407.

# Contour tools for the parabolic cylinder integrals (DLMF 12.5.5–12.5.7)

* Vertical lines `t = c + iy`, `c > 0`: a Gaussian majorant `pcfCt_dom` for
  `e^{-zt+t²/2} t^p`, locally uniform in `z` and `p` (`pcfCt_vert_le`), and the shifted
  Gaussian integral `∫ e^{-wt+t²/2} dy = √(2π) e^{-w²/2}` (`pcfCt_gauss_vertical`).
* DLMF 12.5.6 in integral form (`pcfCt_vertical`): for `re a > -1/2`, Euler's integral
  `Γ(a+1/2) t^{-a-1/2} = ∫₀^∞ s^{a-1/2} e^{-ts} ds` (complex scale, `integral_cpow_mul_cexp_neg_mul_Ioi`),
  Fubini and the Gaussian reduce the vertical integral to DLMF 12.5.1 (`pcfU_eq_integral`);
  holomorphy in `a` (`pcfCt_vertical_differentiable`) and the identity theorem give all `a`.
* The horizontal lines `t = x ± ic` of DLMF 12.5.7 are the vertical lines rotated by `±π/2`
  (`pcfCt_horizontal_upper`, `pcfCt_horizontal_lower`).
* The Hankel loop of DLMF 12.5.5: in the variable `w = log t` the loop integrand is the entire
  function `pcfCt_F`, and the circle part `pcfCt_C` at radius `r` is its integral over the
  segment `log r + iθ`, `|θ| ≤ π`. Cauchy's theorem on the rectangle between two radii gives
  `pcfCt_C r₂ - pcfCt_C r₁ = κ(a) ∫_{r₁}^{r₂} t^{a-1/2} e^{-t²/2-zt} dt` (`pcfCt_C_sub`), with
  the jump `κ(a) = e^{-iπ(a-1/2)} - e^{iπ(a-1/2)}`. For `re a > -1/2` the circle shrinks to zero
  (`pcfCt_loop_limit_of_re`), and DLMF 12.5.1 with the reflection formula
  (`pcfCt_kappa_Gamma`) gives the value; holomorphy in `a` of the tail and of the circle part
  extends it to all `a` (`pcfCt_loop_value`).
* The kernel of DLMF 12.12.3 (`pcfCt_kernel`): for `0 < re μ < 2`, `x > 0`, `σ ≥ 0`,
  `∫₀^∞ t^{μ-1} cos(tσ + π/2 - πμ/2)/(x²+t²) dt = (π/2) x^{μ-2} e^{-xσ}`. In `w = log t` the
  two exponential halves are integrals of `pcfCt_Phi` over the lines `Im w = 0` and `Im w = π`;
  the vertical-shift residue lemma `Complex.barnesRes_vertical_shift` (after rotating by `i`)
  relates them through the residue at `w = log x + iπ/2` (`pcfCt_kernel_shift`).
* `pcfCt_U_decay`: `|e^{-t²/4} U(a,t)| ≤ M e^{-t}` on the real line, locally uniformly in `a`.

# Tools for the cylinder Laplace integrals (DLMF 12.5.2–12.5.3)

The integral `pcfInt_F c p w = ∫₀^∞ t^{c-1} e^{-t} (w+2t)^p dt` is holomorphic in `w` on the
slit plane (`pcfInt_differentiableOn`, by locally uniform domination). For real `x > 0` the
Laplace integral of Kummer's `U` (`kummerU_laplace`) rescales to it (`pcfInt_laplace_scale`),
giving DLMF 12.5.2–12.5.3 on the positive axis (`pcfInt_U_real_2`, `pcfInt_U_real_3`); the
identity theorem (`pcfInt_eq_of_real`) then extends them to the right half-plane.

For DLMF 12.12.1–12.12.2 the substitution `x = t²/2` (`pcfInt_sq_half_subst`) turns the
integrands into the Laplace kernel of `U(a/2+1/4, 1/2, x)` (`pcfInt_integrand_1`,
`pcfInt_integrand_2`), whose transform is DLMF 13.10.7 (`laplace_kummerU_gauss`); at `z = 2`
the resulting `₂F₁(-b,b;1/2;1/2)` is evaluated by DLMF 15.4.12 (`pcfInt_laplace_two`).

For DLMF 12.5.8 the Barnes integral of Kummer's `U` (DLMF 13.4.17, `kummerU_barnes`) and the
duplication formula give the real case (`pcfInt_B_real`); a uniform bound for the integrand
(`pcfInt_norm_B_le`) gives holomorphy on the sector `|arg z| < 3π/4` (`pcfInt_B_differentiableOn`)
and the identity theorem the general case (`pcfInt_B_integral`).

# Sector asymptotics of `U(a,z)` past `|ph z| = π/2` (DLMF 12.9)

For `re a > -1/2` and `|θ| < π/4`, rotating the ray in the Laplace integral DLMF 12.5.1 gives

`Γ(1/2 + a) e^{z²/4} U(a,z) = e^{iθ} ∫₀^∞ e^{-z e^{iθ} r} (r e^{iθ})^{a-1/2} e^{-(r e^{iθ})²/2} dr`

for every complex `z` (`pcfSect_integral_rotate`). Watson's lemma along the rotated rays
(`hasAsymptoticExpansion_integral_cexp_smul_rotate_comap`) then gives the Poincaré expansion
DLMF 12.9.1 of `e^{z²/4} z^{a+1/2} U(a,z)` uniformly in `|ph z| ≤ 3π/4 - δ`; the recurrence
DLMF 12.8.1 removes the restriction on `a` (`pcfSect_U_sector`).

We also record the expansion along the logarithmic plane (`pcfSect_U_logWedge`), which is the
input for the two-exponential expansions DLMF 12.9.3–12.9.4 obtained from the connection
formulas 12.2.19–12.2.20, and DLMF 12.9.2 for `V(a,z)` from 12.2.20 (`pcfSect_V_sector`); there
the `U(a,z)` contribution is exponentially small (`pcfSect_exp_neg_sq_mul_cpow_isBigO`).
The expansion 12.9.1 holds for every `δ > 0` (no upper bound on `δ` is needed).

# Olver's uniform expansion of `U(-½μ², μt√2)` for `t > 1` (DLMF 12.10.3)

With `a = -½μ²` and `z = μ t √2`, Weber's equation becomes `d²w/dt² = μ⁴ (t²-1) w`. We apply the
Liouville–Green expansion with error bounds (`LiouvilleGreen.exists_solution_expansion_exp`,
Olver, *Asymptotics and Special Functions*, Ch. 10, Thm. 3.1) with `u = μ²`,
`A = (t²-1)^{-1/4}`, `g = 0` and the coefficients `(-1)^s A_s(t)`, `A_s = u_s(t)/(t²-1)^{3s/2}`
(DLMF 12.10.8). The polynomial recursions DLMF 12.10.11–12.10.12 are exactly the Liouville–Green
recursion `A² A_s'' + 2AA'A_s' + AA''A_s = 2A_{s+1}'` (`pcfLG_recursion`). The constructed
solution is identified with `U` as the recessive solution at `+∞`: a Wronskian argument
(`pcfLG_eq_mul_of_tendsto`) together with the large-`t` limit
`U/(A e^{-μ²ξ}) → h(μ)` (`pcfLG_tendsto_U_div`, from DLMF 12.9.1). The normalizer is
`g = h/Φ(μ²)`, where `Φ` realizes the formal series `∑ c_s u^{-s}`, `c_s = lim_{t→∞} A_s(t)`
(`pcfLG_exists_asymptotic`, a Borel-type lemma).

## Main results

* `pcfLG_core`: the uniform estimate for each truncation order.
* `pcf_negative_parameter_uniform_U`: DLMF 12.10.3 with the normalizer
  `g(μ) ∼ h(μ)/∑ c_s μ^{-2s}`.

DLMF 12.10.14 (`IsCylinderGNormalizer`) additionally requires the identity
`(∑ c_s u^{-s})·(1 + ½∑ γ_s (u/2)^{-s}) ∼ 1`, which is not proved here.

# Uniform expansions of parabolic cylinder functions: second stage

A general form of the recessive Liouville–Green core of `DLMF.ParabolicCylinder.UniformLG`
(`pcfLG2_core`): for any amplitude `A` with `ξ' = A⁻²` on `(b, ∞)`, any coefficient family
satisfying the Liouville–Green recursion with uniform bounds and limits at `+∞`, and any solution
`U` of `U'' = μ⁴A⁻⁴U` normalised at `+∞`, the expansion of `U` and of `U'` holds with explicit
constants. It is applied here to Temme's form of the expansion of `U(-½μ², μt√2)` (DLMF 12.10.31),
whose coefficients `φ_s(τ(t))` satisfy the Liouville–Green recursion by the polynomial recursion
DLMF 12.10.33 (`pcfLG2_temme_rec`) and tend to `0` at `t = ∞` for `s ≥ 1`, so that the
normalizer is exactly `h(μ)`.

For positive parameter `a = ½μ²` the equation `w'' = μ⁴(t²+1)w` has no turning points, and the
core applies on every half-line `(b, ∞)` with constants uniform in `b`
(`pcfLG2_pos_core`), with the real coefficients `Ā_s = Re(i^s u_s(-it))/(t²+1)^{3s/2}`
(DLMF 12.10.27). Comparing the limits at `+∞` (DLMF 12.9.1) and at `-∞` (DLMF 12.2.15 with
DLMF 12.9.1–12.9.2) gives the formal identity `(∑ γ_j (u/2)^{-j})(∑ c_s u^{-s}) =
∑ (-1)^s c_s u^{-s}` (`pcfLG2_gamma_identity`), where `c_s` is the coefficient of `t^{3s}` in
`u_s`. Since the even `c_s`, `s ≥ 2`, vanish, this yields DLMF 12.10.14 for the normalizer of
DLMF 12.10.3.

# The polylogarithm (Duverney Chapter 8; DLMF §25.12)

`Li_n(z) = ∑_{k ≥ 1} z^k/k^n` on the closed unit disk (`n ≥ 2`) or the open disk. This file
proves `Li₁(z) = -log(1-z)`, the termwise derivative `Li_{n+1}' = Li_n/z`, `Li_n(1) = ζ(n)`, the
duplication formula `Li_n(z) + Li_n(-z) = 2^{1-n} Li_n(z²)`, the value
`Li_n(-1) = -(1 - 2^{1-n})ζ(n)`, and the identification with Mathlib's `expZeta` on the circle.

# The real dilogarithm (Duverney §8.1.2; DLMF §25.12(i))

`Real.dilog x = ∫₀ˣ -log(1-t)/t dt` is defined for real `x ≤ 1`; the kernel is extended by its limit
`1` at `t = 0` (`dslope`). On `[-1, 1]` it agrees with the series `Li₂` of `DLMF.Polylog.Basic`;
the endpoints use integrability of the nonnegative kernel against the continuous series. Euler's
reflection formula, Landen's identity, the inversion formula and the duplication formula follow by
the derivative-equals-zero method, giving `Li₂(1/2)` and the golden-ratio values.

# The real trilogarithm (Duverney §8.1.3)

`Real.trilog x = ∫₀ˣ Li₂(t)/t dt` for real `x ≤ 1`, with the kernel extended by `1` at `t = 0`.
It agrees with the series `Li₃` on `[-1, 1]` (on the open interval by the derivative, at the
endpoints by continuity), so `Li₃(1) = ζ(3)` and `Li₃(-1) = -¾ζ(3)`. Landen's identity for `Li₃`
(Duverney (8.33)) follows from the reflection, inversion and Landen identities for `Li₂` by the
derivative-equals-zero method, with the constant fixed by the limit `x → 1⁻`; at `x = 1/2` it gives
`Li₃(1/2) = (7/8)ζ(3) - (π²/12) ln 2 + (ln 2)³/6`.

# Polylogarithms (Duverney Chapter 8; DLMF §25.12)

Mathlib has the values `ζ(2k)`, `expZeta` and the series of `log` and `arctan`, but no
polylogarithm. This area defines `Li_n(z) = ∑ z^k/k^n` on the unit disk (`DLMF.Polylog.Basic`) and
the real dilogarithm `Li₂(x) = -∫₀ˣ log(1-t)/t dt` for `x ≤ 1` (`DLMF.Polylog.Dilog`), with:
* `Li₁(z) = -log(1-z)`, `Li_{n+1}' = Li_n/z`, `Li_n(1) = ζ(n)`, `Li_n(-1) = -(1-2^{1-n})ζ(n)`,
  the duplication formula, and `Li_n(e^{2πia}) = expZeta a n`;

* the real trilogarithm (`DLMF.Polylog.Trilog`): `Li₃(±1)`, Landen's identity for `Li₃` and

# q-Appell functions and their transformations (DLMF §§17.4(iii),17.11)

All four functions use the actual double series. Their bidisc convergence is
asserted separately, so totalized `tsum` is never used to claim continuation.

# Gaussian `q`-binomial coefficients (Duverney §10.1.1)

`qBinom q n k = [n k]_q` is defined by the `q`-Pascal rule (Duverney (10.6)–(10.7)). This file
proves `[n k]_1 = C(n,k)`, the product form `[k+m, k]_q (q;q)_k (q;q)_m = (q;q)_{k+m}`
(Duverney (10.4)), and Cauchy's finite `q`-binomial theorem
`(x;q)_n = ∑_k [n k]_q (-1)^k q^{k(k-1)/2} x^k` (Duverney (10.8)), and the limit
`[n k]_q → C(n,k)` as `q → 1` (10.5). Mathlib has no Gaussian binomial coefficients.

# `q`-derivative and the `q`-fundamental theorem (Duverney §10.1.2)

`qDeriv q f x = (f(x) - f(qx))/((1-q)x)` is Jackson's `q`-derivative. This file proves
`δ_q xⁿ = [n]_q x^{n-1}`, linearity, the `q`-product rule, and `δ_q f(x) → f'(x)` as `q → 1`.
It also proves both halves of the `q`-fundamental theorem of calculus for the existing Jackson
integral `jacksonIntegral`: `δ_q ∫₀ˣ f d_q t = f(x)` and `∫₀ˣ δ_q f d_q t = f(x) - f(0)`.

# Euler's second `q`-exponential (Duverney §10.1.3)

`E_q(x) = ∑ q^{n(n-1)/2} xⁿ/(q;q)_n = (-x;q)_∞` for `|q| < 1` and every complex `x`. The proof lets
`N → ∞` in Cauchy's finite `q`-binomial theorem `(-x;q)_N = ∑_k [N k]_q q^{k(k-1)/2} x^k`, by
Tannery's theorem: `[N k]_q = (q^{N-k+1};q)_k/(q;q)_k → 1/(q;q)_k`, with a uniform bound. Together
with Euler's first identity this gives `e_q(x) E_q(-x) = 1`.

# The `q`-Pfaff–Saalschütz sum (AAR §10.?, Gasper–Rahman (II.12))

The terminating balanced `₃φ₂` sum, proved here as a polynomial identity valid for every `q`:
for all `q, x, r, s`,
`∑_m [n m]_q (r;q)_m (s;q)_m (x;q)_{n-m} (xrsq^m;q)_{n-m} x^m = (xr;q)_n (xs;q)_n`.
Dividing by `(q;q)_n (xrs q;q)_n` gives the usual quotient form, in which `x = aq/(rs)`; this is
the form used for Bailey's lemma.

The proof is by induction on `n`, generalizing `x`, with the explicit telescoping certificate
`G(m) = -[n, m-1]_q x^m (r;q)_m (s;q)_m (xq;q)_{n+1-m} (xrsq^m;q)_{n+1-m}`.

# Riemann theta functions (DLMF §§21.1–21.2)

For a finite index type `ι` (DLMF's genus `g = card ι`), a *Riemann matrix* is a complex
symmetric `ι × ι` matrix whose imaginary part is positive definite (DLMF §21.1); these form
the Siegel upper half-space `siegelUpperHalfSpace ι`. The Riemann theta function
`riemannTheta z Ω = ∑_{n ∈ ℤ^ι} exp(2πi(½ n·Ω·n + n·z))` (DLMF 21.2.1) and the theta function
with real characteristics `riemannThetaChar α β z Ω` (DLMF 21.2.5) are defined as `tsum`s over
the lattice `ι → ℤ`.

The central analytic result of §21.2(i) is proved in `Convergence`: the defining series converges
absolutely, and uniformly on compact subsets of `ℂ^ι × 𝔖_ι`; the limit is continuous there
and holomorphic in each component of `z` and each entry of `Ω`. The proof uses a positive
lower bound for the imaginary quadratic form near a Riemann matrix and a product majorant
built from Mathlib's one-variable bound `summable_pow_mul_jacobiTheta₂_term_bound`.

The `g = 1` case reduces to the one-variable theta functions of DLMF §20.2
(`DLMF.Elliptic.jacobiThetaThreeTau` etc., built on Mathlib's `jacobiTheta₂`), see 21.2.8–12.

`tsum` is totalized: outside the convergence region the defined value is `0`, and all
identities state the hypothesis `Ω ∈ siegelUpperHalfSpace ι` where it is needed.

Analytic properties are proved in `DLMF.RiemannTheta.Convergence`; scaled functions and characteristic identities are developed in `Scaled` and `Characteristics`.

## Corrections and branch conventions

* **21.5.4 as printed is false for general symplectic `Γ`.** For `Γ = [[I, B], [0, I]]` with
  `B` of odd diagonal, 21.5.7 gives `θ(z|Ω+B) = θ(z + ½ diag B|Ω)`, which is not a constant
  multiple of `θ(z|Ω)` (numerically, for `g = 2`, `B = [[1,3],[3,-1]]`, the ratio
  `θ(z|Ω+B)/θ(z|Ω)` changes with `z`). The general formula is 21.5.9 with `α = β = 0`, which
  shifts the characteristics by `½ diag(CDᵀ)`, `½ diag(ABᵀ)`; 21.5.4 holds when both diagonals
  are even (the theta group). That corrected form is acquired.
* The square root `√det(CΩ+D)` in 21.5.4 and 21.5.9 is a continuous branch on the Siegel
  space (any such branch, the constant `ξ` or `κ` absorbing its sign).
* **21.5.8 with the principal square root fails for `g ≥ 3`.** For `Ω = τ I₃`,
  `τ = -1.1√3 + i`, `det(-iΩ) = (1 + 1.1√3 i)³` has argument beyond `π`, and the principal value
  of the root has the wrong sign (verified numerically). The correct factor is the continuous
  branch with value `1` at `Ω = iI`, i.e. the product of the principal roots of the
  eigenvalues of `-iΩ`. For `g ≤ 2` the principal value is that branch. Both the general
  branch form and the principal-value form for `g ≤ 2` are acquired; `g = 1` is proved.

# The Selberg and Aomoto integrals (AAR §§8.1–8.4)

## Proof of Selberg's integral

We follow Aomoto's proof (AAR §8.1), completed by Carlson's theorem and a recursion in the
dimension, and extend to the full domain of convergence by analytic continuation.

1. *Integration by parts* in one coordinate (`integral_cube_ibp`), with the Vandermonde factor
   handled off the diagonal, gives **Aomoto's recurrence** (`aomoto_step`) for `Re c ≥ 1/2`,
   and hence the shift `S(a+1) = ∏ⱼ (a+(n-1-j)c)/(a+b+(2n-2-j)c) · S(a)`
   (`selbergInt_add_one`).
2. `S/R` is therefore `1`-periodic in `a`; it is holomorphic and of polynomial growth on
   vertical strips, so it is constant by **Carlson's theorem** (`selbergRatio_eq_one_left`).
   By the symmetry `a ↔ b` it depends on `c` only.
3. A boundary integration by parts gives the **dimension recursion**
   `(a + n c) S_{n+1}(a, 1, c) = S_n(a, 1 + 2c, c)` (`selbergInt_succ_one`), which the
   right-hand side also satisfies, so the constant is `1` (`selbergInt_eq_of_half_le`).
4. The identity extends to `Re c > 0` by analytic continuation in `c`. Integrability on the
   full domain `Re c > -min(1/n, Re a/(n-1), Re b/(n-1))` follows from a **Landau-type
   theorem** for Mellin transforms of positive measures
   (`integrable_mul_rpow_of_analytic`), after which the identity theorem gives
   `selberg_integral`.

The evaluation proof is organized in `DLMF.Selberg.IntegrationByParts`, `DimensionAndParameters` and `ContinuationAndAomoto`.

# Gegenbauer's addition theorem for Bessel functions (DLMF 10.23.8)

For complex `ν` with `Re ν > 0`, positive radii `r, ρ` and `w² = r² + ρ² - 2rρ cos φ > 0`,

$$
\frac{J_ν(w)}{w^ν} = \frac{2^ν Γ(ν)}{(rρ)^ν}
  \sum_{n=0}^∞ (ν+n) J_{ν+n}(r) J_{ν+n}(ρ) C^{(ν)}_n(\cos φ).
$$

The proof is by power series and works directly at complex `ν`. Write `F_c = ₀F̃₁(;c;·)`, so
that `J_ν(w)/w^ν = 2^{-ν} F_{ν+1}(x + y + z)` with `x = -r²/4`, `y = -ρ²/4`, `z = rρ cos φ / 2`.

* Taylor's theorem for the entire function `F_{ν+1}` gives `F_{ν+1}(s + z) = ∑ zᵏ/k! F_{ν+1+k}(s)`
  (`shBes_hasSum_shift`).
* Each `(2t)ᵏ` is expanded in Gegenbauer polynomials (`monomial_ultrasphPoly_expansion`, DLMF
  18.18.17), and the absolutely convergent double series is regrouped by the Gegenbauer degree

# Addition theorems, Funk–Hecke, Poisson, and `SU(2)` (AAR §§9.6–9.16)

Mathlib has the Poisson kernel of the *disk* (`poissonKernel`) and `Matrix.specialUnitaryGroup`,
but not the spherical addition theorem, Funk–Hecke, or the identification of Jacobi polynomials
with matrix coefficients of `SU(2)`.
The ball Poisson representation uses the Tau Ceti contributors’ Poisson kernel,
boundary convergence and Dirichlet uniqueness. The continuous extension argument
is adapted from their unit-ball Dirichlet theorem. The `SU(2)` double cover transports
their compact Spin cover through their Spin–unitary and coordinate equivalences.
Gegenbauer's addition theorem is proved by induction on the degree: both sides have the same
derivative in `cos ψ` (by the derivative formula and the induction hypothesis at `λ + 1`), and the
constant term is fixed by integrating against `sin^{2λ-1} ψ`, using the proved product formula
(DLMF 18.17.5) and the vanishing of the integrals of `C_j^{λ-1/2}(cos ψ)`, `j ≥ 1`.

## Design notes

* `γ²` is a real parameter (DLMF §30.1), written `γ2 : ℝ`. Prolate: `γ2 > 0`, oblate:
  `γ2 < 0`. The degree comes before the order (`n m`, as for the project's `ferrersP ν μ x`),
  followed by DLMF's arguments `(x, γ²)`.
* **Eigenvalues (choice flagged).** DLMF §30.3(i) characterizes `Ps^m_n` as the solutions of
  30.2.1 with `μ = m` of the form `(1-x²)^{m/2} g(x)`, `g` entire; such solutions exist only for
  the eigenvalues `λ^m_n(γ²)`, `n = m, m+1, …`, ordered by 30.3.1. Here
  `spheroidalSpectrum m γ2` is the set of real `λ` for which the transformed equation
  `(1-z²)g'' - 2(m+1)zg' + (λ - m(m+1) + γ²(1-z²))g = 0` has a nonzero entire solution, and
  `spheroidalEigenvalue n m γ2` is the element of the spectrum with exactly `n - m` smaller
  elements (junk `0` if there is none). The theorem `exists_spheroidalEigenvalue` (in
  `DLMF.Spheroidal.Existence`, proved via `DLMF.Spheroidal.P3lSpectrum` by a Frobenius
  solution at `z = 1` and Sturm oscillation)
  asserts that it exists; the ordering 30.3.1 is then proved.
* **Eigenfunctions (choice flagged).** `spheroidalPsFactor n m γ2` is the entire function `g`
  with the eigenvalue `λ^m_n(γ²)`, real on `ℝ`, with `∫_{-1}^1 (1-x²)^m g(x)² dx` given by
  30.4.1 and the sign of `g(0)` (`n - m` even) or `g'(0)` (`n - m` odd) of §30.4(i); it is
  defined by choice, with existence and uniqueness proved in
  `existsUnique_isSpheroidalPsFactor` (`DLMF.Spheroidal.Existence`; simplicity and parity of the
  eigenvalues,
  `DLMF.Spheroidal.P3lParity`). Since
  `(1 - x²)^{m/2}` has derivative `0` at `x = 0`, the signs of `g(0)`, `g'(0)` are those of
  `𝖯s(0)`, `𝖯s'(0)`.
* `𝑃s^m_n(z, γ²) = (-1)^m (z-1)^{m/2} (z+1)^{m/2} g(z)` with principal powers: this is real on
  `(1, ∞)`, analytic on `ℂ ∖ (-∞, 1]`, and has the boundary values 30.6.4; at `γ = 0` it is

# Parity and simplicity of the spheroidal eigenvalues (DLMF §30.3(i), §30.4(i))

Continuing `DLMF.Spheroidal.P3lSpectrum`, with `p(λ) = Y(0)` and `q(λ) = Y'(0)` for the

* **Green's identity in `λ`** (`p3l_green`):
  `p(λ₁) q(λ₂) - p(λ₂) q(λ₁) = (λ₂ - λ₁) ∫₀¹ (1-x²)^m y₁ y₂ dx`, hence the Wronskian
  `p q' - q p'` in `λ` is positive (`p3l_wron_pos`);
* the zeros of `p` and `q` interlace (`ODE.sturmCount_existsUnique_zero_between`), the lowest
  element of the spectrum is a zero of `q` (`p3l_first`), so the element with `k` smaller
  elements has an even eigenfunction iff `k` is even (`p3l_parity`);
* an entire solution at an eigenvalue is a multiple of a real solution with data `(1, 0)` or
  `(0, 1)` at `0` (`p3l_exists_unit`), and two real normalized solutions with the same sign
  agree (`p3l_unique`).

These give `DLMF.Spheroidal.existsUnique_isSpheroidalPsFactor`.

# The spectrum of the spheroidal factor equation (DLMF §30.3(i))

For `m ∈ ℕ` and real `γ²`, `λ`, consider the equation of the entire factor `g` of
`(1 - z²)^{m/2} g(z)` (DLMF §30.3(i)):

`(1 - z²) g'' - 2(m+1) z g' + (λ - m(m+1) + γ²(1 - z²)) g = 0`.

We prove that the set `p3lSpec m γ²` of real `λ` for which it has a nonzero entire solution is
infinite and meets every half-line `(-∞, x)` in a finite set (`p3lSpec_infinite`,
`p3lSpec_Iio_finite`). This gives the existence of the eigenvalues `λ^m_n(γ²)`
(`DLMF.Spheroidal.exists_spheroidalEigenvalue`).

## Method

* **Frobenius solution at `z = 1`** (exponent `0`): `Y(z) = ∑ f_k (z - 1)^k` with the
  recurrence `2(k+1)(k+m+1) f_{k+1} = (c - k(k+2m+1)) f_k - 2γ² f_{k-1} - γ² f_{k-2}`,
  `c = λ - m(m+1)`, convergent for `|z - 1| < 5/3` (majorants, uniformly for `|c| ≤ K`).
* **Entire solutions force `Y(0) Y'(0) = 0`**: the Wronskian `(1-z²)^{m+1}(g Y' - g' Y)` is
  constant on the disc and vanishes at `z = 1`; applied to `g(z)` and `g(-z)`.
* **Conversely**, if `Y(0) = 0` (`Y'(0) = 0`), `Y` and `∓Y(-z)` agree on the lens between the
  discs about `±1` and glue to a solution on `|z| ≤ 6/5`; its Taylor coefficients at `0` satisfy
  a three-term recurrence and decay geometrically, hence superexponentially
  (`p3l_superexp`), so the solution is entire.
* **Discreteness and lower bound**: `λ ↦ Y(0) Y'(0)` is entire in `λ`; for
  `λ < m(m+1) - |γ²|` it does not vanish (monotonicity of `(1-x²)^{m+1} y y'` on `[0, 1]`).
* **Infinitely many eigenvalues**: by Sturm comparison with `sin(ω s(x))`,
  `s' = (1-x²)^{-m-1}`, the real solution has at least `J` zeros in `(0, 1/2)` for large `λ`;
  the zero count in `[0, 1]` is locally constant in `λ` while `Y(0) ≠ 0`
  (`ODE.sturmDef_ncard_eq_of_isPreconnected`), so `Y(0) = 0` for arbitrarily large `λ`.

Uses the power-series helpers of `DLMF.Hypergeometric.Series` and the Sturm tools of
`DLMFMathlib/Analysis/ODE`. Proof round 3, agent `ls` (prefix `p3l_`).

# The continued fraction for `Γ(a,x)` (Temme §11.2.2; DLMF 8.9.2)

For real `a < 1` and `x > 0` this file proves that the convergents of Legendre's continued fraction
`Γ(a,x) = x^a e^{-x}/(x + (1-a)/(1 + 1/(x + (2-a)/(1 + 2/(x + ⋯)))))` converge to `Γ(a,x)`.
All partial numerators and denominators are then positive.

* **Exact tails.** Let `J_m(σ) = ∫₀^∞ t^m (1+t)^σ e^{-xt} dt`. Then `Γ(a,x) = x^a e^{-x} J₀(a-1)`
  (`upperIncGamma_eq_gammaTail`). Integration by parts gives
  `x J_m(σ) = 0^m + m J_{m-1}(σ) + σ J_m(σ-1)`
  (`gammaTail_ibp`), and `(1+t)^σ = (1+t)^{σ-1}(1+t)` gives `J_n(σ) = J_n(σ-1) + J_{n+1}(σ-1)`
  (`gammaTail_split`). Together these provide a positive backward solution `w` of the three-term
  recurrence of the fraction, with `Γ(a,x) = a₀ w₁ / w₀` (Temme's Exercise 11.5 route, without
  Kummer's `U`).
* **General convergence theorem** (`posContFract_tendsto`). For `a₀/(b₀ + a₁/(b₁ + ⋯))` with
  positive elements and a positive backward solution `w`, Pincherle-type invariants and the
  determinant formula bound the error by `∏ a_k / (B_{m+1} B_m)`. Scaling the denominators
  reduces this to the Seidel–Stern growth lemma `tendsto_mul_of_seidelStern`, which needs the
  divergence of `∑ b_k d_k / d_{k+1}`.
* For the `Γ(a,x)` fraction, `d_{2j}/d_{2j+1} ≥ c/(j+1)`, so the divergence follows from the
  harmonic series (`gammaInc_seidelStern_div`).

DLMF states convergence for every complex `a` and `|ph z| < π`. The positive real case proved here
is the one where all elements are positive.

# Incomplete Beta functions with complex parameters (Temme §11.3; DLMF §8.17)

For complex `a, b` with positive real parts and `0 ≤ x ≤ 1`,

`B_x(a,b) = ∫₀ˣ t^{a-1} (1-t)^{b-1} dt`,  `I_x(a,b) = B_x(a,b) / B(a,b)`,

where `B(a,b)` is Mathlib's `Complex.betaIntegral` (DLMF 8.17.1–8.17.2). TauCeti treats the real
case; `Real.normIncBetaI_ofReal` identifies the two.

## Main results

* `Real.incBeta_one`, `Real.normIncBetaI_one`: `B_1(a,b) = B(a,b)`, `I_1(a,b) = 1`.
* `Real.incBeta_add_incBeta_one_sub`, `Real.normIncBetaI_symm`:
  `I_x(a,b) + I_{1-x}(b,a) = 1` (DLMF 8.17.4).
* `Real.incBeta_one_right`, `Real.normIncBetaI_one_right`: `I_x(a,1) = x^a`.
* `Real.incBeta_eq_add`: `B_x(a,b) = B_x(a+1,b) + B_x(a,b+1)`.
* `Real.incBeta_parts`: `a B_x(a,b+1) - b B_x(a+1,b) = x^a (1-x)^b`.
* `Real.normIncBetaI_add_one_left`, `Real.normIncBetaI_add_one_right`: the recurrences
  DLMF 8.17.20–8.17.21.
* `Real.normIncBetaI_nat`: the binomial sum `I_p(m, n-m+1) = ∑_{j=m}^n C(n,j) p^j (1-p)^{n-j}`
  (DLMF 8.17.5).
* `Real.incBeta_eq_ordinaryHypergeometric`: `B_x(a,b) = xᵃ/a · F(a, 1-b; a+1; x)` for
  `0 < x < 1` (DLMF 8.17.7), from Euler's integral.

# Regularized incomplete Gamma functions (Temme §11.2; DLMF §§8.2–8.8)

The normalized functions `P(a,z) = γ(a,z)/Γ(a)` and `Q(a,z) = Γ(a,z)/Γ(a)` (DLMF 8.2.4) are the
distribution function of the Gamma distribution and its complement. This file defines them for
complex `a` and `z` from the project's `lowerIncGamma` and `upperIncGamma`.

## Main results

* `normIncGammaP_add_normIncGammaQ`: `P(a,z) + Q(a,z) = 1` (DLMF 8.2.5).
* `lowerIncGamma_add_one`: `γ(a+1,z) = a γ(a,z) - z^a e^{-z}` (DLMF 8.8.1).
* `normIncGammaP_add_one`, `normIncGammaQ_add_one`: the recurrences DLMF 8.8.5–8.8.6.
* `normIncGammaQ_nat_succ`, `normIncGammaP_nat_succ`: `Q(n+1,z) = e^{-z} ∑_{k ≤ n} z^k/k!`
  (DLMF 8.4.10), the Poisson tail.
* `lowerIncGamma_eq_tsum`: `γ(a,z) = z^a e^{-z} ∑ zⁿ/(a (a+1)ₙ)` (DLMF 8.7.1).
* `normIncGammaP_ofReal`, `normIncGammaQ_ofReal`: `P` restricts to TauCeti's `regularizedGamma`.
* `hasDerivAt_lowerIncGamma_ofReal`: `∂ₓ γ(a,x) = x^{a-1} e^{-x}` (DLMF 8.8.13).
* `scIncGamma`: Tricomi's entire function `γ*(a,z) = e^{-z} 𝐌(1, a+1, z)`, with the series
  `e^{-z} ∑ zᵏ/Γ(a+k+1)` (DLMF 8.7.1), `γ* = z^{-a} γ(a,z)/Γ(a) = z^{-a} P(a,z)` (DLMF 8.2.6–8.2.7)
  and `γ*(-n,z) = zⁿ` (DLMF 8.4.12).

# The noncentral chi-squared distribution and Marcum's Q-function (Temme §11.4)

Temme writes the noncentral chi-squared distribution with `2μ` degrees of freedom and
noncentrality `2x` as Poisson mixtures of incomplete Gamma ratios,

`P_μ(x,y) = ∑ₙ e^{-x} xⁿ/n! · P(μ+n, y)`,  `Q_μ(x,y) = ∑ₙ e^{-x} xⁿ/n! · Q(μ+n, y)`,

for `μ > 0` and `x, y ≥ 0`, where `P = TauCeti.regularizedGamma` and `Q = 1 - P`. `Q_μ` is the
generalized Marcum Q-function `Q_μ(√(2x), √(2y))`.

## Main results

* `hasSum_poissonWeight`: the Poisson weights `e^{-x} xⁿ/n!` sum to `1`.
* `marcumP_add_marcumQ`: `P_μ(x,y) + Q_μ(x,y) = 1`.
* `marcumP_nonneg`, `marcumP_le_one`: `0 ≤ P_μ(x,y) ≤ 1`.
* `marcumP_zero_left`: `P_μ(0,y) = P(μ,y)`.
* `marcumQ_add_one`: `Q_{μ+1}(x,y) = Q_μ(x,y) + (y/x)^{μ/2} e^{-x-y} I_μ(2√(xy))` (Temme (11.64)).
* `marcumQ_recurrence`: `x Q_{μ+2} = (x-μ) Q_{μ+1} + (y+μ) Q_μ - y Q_{μ-1}` (Temme (11.65)).
* `marcumQ_eq_integral`: `Q_μ(x,y) = ∫_y^∞ (t/x)^{(μ-1)/2} e^{-t-x} I_{μ-1}(2√(xt)) dt`
  (Temme (11.63)).

# Statistical distribution functions (Temme Chapter 11; DLMF §§8.2–8.17)

TauCeti provides the real error function, the real regularized incomplete Gamma and Beta
functions and closed-form distribution functions for the standard laws; the project's
`DLMF.Confluent` area provides complex `erf`, `erfc`, `γ(a,z)` and `Γ(a,z)`. This area adds:

* `DLMF.Statistical.IncompleteGamma`: the complex regularized functions `P(a,z)`, `Q(a,z)`, their
  recurrences, the Poisson tail `Q(n+1,z)`, the series DLMF 8.7.1 and the derivative 8.8.13, and
  Tricomi's entire function `γ*(a,z)` (DLMF 8.2.6–8.2.7, 8.4.12).
* `DLMF.Statistical.ContinuedFraction`: convergence of Legendre's continued fraction for `Γ(a,x)`
  (DLMF 8.9.2) for real `a < 1`, `x > 0`, from a general convergence theorem for continued
  fractions with positive elements and a positive backward solution (Pincherle-type invariants
  and Seidel–Stern growth).
* `DLMF.Statistical.IncompleteBeta`: `B_x(a,b)` and `I_x(a,b)` for complex parameters with
  positive real parts: symmetry, the recurrences DLMF 8.17.20–21, the binomial sum 8.17.5 and the
  bridge to TauCeti.
* `DLMF.Statistical.MarcumQ`: the noncentral chi-squared distribution `P_μ(x,y)`, `Q_μ(x,y)` of
  Temme §11.4, with its Bessel recurrences (11.64)–(11.65) and the Bessel integral (11.63).

# Tools for the Struve and Anger–Weber asymptotics

The substitution `s = sinh t` turns the Schläfli-type integral (DLMF 11.10.4 via 11.10.1)
`A_ν(z) = π⁻¹ ∫₀^∞ e^{-νt - z sinh t} dt` into a Laplace transform

`A_ν(z) = π⁻¹ ∫₀^∞ e^{-zs} K_ν(s) ds`,  `K_ν(s) = (s + √(1+s²))^{-ν} (1+s²)^{-1/2}`

(`struveAs_angerA_eq_integral`). The kernel is holomorphic off the cuts `±i[1, ∞)`, grows at
most polynomially in closed sectors `|arg s| ≤ α < π/2`, and satisfies
`(1+s²) K'' + 3 s K' + (1-ν²) K = 0` (`struveAs_ode`), so its Taylor coefficients at `0` are
`dₙ/n!` with `d₀ = 1`, `d₁ = -ν`, `d_{n+2} = (ν² - (n+1)²) dₙ` (`struveAs_iteratedDeriv_kernel`).
Rotating the ray (`struveAs_angerA_eq_rot`, by analytic continuation in `z` at nonintegral
order and continuity in the order at integral order) and Watson's lemma give
`A_ν(z) ~ π⁻¹ ∑ dₙ z^{-n-1}` in every rotated sector (`struveAs_angerA_hasAsymptoticExpansion`),
the basis of DLMF 11.11.2–11.11.4.

# Large-order tools for the Anger–Weber coefficients

The coefficients `A_k(λ)` of the scaled Anger–Weber expansion DLMF 11.11.8 are the Taylor
coefficients `[u^{2k}] dt/du` of the inverse of `u = t + λ sinh t`; by Lagrange inversion
`A_k(λ) = Res_{t=0} (t + λ sinh t)^{-(2k+1)}`. This file works with the circle integrals

`I_m(λ) = ∮_{|t|=r} g(t) (t + λ sinh t)^{-m} dt`  (`struveLO_I`)

on a small circle on which `t + λ sinh t = t (1 + λ σ(t))`, `σ = dslope sinh 0`, has no zero
other than `t = 0` for all `λ` in a closed disc around `λ₀ ≠ -1` (`struveLO_Good`,
`struveLO_good_exists`). The integrals are holomorphic in `λ`
(`struveLO_hasDerivAt_I`, by differentiation under the integral sign,
`struveLO_hasDerivAt_circleIntegral`), `I_1 = 2πi/(1+λ)` (`struveLO_I_one`, Cauchy's
formula), and since

`λ² n(n+1) sinh² t u^{-n-2} - λ n sinh t u^{-n-1} - (1-λ²) n(n+1) u^{-n-2}
  = d/dt [-n (λ cosh t - 1) u^{-n-1}]`

(`struveLO_hasDerivAt_exact`), the identity
`θ² I_n = (1-λ²) n(n+1) I_{n+2}`, `θ = λ d/dλ`, holds (`struveLO_recurrence`). This is the
recurrence DLMF 11.11(iii) for `A_k = (2πi)⁻¹ I_{2k+1}`, and it shows that the singularity of
the recurrence at `λ = 1` is removable (`angerScaledA_removable` in `DLMF.Struve.Asymptotics`).

The second part treats the large-order expansions DLMF 11.6.6–11.6.7 of `𝐊_ν(λν)` and
`𝐌_ν(λν)` by expanding `(1 ± t²)^{ν-1/2}` binomially inside the integrals 11.5.2 and 11.5.4.
For complex `a` and real `u > -1` the remainder `R_N(a, u) = (1+u)^a - ∑_{j<N} (a choose j) u^j`
(`struveLO_R`) satisfies `|R_N(a,u)| ≤ ∏_{i<N} |a-i| |u|^N (1 + max u 0)^{re a - N}` for
`N ≤ re a` (`struveLO_norm_R_le`, by induction with the mean value inequality). Integrating
against `e^{-zt}` gives explicit error bounds for
`∫₀^∞ e^{-zt} (1+t²)^a dt` (`struveLO_K_integral_bound`, `re a < re z`) and for
`∫₀¹ e^{-zt} (1-t²)^a dt` (`struveLO_M_integral_bound`, `re z > 0`), uniform in complex `a`, `z`.
