# Jacobi theta functions, constants, nome forms and lattice data

# Theta functions: definitions and periodic properties (DLMF §§20.1–20.2)

The project's theta functions are `DLMF.Elliptic.jacobiThetaOneTau … jacobiThetaFourTau`
(`θⱼ(z|τ)` in DLMF normalization, defined from Mathlib's `jacobiTheta₂`; `q = e^{iπτ}`,
period `π` in `z`). As in Mathlib, they are totalized: for `Im τ ≤ 0` they vanish.

This module adds

* the nome forms `jacobiThetaOneQ … jacobiThetaFourQ` (`θⱼ(z,q)`, DLMF §20.1), defined by their
  Fourier series in `q`. DLMF's convention `q^α = e^{iαπτ}` presupposes a known `τ`; for `θ₁, θ₂`
  we use the principal `q^{1/4}`, so `θⱼ(z, e^{iπτ}) = θⱼ(z|τ)` holds for `-1 < Re τ ≤ 1`
  (`jacobiThetaTwoQ_cexp`), while for `θ₃, θ₄` it holds for every `τ`;
* the theta constants `θⱼ(0|τ)`, `θ₁'(0|τ)` (`…NullTau`, `…DerivNullTau`) and their nome forms;
* the Fourier series 20.2.1–20.2.4 in DLMF's sine/cosine form, the lattice quasi-periodicity
  20.2.6–20.2.9, the half-period translations 20.2.10–20.2.14 and the `z`-zeros of §20.2(iv).

Statements are given in the lattice-parameter form `θⱼ(z|τ)`, which avoids the branch of `q^{1/4}`;
results with `q²`, `iq`, … are stated with `2τ`, `τ + 1/2`, … accordingly.

The series, periodicity and zero theorems are in `DLMF.Theta.SeriesAndZeros`.

# Theta functions: generalizations and analogs (DLMF §20.11)

The Gauss sum `G(m,n)` and its reciprocity law (20.11.1–20.11.2), Ramanujan's theta function
`f(a,b)` (20.11.3–20.11.4), Ramanujan's change of base `₂F₁(1/2,1/2;1;k²) = θ₃²(0|τ)` (20.11.5,
rectangular case `τ = it` with Mathlib's series `₂F₁`), and the twelve combined theta functions
`φ_{m,n}` of Carlson with their permutation symmetry (20.11.6–20.11.9).

Theta functions with characteristics (§20.11(iv)) are the one-dimensional case of the Riemann theta
functions of DLMF Chapter 21 and are acquired there.

# Theta functions: identities (DLMF §§20.7–20.8)

Sums of squares, addition and duplication formulas, reduction formulas, Watson's identities, the
Landen transformations, the derivative of `θ₂/θ₄`, the transformations `τ ↦ τ + 1` and
`τ ↦ -1/τ` of the lattice parameter, and Watson's expansion 20.8.1.

DLMF writes most of these identities in the nome form `θⱼ(z, q)`, `θⱼ(z, q²)`, `θⱼ(z, iq)`.
Following DLMF's convention `q^α = e^{iαπτ}` they are stated in the lattice form: `q ↦ q²` is
`τ ↦ 2τ` and `q ↦ iq` is `τ ↦ τ + 1/2`. Quotients carry a nonvanishing hypothesis on their
denominator where it can vanish; theta constants `θ₂(0|τ), θ₃(0|τ), θ₄(0|τ)` never vanish for
`Im τ > 0` (`DLMF.Theta.jacobiThetaTau_eq_zero_iff`).

**Source correction (20.7.34).** With principal square roots the printed 20.7.34 holds only up to
sign: numerically (mpmath) it fails, e.g., for `τ = -2.19 + 1.29i` and `τ = 2.03 + 0.90i`, where the
left side equals minus the right side. We acquire the branch-free squared identity for all `τ`,
the printed form in the rectangular case `τ = it`, `t > 0`, where it holds, and the full-domain
corrected form `jacobiTheta_reduction_iq_eta`, in which the square root is the explicit
eta-quotient `e^{-iπ/8} η(τ)η(4τ)/η(2τ)` (checked with mpmath at 200 random points).

The transformations 20.7.26–20.7.33 are proved: `τ ↦ τ + 1` from the series, and `τ ↦ -1/τ` from
Mathlib's `jacobiTheta₂_functional_equation` and the half-period translations of §20.2(iii).

# Theta functions: integrals (DLMF §20.10)

Mellin transforms (20.10.1–20.10.3) and Laplace transforms (20.10.4–20.10.5) with respect to the
lattice parameter. Integrals are Bochner integrals over `(0, ∞)` and are stated together with
integrability, so that Lean's convention `∫ = 0` for non-integrable functions plays no role.
Powers `x^{s-1}`, `2^s`, `π^{-s/2}` and `√s` are principal complex powers.

**Exceptional point (20.10.3).** For `Re s > 0` the right side `(1 - 2^{1-s}) π^{-s/2} Γ(s/2) ζ(s)`
is meant as its analytic continuation, which is removable at `s = 1`, where Mathlib's totalized
`riemannZeta 1` gives the wrong value `0`. We state 20.10.3 for `s ≠ 1` and the value at `s = 1`,
`∫₀^∞ (1 - θ₄(0|ix²)) dx = ln 2`, separately.

# Separating the Helmholtz equation (Temme Chapter 10)

Temme separates `Δu + k²u = 0` in cylindrical and spherical coordinates. The radial factors are
Bessel functions, and for integer azimuthal order the separated solutions are, in Cartesian form,
`(x+iy)ⁿ ₀F̃₁(n + d/2; -k²r²/4)` with `d = 2` or `3`. These expressions are entire in the
Cartesian coordinates, so the Helmholtz equation can be checked at every point, including the
axis and the origin. This file proves:
* `helmholtz_cylinderWave`: the cylinder wave solves `Δu + k²u = 0` on `ℝ²`, and
  `cylinderWave_polar` identifies it with `(2/k)ⁿ J_n(kr) e^{inφ}` (Temme §10.2.1).
* `helmholtz_cylinderWave_exp`: with the axial factor `e^{iβz}` it solves
  `Δu + (κ² + β²)u = 0` on `ℝ³`.
* `helmholtz_sphericalWave`: the spherical wave solves `Δu + k²u = 0` on `ℝ³`, and
  `sphericalWave_spherical` identifies it with `(r sin θ)ⁿ e^{inφ} (kr/2)^{-(n+1/2)} J_{n+1/2}(kr)`,
  a multiple of `j_n(kr) Pⁿₙ(cos θ) e^{inφ}` (Temme §10.2.2).
* `heatMode_pde`, `heatMode_boundary`: Temme's cooled-cylinder modes `J₀(jr) e^{-j²t}` (§10.3.1).

The Laplacians `laplacian2`, `laplacian3` are written with iterated one-variable derivatives.
In each case the computation reduces to the contiguous relation
`₀F̃₁(c; w) = c ₀F̃₁(c+1; w) + w ₀F̃₁(c+2; w)`.

# Weierstrass lattices, `℘`, `ζ` and `σ` (DLMF §§23.2–23.3(i))

DLMF describes a lattice `𝕃` by half-periods `ω₁, ω₃` with `ℑ(ω₃/ω₁) > 0`; the lattice
generators are `2ω₁, 2ω₃` and `ω₂ = -ω₁ - ω₃` (23.2.1). Mathlib's `PeriodPair` instead stores
the *full* periods `ω₁, ω₂` (with no orientation condition). The structure `HalfPeriods`
records DLMF's data and `HalfPeriods.periodPair` is the bridge: its Mathlib periods are
`2ω₁` and `2ω₃`. Mathlib's names for full periods are therefore *not* DLMF's names; in this
area `H.ω₁, H.ω₂, H.ω₃` always denote DLMF's half-periods.

The Weierstrass `℘` and `℘'` are Mathlib's `PeriodPair.weierstrassP` and
`PeriodPair.derivWeierstrassP`; the invariants `g₂ = 60 G₄`, `g₃ = 140 G₆` are Mathlib's
`PeriodPair.g₂`, `PeriodPair.g₃`. Mathlib sums over all lattice points; the `w = 0` term is
`1/z²` in `℘` and vanishes in `G n` (`n ≥ 1`) because `0⁻¹ = 0`, which reproduces DLMF's sums
over `𝕃 ∖ {0}`. The same convention defines `weierstrassZeta` (23.2.5) and
`weierstrassSigma` (23.2.6) here: the `w = 0` summand of `ζ` is `1/z`, and the `w = 0` factor
of the product for `σ` is `1`. At lattice points the totalized values are junk where DLMF has
poles; the theorems state their domains.

The invariants-form `℘(z; g₂, g₃)` (23.3.8) is defined through a chosen lattice with the given
invariants; it agrees with `℘(z|𝕃)` for every lattice with those invariants, which uses the
uniqueness of the lattice proved in `EllipticFunctionsAndInvariants`.

The lattice, sigma and invariant developments are in `DLMF.Weierstrass.LatticesAndSigma` and `DLMF.Weierstrass.EllipticFunctionsAndInvariants`.

# Elliptic modular functions (DLMF §§23.15–23.19)

We define the elliptic modular function `λ(τ)` (23.15.6) and Klein's complete invariant `J(τ)`
(23.15.7) from the project's theta functions in lattice-parameter form `θⱼ(0|τ)`
(`DLMF.Theta.jacobiThetaTwoNullTau` etc.); Dedekind's eta function is Mathlib's
`ModularForm.eta`. DLMF writes `θⱼ(0, q)` with `q = e^{iπτ}`; the nome form of `θ₂` and of `θ₁'`
carries a branch of `q^{1/4}` which only changes them by a fourth root of unity, and `λ`
(fourth powers) and `J` (eighth powers) are unaffected by it.

The bilinear transformation `𝒜τ = (aτ + b)/(cτ + d)` of 23.15.3 is the Möbius action of
`SL(2, ℤ)` on the upper half-plane (`A • τ` for `A : SL(2, ℤ)`, `τ : ℍ`); `mobius_coe` is the
bridge to the explicit formula.

The general notions of 23.15(i) are formalized literally: the level `ℓ` is an integer or half
an odd integer, which we encode by the integer `ℓ₂ = 2ℓ`, with `(cτ + d)^ℓ` the principal
power. "Analytic at `q = 0` as a function of `q`" means that `f(τ) = F(e^{iπτ})` with `F`
analytic at `0`.

**Terminology in 23.18.** DLMF calls `J` "a modular form of level zero for `SL(2, ℤ)`", but by
23.17.5 `J` has a pole `q⁻²/1728` at `q = 0`, so it is not a modular form in the sense of
23.15(i); it is a modular function (`isModularFunction_kleinJ`).

# Quarter periods (DLMF §23.7)

DLMF gives `℘(ω_j/2)` in two forms, a square-root form and a Jacobian form, with `k, k'` and
the square roots real and positive for rectangular lattices and "determined by continuity"
otherwise. Here the branch is made precise as follows.

* The Jacobian forms hold for every pair of generators with the lattice quantities
  `K = (π/2)θ₃²(0|τ)`, `k = θ₂²(0|τ)/θ₃²(0|τ)`, `k' = θ₄²(0|τ)/θ₃²(0|τ)` (these are the
  analytic continuations in `τ` of the rectangular values; checked numerically for several
  generator pairs of one lattice, including `τ` outside `-1 < ℜτ ≤ 1`).
* The squares of the square-root forms hold for every lattice, branch-free.
* For rectangular lattices the square-root forms hold with principal (positive) roots.

# Relations to theta and Jacobian elliptic functions (DLMF §23.6)

Theta functions are the project's lattice-parameter forms `θⱼ(z|τ)`
(`DLMF.Elliptic.jacobiThetaOneTau … jacobiThetaFourTau`), which are DLMF's `θⱼ(z, q)` with

`e^{iπτ/4}` below). Derivatives at `0` are Lean derivatives in `z`
(`DLMF.Theta.jacobiThetaOneDerivNullTau`, `iteratedDeriv 3`), and `d/dz ln θ₁` is the
logarithmic derivative `θ₁'/θ₁`.

**Jacobian functions (§23.6(ii)).** DLMF states 23.6.16–23.6.26 for *any* pair of generators
with `K = K(k)` the complete elliptic integral of the modulus. The squared quantities in
23.6.17 hold for every pair of generators only if `K` denotes the lattice quarter period
`K = (π/2)θ₃²(0|τ)` (`DLMF.JacobiElliptic.compEllIntKTau`), not the principal integral of
`k = θ₂²/θ₃²`: `k²` is invariant under `τ ↦ τ/(2τ + 1)` while `ω₁²(e₁ - e₃)` is not

`K(k)² - ω₁²(e₁ - e₃) ≈ 11.0 - 13.7i`). The lattice forms are therefore acquired for all
generators, and the literal principal form under the hypothesis `τ = iK'(k)/K(k)`.

**Source correction.** In 23.6.29 the last term has the wrong sign: the correct identity is
`ζ(z|𝕃₃) - ζ(z + 2iK'|𝕃₃) + ζ(2iK'|𝕃₃) = cs(z, k)` (the printed `- ζ(2iK'|𝕃₃)` fails
numerically, e.g. by `-0.49i` for `k² = 0.3`, `z = 0.37 + 0.21i`; the corrected form agrees to
`10⁻¹⁰`). The correction also follows from the oddness of `cs` and `ζ` and 23.2.11.

# Wigner `3j`, `6j` and `9j` symbols: definitions (DLMF Chapter 34)

This file holds the definitions of DLMF Chapter 34 (namespace `DLMF.WignerSymbols`).

## Representation

Angular momenta `j` and projective quantum numbers `m` are rational numbers. DLMF's
standing conditions are predicates:

* `IsNatQ x`: `x` is a nonnegative integer; `IsAngularMomentum j`: `2j ∈ ℕ`;
* `IsProjection j m` (34.2.2): `j - m ∈ ℕ` and `j + m ∈ ℕ`, i.e. `m ∈ {-j, -j+1, …, j}`;
* `IsTriad j₁ j₂ j₃` (34.2.1 with the parity condition of §34.2): the three numbers
  `j₁ + j₂ - j₃`, `j₁ - j₂ + j₃`, `-j₁ + j₂ + j₃` are nonnegative integers. This is
  equivalent to: each `jᵣ` is a nonnegative integer or half-odd integer, the triangle
  conditions hold, and `j₁ + j₂ + j₃` is an integer (`isTriad_iff` in
  `DLMF.WignerSymbols.ThreeJ`).

Factorials, reciprocal factorials and signs of rational arguments are `factQ`, `invFactQ`
and `signPow`; they are only used at integer arguments, where they are `n!`, `1/n!`
(`0` for negative `n`) and `(-1)ⁿ`.

## Definitions

* `wigner3j j₁ j₂ j₃ m₁ m₂ m₃` (34.2.4, Racah's formula with `triangleDelta` of 34.2.5). It is
  `0` unless `IsAdmissible3j` holds: the triangle conditions (34.2.1), the projection
  conditions (34.2.2) and `m₁ + m₂ + m₃ = 0` (34.2.3). DLMF: "If either of the conditions
  (34.2.1) or (34.2.3) is not satisfied, then the 3j symbol is zero"; outside the
  projection ranges 34.2.2 DLMF defines nothing and the value `0` is the convention used by
  all summation formulas of the chapter.
* `clebschGordan` (34.1.1).
* `wigner6j` (34.4.2, the single-sum formula), zero unless the four triads of 34.4.1 satisfy
  the triangle conditions (DLMF §34.10).
* `wigner9j` (34.6.2, the sum of products of three `6j` symbols).
* `projections j`, `halfIntegersUpTo x`: the finite ranges of summation used in the
  orthogonality relations and sum rules.
* `largeParameterAngle` (34.8.2).
* `sixJRecursionE` (34.5.13), the coefficient of the three-term `6j` recursion 34.5.12.
* `w34_S`: an internal helper, the Racah sum of 34.2.4 written symmetrically as a `finsum`
  over `ℤ`; it is used to prove the symmetries of the `3j` symbol.

# Approximations for large parameters: DLMF §34.8

tend to infinity". It is acquired as an iterated limit: first the `jᵣ` tend to infinity with
`l₃` fixed, then `l₃` tends to infinity, uniformly for `θ` (34.8.2, `largeParameterAngle`)
bounded away from `0` and `π` (`sin θ ≥ δ`; near `θ = 0, π` the prefactor `(sin θ)^{-1/2}`
is singular and the approximation is not uniform). The statement is checked numerically
with exact `6j` values up to `j ≈ 1600` (see the ledger).

# Asymptotic approximations of the Riemann zeta function (DLMF §25.9)

The approximate functional equation of Hardy and Littlewood (25.9.1) with the factor
`χ(s) = π^{s-½} Γ(½ - s/2)/Γ(s/2)` (25.9.2) of the functional equation `ζ(s) = χ(s) ζ(1-s)`, and
its symmetric case on the critical line (25.9.3).

The `O`-terms of 25.9.1 are uniform in `x, y ≥ 1` subject to `2πxy = t`: the statement gives a
constant `C` and a threshold `T₀`, depending only on `σ`, with the error bounded by
`C (x^{-σ} + y^{σ-1} t^{½-σ})` for all `t ≥ T₀`. Sums `∑_{1 ≤ n ≤ x}` are over
`n ∈ [1, ⌊x⌋]`. 25.9.3 is proved from 25.9.1.

# Dirichlet `L`-functions (DLMF §25.15)

DLMF's `L(s, χ)` for a Dirichlet character `χ (mod k)` is Mathlib's
`DirichletCharacter.LFunction χ s` (`χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ k`), the meromorphic continuation of
`LSeries χ`; it is *defined* in Mathlib as `k^{-s} ∑_{j mod k} χ(j) ζ(s, j/k)` with Mathlib's
Hurwitz zeta function, which is DLMF 25.15.3. The principal character `χ₁ (mod k)` is `1`, the
complex conjugate character `χ̄` is `star χ` (`= χ⁻¹`, `MulChar.star_eq_inv`), and DLMF's Gauss sum
`G(χ) = ∑_{r=1}^{k-1} χ(r) e^{2πir/k}` (25.15.6) is `gaussSum χ ZMod.stdAddChar` for `k ≥ 2`
(`gaussSum_stdAddChar_eq_sum`).

**Implicit conditions.** For the modulus `k = 1` (the trivial character, which is primitive and
principal) DLMF's finite sums `∑_{r=1}^{k-1}` are empty, so 25.15.3, 25.15.6 (hence 25.15.5) and
the case `χ = χ₁` of 25.15.10 (`L(0, χ₁) = 0`; in fact `L(0, χ₁) = ζ(0) = -1/2` for `k = 1`) need
`k ≥ 2`; 25.15.7 at `n = 0` likewise. The functional equation 25.15.5 is stated with Mathlib's Gauss
sum, which makes it valid also for `k = 1`; it needs `s ≠ 0, -1, -2, …` (implicit: there `Γ(s)` has
a pole and the right side is a limit).

Upstream pointers for 25.15.1, 25.15.2, 25.15.4, 25.15.8, 25.15.9 and the analyticity statements
of §25.15(i) are in `DLMF.Zeta.MathlibCoverageB`.

# The Hurwitz zeta function: definition, Euler–Maclaurin forms, special values, derivatives
(DLMF §25.11(i)–(vi))

## Two Hurwitz zeta functions

* Mathlib's `HurwitzZeta.hurwitzZeta (a : UnitAddCircle) s` is the meromorphic continuation in `s`
  of `∑ (n + a)^{-s}` **for real `0 ≤ a ≤ 1`**; its parameter lives in `ℝ/ℤ`, so it is periodic in
  `a` and agrees with DLMF's `ζ(s, a)` only for `0 < a ≤ 1` (and `hurwitzZeta 0 = ζ(s, 1)`).
* DLMF's `ζ(s, a)` (25.11.1) is defined for complex `a ≠ 0, -1, -2, …` with principal powers. The
  project's definition is `DLMF.Confluent.hurwitzZetaComplex s a`
  (`DLMF/IncompleteGamma/ZerosIntegrals.lean`, made for DLMF 8.15.2), the limit as `N → ∞` of the
  Euler–Maclaurin form `∑_{n<N} (a+n)^{-s} + (a+N)^{1-s}/(s-1) + (a+N)^{-s}/2 + ∑_{k<M} …`
  with `M` large enough for `Re s`. It is reused here, not redefined. Its bridge to Mathlib for
  `0 < a ≤ 1` is `DLMF.Zeta.r25b_hurwitzZetaComplex_mathlib` (a proved form of the admitted
  `DLMF.Confluent.hurwitzZetaComplex_mathlib`).

Convention used below: a DLMF formula whose parameter range is contained in `0 < a ≤ 1` is stated
with Mathlib's `hurwitzZeta` (this is DLMF's function there); a formula for complex `a` or for
unbounded real `a > 0` is stated with `hurwitzZetaComplex`.

The existence of the defining limit (`tendsto_hurwitzZetaComplex`, the content of the continuation
statement in §25.11(i)) is proved in `DLMF.Zeta.R25bHurwitzContinuation` by the one-interval
Euler–Maclaurin formula; the recurrences 25.11.3 and 25.11.4 follow from it.

# The Hurwitz zeta function: integrals, sums and `a`-asymptotics (DLMF §25.11(vii)–(xii))

Statements use DLMF's `ζ(s, a)` in the form `DLMF.Confluent.hurwitzZetaComplex s a` for complex
`a` (see `DLMF.Zeta.Hurwitz`), and Mathlib's `hurwitzZeta` where DLMF's range is `0 < a ≤ 1`.

* Integrals `∫_0^a` with complex `a` are taken along the segment `[0, a]`, written
  `∫_0^1 a f(ta) dt`.
* Conditionally convergent series and improper integrals are stated as limits of partial sums or of
  `∫_0^X` (resp. `∫_{-a}^X`) as `X → ∞`.
* Asymptotic expansions (25.11.43–25.11.45) are stated for each truncation order `K`, with remainder
  `O` of the next power, as `a → ∞` in the sector `|ph a| ≤ π - δ`.
* 25.11.37 involves `ln Γ` of complex arguments. With principal logarithms it holds only modulo
  `2πi` (mpmath, e.g. `n = 2`, `a = 4 - 9i`); it is stated exactly with principal logarithms for
  real `a ≥ 1` (where every logarithm is of a positive real) and in exponentiated form for complex
  `Re a ≥ 1` (the identity with the analytic branch of `ln Γ` is equivalent to it plus a
  continuity statement).
* The removable singularities at `s = 1` in 25.11.31 and 25.11.35 (differences of two Hurwitz
  functions) are excluded by a hypothesis `s ≠ 1`, since Lean's value at the pole is junk.

# The Riemann zeta function at integer arguments (DLMF §25.6)

# Integral representations of the Riemann zeta function (DLMF §25.5)

Conventions.
* Integrals over `(0, ∞)` are Bochner integrals `∫ x in Ioi 0`, stated together with the
  integrability of the integrand, so that Lean's convention `∫ = 0` for non-integrable functions
  plays no role. Powers `x^{s-1}`, `(1+x²)^{s/2}`, `2^s`, `π^{s/2}` are principal complex powers
  of positive reals.
* 25.5.5 converges only conditionally at `∞` (for `-1 < Re s < 0`); it is stated as the limit of
  `∫₀^R` as `R → ∞`.
* Where DLMF divides by `1 - 2^{1-s}` (25.5.3, 25.5.4, 25.5.10, 25.5.21), which vanishes at
  `s = 1 + 2πik/ln 2`, the multiplied form is stated. It is equivalent to the printed form where
  the factor is nonzero and also holds at its zeros (stronger than DLMF).
* `1/Γ(s)` is kept as printed; Lean's `1 / Γ(s) = 0` at the poles of `Γ` agrees with the
  reciprocal Gamma function, so 25.5.6 and 25.5.7 hold also at `s = 0, -1, -2, …`.
* 25.5.13 has a removable singularity at `s = 0`, which is excluded.
* `ψ = Complex.digamma` and `ψ^{(m)} = DLMF.Gamma.polygamma m` (iterated derivatives of `ψ`).
* The loop integrals 25.5.20–25.5.21 are taken over the keyhole contours `keyholeLoopIntegral`
  (the two edges of the cut `(-∞, -δ]` and the circle `|z| = δ`), for every admissible radius
  `δ`; DLMF allows any loop of the stated kind, and the independence of the loop (Cauchy's
  theorem) is not formalized.

# Lerch's transcendent (DLMF §25.14)

* `lerchPhiSeries z s a = ∑_{n≥0} zⁿ/(a+n)^s` (DLMF 25.14.1), principal powers, as a `tsum`.
* `lerchPhi z s a` is DLMF's `Φ(z, s, a)`: for fixed `s`, `a` the analytic continuation in `z` of
  the series from the unit disk to the cut plane `ℂ \ [1, ∞)`, chosen as for `DLMF.Zeta.polylog`
  (`z25b_slitContinuation`), and the series itself on `[1, ∞)` (so `Φ(1, s, a) = ζ(s, a)` for
  `Re s > 1`). DLMF's parameter conditions (`|ph a| < π` if `s ∉ ℤ`; `a ≠ 0, -1, -2, …` if
  `s = 1, 2, …`; any `a` if `s = 0, -1, -2, …`) are `z25b_lerchParamOK s a`. The existence of the
  continuation, together with the convergence of the series in the disk, is the admitted
  `exists_lerchPhi_continuation` (DLMF §25.14(i), "defined by analytic continuation").

**Domain of Lerch's transformation formula 25.14.7.** DLMF prints no conditions. Numerically
(mpmath, 150 sample points) the formula holds for `0 < Re a < 1` and `0 < |z| < 1` and fails in
general for `Re a ∉ (0, 1)` (e.g. `a = 1.6 + 0.2i`, `a = -0.4 + 0.3i`, `a = 1`) and for `|z| ≥ 1`
(e.g. `z = 0.6 - 0.8i`, `z = 3 + 0.4i` with `Im a < 0`); it is acquired on the verified domain.

**25.14.9** is a convergent expansion for `|z| > 1` (the second sum diverges for `|z| < 1`); it is
acquired as an exact identity for `|z| > 1`, `|ph z| < π` (for `m ≥ 1` also `a ≠ 1, 2, …`, as
DLMF requires, and `a ≠ 0, -1, …`, needed for `Φ(-z, m, a)`).

# Analytic continuation of Lerch's series (DLMF §25.14(i), §25.12(ii))

For all complex `s` and `a`, the power series `∑_{n≥0} zⁿ/(a+n)^s` (principal powers) extends
from the open unit disk to an analytic function on the cut plane `ℂ \ [1, ∞)`:

* for `Re a > 0`, `Re s > 0` the continuation is the integral 25.14.5,
  `(1/Γ(s)) ∫_0^∞ x^{s-1} e^{-ax}/(1 - z e^{-x}) dx` (`q25b_lerchInt`), which also sums the series
  on the closed disk when `Re s > 1`;
* the order is lowered by `Φ(z, s-1, a) = (z ∂_z + a) Φ(z, s, a)`;
* the parameter `a` is shifted into `Re a > 0` by 25.14.4.

The cut plane is connected (star-shaped about `0`), so continuations are unique
(`q25b_eqOn_slit`). These results give the continuations behind `DLMF.Zeta.polylog` and
`DLMF.Zeta.lerchPhi`.

# Continuation of the Hurwitz zeta function by Euler–Maclaurin summation (DLMF §25.11(i))

The project's `DLMF.Confluent.hurwitzZetaComplex s z` is defined as the limit of the
Euler–Maclaurin sequence
`E_N(s, z) = ∑_{n<N} (z+n)^{-s} + (z+N)^{1-s}/(s-1) + (z+N)^{-s}/2
  + ∑_{k<M} B_{2k+2}/(2k+2)! (s)_{2k+1} (z+N)^{-s-2k-1}`.
This file proves that the limit exists, for every `s ≠ 1` and every `z`, and is the same for every
admissible number `M` of correction terms (`Re s > -2M`). The engine is the one-interval
Euler–Maclaurin identity for `t ↦ (w+t)^{-s}` on `[0, 1]` (`r25b_emF_diff`), which gives
`E_{N+1} - E_N = O(N^{-Re s - 2M - 1})` locally uniformly in `(s, z)`
(`r25b_tendstoUniformlyOn_hurwitz`). Consequences: holomorphy in `s ≠ 1` for
`z ≠ 0, -1, -2, …` and in `z` on `Re z > 0`, and the derivative `∂_z ζ(s, z) = -s ζ(s+1, z)`.

The general parts, and the definition of `DLMF.Confluent.hurwitzZetaComplex` itself, live in
`DLMF.Zeta.S25bHurwitzCore` (imported by `DLMF.IncompleteGamma.ZerosIntegrals`); this file
restates them under their `r25b_` names.

# Dirichlet's test for Dirichlet series with bounded partial sums

If the partial sums of `c : ℕ → ℂ` are bounded and `a > 0`, the series `∑ c n (n + a)^{-s}`
converges for `Re s > 0`, as a limit of partial sums, to a function holomorphic on `Re s > 0`
(`DLMF.Zeta.s25b_dirichlet_test`). The proof is summation by parts together with the mean-value
bound `|(x+1)^{-s} - x^{-s}| ≤ |s| x^{-Re s - 1}`, which makes the transformed series locally
uniformly absolutely convergent. Used for the conditionally convergent series of DLMF §25.11 and
§25.13 (25.11.8, 25.11.9, 25.13.1); in particular the partial sums of `∑_{n≥1} e^{2πinx}/n^s` tend
to Mathlib's `expZeta x s` for `x ∉ ℤ`, `Re s > 0` (`DLMF.Zeta.s25b_tendsto_expZeta`).

# Euler–Maclaurin continuation of the Hurwitz zeta function: the core (DLMF §25.11(i))

This module holds the part of `DLMF.Zeta.R25bHurwitzContinuation` that does not depend on
`DLMF.IncompleteGamma.ZerosIntegrals`, so that the latter can import it. It holds the
definition of `DLMF.Confluent.hurwitzZetaComplex s z` (moved here from
`DLMF.IncompleteGamma.ZerosIntegrals` on 2026-10-26), the limit of the Euler–Maclaurin sequence
`E_N(s, z) = ∑_{n<N} (z+n)^{-s} + (z+N)^{1-s}/(s-1) + (z+N)^{-s}/2
  + ∑_{k<M} B_{2k+2}/(2k+2)! (s)_{2k+1} (z+N)^{-s-2k-1}`,
and proves that the limit exists for every `s ≠ 1` and every `z`, that it is the same for every
admissible number `M` of correction terms (`Re s > -2M`), that it is holomorphic in `s ≠ 1` for
`z ≠ 0, -1, -2, …`, and that it agrees with Mathlib's `hurwitzZeta` for real `0 < x ≤ 1`
(`s25b_hzc_mathlib`).

# Sums involving the Riemann zeta function (DLMF §25.8)

The power series 25.8.5–25.8.8 are derived from the project's Taylor series of `ψ(1+z)` and

# Zeros of the Riemann zeta function (DLMF §25.10)

§25.10(i). Mathlib proves `ζ(s) ≠ 0` for `Re s ≥ 1` (`riemannZeta_ne_zero_of_one_le_re`) and the
trivial zeros `ζ(-2n) = 0` (`riemannZeta_neg_two_mul_nat_add_one`); pointers are in
`DLMF.Zeta.MathlibCoverage`. This file proves that `ζ(s) ≠ 0` for `Re s ≤ 0` except at the trivial
zeros, the two symmetries of the zeros in the critical strip, and acquires the existence of
infinitely many zeros there. The Riemann hypothesis is a conjecture and is not acquired; Mathlib's
`RiemannHypothesis` is the statement (pointer only).

The Riemann–Siegel functions: `riemannSiegelTheta t = ph Γ(¼ + ½it) - ½ t ln π` with the
principal phase, as DLMF prescribes (25.10.2), and `riemannSiegelZ t = e^{iθ(t)} ζ(½ + it)`
(25.10.1). With the principal phase `θ` is discontinuous (it differs from the usual continuous
Riemann–Siegel theta function by integer multiples of `2π`), but `e^{iθ}`, and hence `Z`, do not
depend on the choice. `riemannSiegelZ` equals Mathlib's `hardyZ` (`riemannSiegelZ_eq_hardyZ`), so
`Z` is real, `|Z(t)| = |ζ(½+it)|` and `Z` vanishes exactly at the zeros on the critical line. That
`Z` changes sign infinitely often (Hardy's theorem) is admitted; the infinitude of zeros on the
critical line and in the critical strip is proved from it.

§25.10(ii). `riemannZeroCount T` is `N(T)`, the number of zeros in the critical strip with
`0 < Im s < T`, counted with multiplicity; `criticalLineZeroCount T` counts those on the critical
line. The Riemann–Siegel formula 25.10.3 is stated for the remainder `riemannSiegelRemainder`, and
the first term of its asymptotic series (25.10.4) along `t` with `cos √(2πt) ≠ 0` (at the other `t`
the printed quotient is a removable `0/0` form). The proportion result of Bui, Conrey and Young
(more than 41% of the zeros lie on the critical line) is acquired as an eventual inequality; the
statement about the first ten billion zeros is numerical and excluded.

# Special Functions following the NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions

# Pairing consecutive terms of finite sums

Small general facts used throughout the special-function library: a sum over
`range (2 m)` is the sum of the consecutive pairs `f (2 j) + f (2 j + 1)`, and
`(-1)ⁿ (-1)ⁿ = 1`.

# Real polynomials evaluated at real points of `ℂ`

The complexification of a real polynomial takes real values at real points.

# Asymptotic expansions

Following Poincaré (and Temme, *Special Functions*, §2.2), a function `f` has the asymptotic
expansion `f ~ ∑ aₙ φₙ` along a filter `l` with respect to the scale functions `φₙ` if for
every `N` the remainder after `N` terms is `O(φ_N)`:

`f - ∑_{n<N} φₙ aₙ = O(φ_N)`.

The scale is *asymptotic* if `φₙ₊₁ = o(φₙ)`; then the remainder after `N` terms is also
`o(φ_{N-1})`, and the coefficients are unique as soon as each `φₙ` is frequently nonzero.
The expansion need not converge, and a function determines its expansion but not
conversely.

The scale functions are scalar-valued and the coefficients lie in a normed space, so that
real and complex expansions with vector coefficients are covered.

## Main definitions

* `Asymptotics.IsAsymptoticScale l φ`: `φ (n+1) =o[l] φ n` for all `n`.
* `Asymptotics.HasAsymptoticExpansion l φ a f`: `f ~ ∑ aₙ φₙ` along `l`.

## Main results

* `HasAsymptoticExpansion.add`, `.smul`, `.neg`, `.sub`: linearity.
* `HasAsymptoticExpansion.congr_scale`, `.smul_scale`, `.mul_left`, `.comp_tendsto`: changing,
  rescaling, multiplying and composing the scale.
* `HasAsymptoticExpansion.isLittleO`: the remainder after `N + 1` terms is `o(φ_N)`.
* `HasAsymptoticExpansion.unique`: uniqueness of the coefficients.
* `isAsymptoticScale_rpow_neg`: the scale `x ↦ x^{-(n+μ)}` at `+∞`.

# Asymptotic power series: composition and inversion

An *asymptotic power series* of `f : α → 𝕜` in a small variable `w : α → 𝕜` along a filter `l`
is a Poincaré expansion `f ~ ∑ pₙ wⁿ` (`HasAsymptoticExpansion` with the scale `wⁿ`) whose
coefficients are those of a formal power series `P : 𝕜⟦X⟧`. With `w → 0`, these expansions form
an algebra on which `f ↦ P` acts as a ring homomorphism, and they are closed under composition
(formal substitution `PowerSeries.subst`) and reciprocals.

The main result is asymptotic (Lagrange) inversion: if `H ~ P(σ)` with `P = p₁X + O(X²)`,
`p₁ ≠ 0`, and `y` solves `H(y) = w` with `σ(y) → 0`, then `σ(y) ~ Q(w)` where
`Q = P.substInvOfIsUnit _` is the compositional inverse of `P`; all error bounds `O(wᴺ)` hold.
No a priori expansion of the solution is assumed: the estimate `σ(y) = O(w)` and the formal
identity `Q(P(X)) = X` give every order at once.

The McMahon form treats equations `ξ(x) + G(x) = T` with `G(x) ~ ∑ cₙ ξ(x)⁻ⁿ` (constant phase
shift `c₀` allowed) and a large variable `ξ`; a solution `x(T)` along any filter (for instance
indexed by `k : ℕ` with `T = βₖ → ∞`) satisfies `ξ(x) - T ~ ∑ dₙ T⁻ⁿ` with `d = mcMahonSeries C`,
and `D = mcMahonSeries C` is characterised formally by `D = -C(X (1 + X D)⁻¹)`.
An equation `F(x) = T` with `F(x) ~ x (1 + ∑_{n≥1} cₙ x⁻ⁿ)` is the case `G = F - ξ`.

## Main definitions

* `Asymptotics.HasAsymptoticPowerSeries l w P f`: `f ~ ∑ (coeff n P) wⁿ` along `l`.
* `Asymptotics.mcMahonSeries C`: the inverted coefficients of `x + G(x) = T`.

## Main results

* `HasAsymptoticPowerSeries.add`, `.mul`, `.pow`, `.aeval`, `.recip`, `.mul_var`, `.div_var`:
  algebra of asymptotic power series; `.unique`: uniqueness.
* `HasAsymptoticPowerSeries.comp`: composition `H ∘ y ~ P.subst Q`.
* `HasAsymptoticPowerSeries.analytic_comp`: composition with an analytic function.
* `HasAsymptoticPowerSeries.inversion`: asymptotic inversion.
* `HasAsymptoticPowerSeries.mcMahon`, `hasAsymptoticPowerSeries_mcMahon_atTop`: McMahon-type
  inversion `x = T + ∑ dₙ T⁻ⁿ`; `mcMahonSeries_spec`: the formal fixed-point identity.
* `hasAsymptoticPowerSeries_recip_iff`: translation to the scale `ξ^{-n}` of
  `HasAsymptoticExpansion`.
* `mcMahonSeries_coeff_le_two`: `d₀ = -c₀`, `d₁ = -c₁`, `d₂ = -(c₂ + c₀c₁)`.

Expansions whose coefficients are polynomials in a slowly varying parameter (logarithmic
terms, as in DLMF 7.13.1) are not covered.

# Exponential bounds for primitives on a half-line

An exponential bound with positive rate for a derivative gives an exponential
bound with the same rate for its primitive. One-sided derivatives at zero suffice.

# Integrating power-law asymptotics

A continuous function dominated at infinity by an integrable complex power is
integrable on a positive half-line. Asymptotic equivalence to such a power passes
to the tail integral, by integrating the uniform tail bound on the error.
For nonintegrable powers, asymptotic equivalence instead passes to growing
primitives; the fixed initial segment becomes negligible. The borderline
comparison with `1/x` gives a logarithmic primitive.

# All-order Laplace expansions at a quadratic endpoint

Watson's lemma (`hasAsymptoticExpansion_integral_exp_smul`) treats Laplace transforms
`∫₀^∞ e^{-zt} F(t) dt`. After the saddle substitution `φ(u) = v²/2`, a Laplace integral with a
quadratic minimum of the phase becomes a Gaussian integral `∫₀^{v₀} e^{-z v²/2} G(v) dv`. This
file proves the all-order expansion of such Gaussian integrals and collects the tools used to
produce the substitution.

## Main results

* `Asymptotics.lapSad_hasAsymptoticExpansion_gauss_odd`: if `G(v) ~ ∑ bⱼ v^{2j+1}` as `v → 0⁺`,
  then `∫₀^{v₀} e^{-z v²/2} G(v) dv ~ ∑ j! 2ʲ bⱼ z^{-(j+1)}` as `z → +∞`.
* `Asymptotics.lapSad_hasAsymptoticExpansion_gauss_analytic`: the same for the odd amplitude
  `v (-U(-v) - U(v))` built from an analytic substitution `U`, with coefficients read off from
  the power series of `U` (`Asymptotics.lapSad_isBigO_odd_part`).
* `Asymptotics.lapSad_coeff_eq_zero_of_isBigO`: uniqueness of truncated power expansions, used
  to identify Taylor coefficients of implicitly defined substitutions.

# Bounds for partial sums of real powers

Integral comparison bounds the partial sums of `j^p`, with the logarithmic
case stated separately. These estimates do not require an asymptotic expansion.

# Stationary phase at a cubic stationary point

For a real phase `φ` on `[0, b]` with `φ(x) = c x³ + O(x⁴)` (`c > 0`), `φ'' ≥ 0` and
`φ'(x) ≥ m x²`, the oscillatory integral satisfies

`λ^{1/3} ∫₀^b e^{iλφ(x)} dx → Γ(4/3) c^{-1/3} e^{iπ/6}`   (`λ → +∞`).

The proof splits `[0, b]` at `δ = λ^{-3/10}`. On `[δ, b]` one integration by parts
(`statPh_norm_integral_le`, the first-derivative test) gives `O(λ^{-1/15})` after scaling; on
`[0, δ]` the phase is replaced by `c x³` at cost `O(λ^{-1/6})`, and the model integral is
rescaled to `∫₀^R e^{it³} dt`. Its limit `Γ(4/3) e^{iπ/6}` (`statPh_tendsto_integral_exp_cube`)
is obtained by rotating the ray `arg t = α`, `0 < α < π/9`, to `arg t = π/6`
(`Complex.integral_Ioi_eq_exp_mul_integral_Ioi_rotate`) and letting `α → 0` with a uniform
tail bound `4/(3R²)`.

This is the leading term of the classical stationary-phase method at a degenerate stationary
point (Olver, *Asymptotics and Special Functions*, Ch. 3, §13; Temme, *Special Functions*,
§2.5); it is used for the Anger–Weber functions `𝐉_ν(ν)`, `𝐄_ν(ν)` (DLMF 11.11.18–19).

## Main results

* `Complex.statPh_norm_integral_le`: `‖∫_a^b ψ φ' e^{iφ}‖ ≤ 2ψ(a)` for nonincreasing `ψ ≥ 0`.
* `Complex.statPh_tendsto_integral_exp_cube`: `∫₀^R e^{it³} dt → Γ(4/3) e^{iπ/6}`.
* `Complex.statPh_tendsto_cubic`: the stationary-phase limit above.

# Remainders of Stieltjes transforms

For a nonnegative density `φ` on `(0, ∞)` with finite moments `m_k = ∫ τ^k φ(τ) dτ`, the
Stieltjes-type transform

  `F(S) = ∫₀^∞ φ(τ) / (1 + τ/S) dτ`,   `S ∉ (-∞, 0]`,

has the asymptotic expansion `Σ (-1)^k m_k S^{-k}`, and its remainder after `N` terms is exactly
`(-1)^N S^{-N} ∫ τ^N φ(τ) / (1 + τ/S) dτ`. Since `|1 + τ/S| ≥ 1` for `re S ≥ 0` and
`|1 + τ/S| ≥ |sin (arg S)|` in general, the remainder is bounded by the first neglected term
times `1`, respectively `|csc (arg S)|` (Olver, *Asymptotics and Special Functions*, Ch. 3 §9;
the bounds of DLMF 9.7.17, 6.12(i) and 2.4 are of this type). On the imaginary axis the real
and imaginary parts are Stieltjes transforms in `S²` and their even and odd remainders are
enclosed by the first neglected term with its sign.

## Main results

* `stRem_remainder_eq`: the exact remainder.
* `stRem_remainder_le`: the bound by the first neglected term divided by `stRem_c S`, where
  `stRem_c S = 1` for `re S ≥ 0` and `|sin (arg S)|` otherwise.
* `stRem_remainder_le_of_re_nonneg`, `stRem_remainder_le_csc`: the two sector cases.
* `stRem_transform_I_mul`: `F(iX) = E(X) + i O(X)` with the even and odd real transforms.
* `stRem_even_remainder`, `stRem_odd_remainder`: signed first-neglected-term enclosures.

All helper names carry the prefix `stRem_`.

# Watson's lemma

Let `F : ℝ → E` have the expansion `F(t) ~ ∑ aₙ t^{n+μ-1}` as `t → 0⁺`, with `μ > 0`, and let
`e^{-ct} F(t)` be integrable on `(0, ∞)` for some `c`. Then the Laplace transform has the
asymptotic expansion

`∫₀^∞ e^{-zt} F(t) dt ~ ∑ Γ(n+μ) aₙ z^{-(n+μ)}`   as `z → +∞`

(Temme, *Special Functions*, Theorem 2.4, for real `z`). The proof splits the remainder
integral at a small `δ`: near `0` the hypothesis gives `O(z^{-(N+μ)})` through the Gamma
integral, and beyond `δ` the factor `e^{-zt}` contributes `O(e^{-δz})`, which is smaller than
any power of `z`.

## Main results

* `integral_exp_neg_mul_mul_rpow_sub_one`: `∫₀^∞ e^{-zt} t^{s-1} dt = Γ(s) z^{-s}`, and its
  complex-exponent version `integral_exp_neg_mul_smul_cpow_sub_one`.
* `isBigO_integral_exp_smul`: if `G(t) = O(t^{s-1})` at `0⁺`, then the Laplace transform of `G`
  is `O(z^{-s})`.
* `hasAsymptoticExpansion_integral_exp_smul`: Watson's lemma.
* `hasAsymptoticExpansion_integral_exp_smul_cpow`: Watson's lemma with a complex exponent `μ`,
  `re μ > 0`, and coefficients in a complex normed space.

# Watson estimates for rapidly decreasing kernels

The substitution `u = t^κ` transports the Laplace remainder estimate to stretched
exponentials. Domination then gives Watson's lemma for kernels bounded by such an
exponential. The moment coefficients are Mellin transforms.

# Logarithmic moments for Watson's lemma

The logarithmic exponential moment is the order derivative of the Gamma integral.
Absolute convergence follows from Mathlib's Mellin differentiation criterion; a positive
dilation gives its exact dependence on the Laplace parameter.

# Watson's lemma along rotated rays

Watson's lemma (`hasAsymptoticExpansion_integral_cexp_smul_sector`) gives the expansion of a
Laplace transform `f(z) = ∫₀^∞ e^{-zt} F(t) dt` in closed subsectors of `|arg z| < π/2`. When `F`
extends holomorphically to a sector `|arg t| ≤ α` with at most polynomial growth, rotating the
ray of integration to `arg t = θ`, `|θ| ≤ α`, gives

`f(z) = e^{iθ} ∫₀^∞ e^{-z e^{iθ} r} F(r e^{iθ}) dr`,

which continues `f` to the half-plane `re (z e^{iθ}) > 0`; Watson's lemma for the rotated
integral then gives the same Poincaré expansion uniformly in closed subsectors of
`|arg z + θ| < π/2`. Taking `θ = ±β` covers closed subsectors of `|arg z| < π/2 + α`
(Temme, *Special Functions*, §2.2; Olver, *Asymptotics and Special Functions*, §4.5).

## Main results

* `differentiableOn_integral_cexp_neg_mul_smul`: a Laplace transform is holomorphic on its
  half-plane of absolute convergence.
* `integral_cexp_neg_mul_mul_eq_rotate`: rotation of the ray in a Laplace integral, for a
  kernel holomorphic in the sector swept, with an integrable singularity at `0` and
  polynomial growth at `∞`.
* `hasAsymptoticExpansion_integral_cexp_smul_rotate`: Watson's lemma along a rotated ray, in
  the rotated variable `w = z e^{iθ}`, for `-π < θ ≤ π`.
* `hasAsymptoticExpansion_integral_cexp_smul_rotate_comap`: the same in the original variable
  `z`, uniformly for `δ |z| ≤ re (z e^{iθ})`, for `|θ| < π/2`.
* `Asymptotics.HasAsymptoticExpansion.sup`, `.of_le_sup`: gluing expansions valid on
  overlapping sectors along functions that agree there (for instance by the identity theorem).
* `Asymptotics.le_sup_comap_rotate`: two rotated sectors cover a closed sector `|arg z| ≤ α`.
* `Asymptotics.HasAsymptoticExpansion.even`, `.odd`: passing to even or odd scale functions
  when the other coefficients vanish.

# Watson's lemma in a sector

The Laplace transform `∫₀^∞ e^{-zt} F(t) dt` has the asymptotic expansion of Watson's lemma as
`z → ∞` in every closed sector `|arg z| ≤ π/2 - δ`, described here by `δ |z| ≤ re z`
(Temme, *Special Functions*, Theorem 2.4).

* `integral_cpow_mul_cexp_neg_mul_Ioi`: `∫₀^∞ t^{s-1} e^{-zt} dt = Γ(s) z^{-s}` for `re s > 0`,
  `re z > 0`.
* `Asymptotics.sectorAtTop`: the filter `z → ∞` with `δ |z| ≤ re z`.
* `hasAsymptoticExpansion_integral_cexp_smul_sector`: Watson's lemma in a sector.

# Boole's summation formula

The alternating analogue of the Euler–Maclaurin formula (Temme, *Special Functions*,
§1.2.2; DLMF 24.17.1 with `h = 0`): for `f : ℝ → E` of class `Cᵐ`, `m ≥ 1`,

`2 ∑_{k<n} (-1)ᵏ f(k) = ∑_{j<m} cⱼ (f⁽ʲ⁾(0) - (-1)ⁿ f⁽ʲ⁾(n))
  + (-1)ᵐ/(m-1)! ∫₀ⁿ Ẽ_{m-1}(x) f⁽ᵐ⁾(x) dx`,

with `c₀ = 1`, `cⱼ = (-1)^{j+1} Eⱼ(0)/j!` for `j ≥ 1`, and the antiperiodic Euler function
`Ẽₖ(x) = (-1)^{⌊x⌋} Eₖ(x - ⌊x⌋)`. Since `Eⱼ(0) = 0` for even `j ≥ 2`, `cⱼ = Eⱼ(0)/j!`.

The proof integrates by parts on `[a, a+1]` against `Eⱼ(x - a)`, using `Eⱼ' = j Eⱼ₋₁` and
`Eⱼ(1) = -Eⱼ(0)` for `j ≥ 1`, and sums with alternating signs, which telescopes.

# Signs of real functions near zeros, and two derivatives

Facts used in zero-counting arguments for real solutions of differential equations:
the sign of the derivative at a zero next to an interval of positivity, nonnegativity at
the endpoints of such an interval, and constancy of sign of a nonvanishing continuous
function on an order-connected set. Also the derivative of the real part of a complex
curve and `x ↦ x²` as a map of `𝓝[<] 1` to itself.

# Truncated expansions of inverse and algebraic functions

Tools for verifying explicit Taylor polynomials of functions defined implicitly, without
computing iterated derivatives. They reduce an expansion `F = P + O(φ)` to a residual estimate
for a polynomial identity satisfied by `F`.

* `invSer_isBigO_sub_of_pow_sub`: if `A → a ≠ 0`, `B → a` and `A^n - B^n = O(φ)`, then
  `A - B = O(φ)` (roots of algebraic relations, e.g. square and cube roots).
* `invSer_isBigO_sub_of_leftInverse`: if `g` is a left inverse of `f` near `x₀` with a strict
  derivative at `f x₀`, then for any approximant `P → x₀` of `g ∘ h`,
  `P - g ∘ h = O(f ∘ P - h)`: a candidate expansion of an inverse function is verified by
  substituting it into `f`.
* `invSer_isBigO_pow_of_eq_mul`: a function of the form `y^n · q(y)` with `q` bounded near the
  point is `O(y^n)`.

# L'Hôpital's rule with an unbounded denominator

The derivative-quotient limit implies the function-quotient limit when the absolute value
of the denominator tends to infinity at a punctured finite point. No limit of the numerator
is required. Cauchy's mean value theorem bounds increments relative to the denominator;
fixed anchors on the two sides of the puncture then contribute vanishing constant terms.
The proof uses Mathlib's `exists_ratio_deriv_eq_ratio_slope` and metric/filter APIs.

# Shifting a vertical line of integration across a simple pole

Let `φ` be holomorphic on the closed strip `c₁ ≤ Re s ≤ c₂` and let `p` be an interior point.
For `f s = φ s / (s - p)`, if `f` is integrable on the two boundary lines and its integrals over
horizontal cross-sections of the strip tend to `0` at `±i∞`, then

`∫ f(c₂ + iy) dy - ∫ f(c₁ + iy) dy = 2π φ(p)`,

i.e. moving the line `Re s = c` to the left past the pole loses `2π` times the residue (the line
integrals carry `dy`, not `ds = i dy`). This is the basic step of Barnes-integral contour shifts.

The proof applies Cauchy's theorem for rectangles to the removable-singularity function
`dslope φ p` and evaluates the rectangle integral of `(s - p)⁻¹` by the explicit primitive
`arctan (t / c) - (i/2) log (c² + t²)` of `(c + it)⁻¹` (the same primitive is used for the Perron
kernel in TauCeti, `TauCeti.NumberTheory.ArithmeticDirichletSeries.Perron.Basic`).

* `Complex.barnesRes_integral_recip`: `∫_{-T}^{T} (c + it)⁻¹ dt = 2 arctan (T / c)`.

* `Complex.barnesRes_vertical_shift_of_differentiableOn`: the pole-free version.
* `Complex.barnesRes_sq_norm_sin` and the lower bounds `|sinh y| ≤ ‖sin (x + iy)‖`,

* `Complex.barnesRes_norm_Gamma_mul_sin_le`: `‖Γ(w)‖ ‖sin πw‖ ≤ π ‖Γ(1-w)⁻¹‖`, with the lower
  bounds `barnesRes_sin_lower_line`, `barnesRes_sin_lower_far` for `‖sin(π(x+iy))‖`.
* `Complex.barnesRes_prod_sub_nat`: `∏_{j<n} (j - n) = (-1)^n n!` (residues of `Γ`).
* `Complex.barnesRes_Gamma_add_nat_succ`: `Γ(w + n + 1) = Γ(w) ∏_{j ≤ n} (w + j)`, the

# Coordinate derivatives of jointly analytic functions

The coordinate partial derivatives of an analytic function on `ℂ × ℂ` are analytic and
its two mixed partial derivatives agree. The proofs express coordinate derivatives as
evaluations of Fréchet derivatives, then apply symmetry of the second Fréchet derivative.

# Mixed derivatives and differential equations of bivariate power series

Mathlib's Cauchy estimate `Complex.norm_iteratedDeriv_le_of_forall_mem_sphere_norm_le`
bounds mixed derivatives on smaller polydiscs. Together with locally dominated
series differentiation, it proves convergence and termwise evaluation of every
mixed derivative. Quadratic coefficient recurrences then give second order
partial differential equations, including points on the coordinate axes.

# Taylor coefficients obstruct separated analytic products

For a convergent bivariate power series, a local representation as `f(x) * g(y)`
forces `c(1, 1) * c(0, 0) = c(1, 0) * c(0, 1)`. The proof restricts the series to
its coordinate axes and diagonal, differentiates term by term, and uses Mathlib's
Leibniz rule `iteratedDeriv_fun_mul`.

# Entire sparse factorial series

Mathlib's summable exponential series and locally uniform holomorphic convergence
supply convergence and differentiability for bounded coefficients and injective exponents.

# Analytic series in a geometric Newton basis

The polynomials `∏ j < n, (w - q^j)` admit a uniform geometric bound on compact discs
when `‖q‖ < 1`. Consequently a series in this basis with geometrically bounded
coefficients is analytic on its expected open disc. The estimate uses Mathlib's
geometric series and `1 + x ≤ exp x`; normal convergence uses the existing locally
dominated holomorphic-series theorem.

# The Lagrange–Bürmann formula at the coefficient level

Let `F` and `Φ` be holomorphic on a closed disc `|t| ≤ r`. For small `z` the equation
`t = z Φ(t)` has a simple root `w` in the disc, and the Lagrange–Bürmann formula reads
`F(w) / (1 - z Φ'(w)) = ∑ₙ zⁿ [tⁿ] (F Φⁿ)`.
We prove it in the following form, which avoids the argument principle: assume a
factorization `t - z Φ(t) = (t - w) g(t)` on the circle `|t| = r` with `|w| < r` and with `g`
holomorphic and zero-free on the closed disc (then `g(w) = 1 - z Φ'(w)`).
Writing `[tⁿ](F Φⁿ)` as a Cauchy integral, summing the geometric series
`∑ (z Φ(t)/t)ⁿ = t / (t - z Φ(t))` under the integral (it converges uniformly when
`|z Φ| ≤ ρ < r` on the circle) and applying Cauchy's integral formula to `F/g` gives

* `Complex.lagB_hasSum_iteratedDeriv`:
  `∑ₙ zⁿ (F Φⁿ)⁽ⁿ⁾(0)/n! = F(w)/g(w)`.

We also record the tool for extending a power-series identity from a small disc to the disc of
holomorphy of its sum:

* `Complex.lagB_hasSum_of_differentiableOn`: if `f` is holomorphic on `|z| < R` and
  `f(z) = ∑ cₙ zⁿ` for `|z| < δ`, then the identity holds for `|z| < R`.

The proofs use Mathlib's Cauchy integral formula (`DiffContOnCl.circleIntegral_sub_inv_smul`,
`DiffContOnCl.circleIntegral_one_div_sub_center_pow_smul`), dominated convergence for interval
integrals, and uniqueness of power series (`HasFPowerSeriesOnBall.exchange_radius`).

# Closing a Mellin–Barnes contour: vertical-line integrals as residue series

Let `F` be meromorphic to the left of the line `Re s = c₀`, with one simple pole `p n` in each
strip `c (n+1) < Re s < c n` of a decreasing sequence of lines `c n`. Write
`F s = φ n s / (s - p n)` on the `n`-th closed strip, with `φ n` holomorphic there. If `F` is
integrable on every line, its integrals over horizontal cross-sections of every strip tend to `0`
at `±i∞`, and the line integrals tend to `0` as `n → ∞`, then

`∫ F(c₀ + iy) dy = 2π ∑ₙ φ n (p n)`,

the sum of the residues (times `2π`; the line integrals carry `dy`, not `ds = i dy`). The series
converges as the limit of its partial sums; it is a `HasSum` when the residue series is known
to be summable. The proof iterates `Complex.barnesRes_vertical_shift`.

For the poles of `Γ(s + a)` at `s = -n - a` we also record the factorization
`Γ(s + a) = Γ(s + a + n + 1) / ∏_{j ≤ n} (s + a + j)` and the residue
`(-1)^n / n!`. Bounds for `Γ` on vertical lines (`|Γ(x+iy)| ≤ C (1+|y|)^K e^{-π|y|/2}`) and for
`1/sin(πs)` are in `DLMF.Gamma.VerticalBounds` and `Complex.barnesRes_sin_lower_line`,
`Complex.barnesRes_sin_lower_far`.

* `Complex.mbSeries_Gamma_mul_eq_div`, `Complex.mbSeries_Gamma_residue`: the residue data of

Bookkeeping for parameters that avoid the integers or the nonpositive integers, and the

# Locally uniform parameter limits from continuous extensions

Joint continuity along a parameter slice gives locally uniform convergence to that slice.
Consequently, an already known pointwise limit is locally uniform whenever the family agrees
near the parameter with such a continuous extension.

# Holomorphy in parameters of series and integrals

Mathlib proves that a series of holomorphic functions of one complex variable with a summable
bound is holomorphic (`differentiableOn_tsum_of_summable_norm`), and that parametric integrals
are differentiable under bounds on the derivative
(`hasFDerivAt_integral_of_dominated_of_fderiv_le`).
This file removes the derivative bounds in the complex setting, for a parameter in an arbitrary
complex normed space (several complex parameters at once):

* `Complex.norm_fderiv_le_of_forall_mem_ball_norm_le`: the Cauchy estimate
  `‖Df(x)‖ ≤ M / r` for `f` holomorphic and bounded by `M` on `ball x r`, obtained from the
  one-variable estimate on complex lines.
* `Complex.differentiableOn_tsum_of_locally_dominated`: a series of holomorphic functions which
  is locally dominated by summable sequences is holomorphic; the `ℕ`-indexed variant
  `Complex.differentiableOn_tsum_of_eventually_dominated` only asks for domination of a tail.
* `Complex.iteratedDeriv_tsum_of_locally_dominated` computes every derivative of a
  locally dominated complex series term by term, using counting-measure integration.
* `Complex.differentiableOn_integral_of_locally_dominated`: a parametric integral of functions
  holomorphic in a finite-dimensional complex parameter, locally dominated by integrable functions,
  is holomorphic; `Complex.differentiableOn_intervalIntegral_of_locally_dominated` and

* `Complex.hasFDerivAt_integral_of_locally_dominated` gives the derivative explicitly;
  `Complex.iteratedDeriv_integral_of_locally_dominated` and its interval form commute every
  parameter derivative with integration. Their bounds use Mathlib’s Cauchy estimate
  `Complex.norm_iteratedDeriv_le_of_forall_mem_sphere_norm_le`.
* `Complex.differentiableOn_of_continuousOn_of_separately` (Osgood's lemma): a continuous function
  on an open subset of `ℂ × E`, `E` finite-dimensional, that is holomorphic in each variable
  separately is jointly holomorphic;
  `Complex.differentiableOn_prod_of_continuousOn_of_separately` is the case `E = ℂ`.
  The proof uses the one-variable Cauchy integral formula and the parametric-integral theorem
  above, not Hartogs' theorem.

# Derivative identities for scalar power-series operations

Mathlib's Cauchy–Taylor coefficients give the differentiated coefficient series near the
center. The principal complex power derivative is written as a first-order differential
identity, convenient for determining coefficients of powers by convolution.

# Rotating the ray of integration

Let `f` be holomorphic on the closed sector between the rays `arg t = 0` and `arg t = α`
(origin excluded), with an integrable singularity `O(|t|^{σ-1})`, `σ > 0`, at the origin and
exponential decay at infinity, uniformly in the sector. Then

`∫₀^∞ f(r) dr = e^{iα} ∫₀^∞ f(r e^{iα}) dr`.

The proof applies Cauchy's theorem for rectangles (`Complex.integral_boundary_rect_eq_zero_of_
differentiableOn`) to `w ↦ f(e^w) e^w` on `[log ε, log R] × [0, α]` and lets `ε → 0`, `R → ∞`.
This is the contour rotation used with Watson's lemma (Temme, *Special Functions*, §2.2).

## Main results

* `integrableOn_ray_of_bounds`: integrability along each ray of the sector.
* `integral_Ioi_eq_exp_mul_integral_Ioi_rotate`: the rotation formula.

# Uniqueness and multiplication of scalar power series

Shared helpers formerly proved independently in the hypergeometric and orthogonal-polynomial
libraries. The proofs use Mathlib's uniqueness of formal multilinear series and its absolutely
summable Cauchy product. They do not depend on any special-function definitions.

# Uniform discs inside a complex sector

A closed sector properly inside an open sector has discs whose radii are a fixed
positive multiple of the norm of their centers. Compactness of the arc of unit
directions supplies the uniform radius. Mathlib's
`Complex.norm_deriv_le_of_forall_mem_sphere_norm_le` then bounds derivatives in
an interior sector.

# Straight-segment primitives of entire functions

The primitive existence theorem and the real fundamental theorem of calculus
are supplied by Mathlib. These adapters identify the normalized straight-segment
integral with an arbitrary primitive and give its complex derivative.

# Geometric predicates for separating infinite contours

These are general point-set and parameterization predicates, independent of any
special function or integral identity. Left and right pole families belong to
distinct connected components of the complement of the contour. Exact tails fix
the orientation; finite indentations are unrestricted. All declarations are definitions.

# Positive real scaling of the principal square root

Mathlib's real-and-imaginary-part formula `Complex.sqrt_eq_real_add_ite`
shows that nonnegative real scaling preserves the selected bank, including on the cut.

# Straight-segment primitives on star-convex domains

For `h` holomorphic on an open set `U` that is star-convex about the origin, the normalized
segment integral `w ↦ w ∫₀¹ h(tw) dt` is a primitive of `h` on `U`. Mathlib supplies primitives
on discs (`DifferentiableOn.isExactOn_ball`) and on the whole plane; this file treats the
star-convex case by differentiating under the integral sign
(`intervalIntegral.hasDerivAt_integral_of_dominated_loc_of_deriv_le`) and applying the
fundamental theorem of calculus to `t ↦ t h(tz)`.

## Main results

* `Complex.starPrim_hasDerivAt`: the derivative of the segment primitive.
* `Complex.starPrim_differentiableOn`: the segment primitive is holomorphic on `U`.

# Parameter derivatives and bounds of Taylor coefficients

Cauchy's circle integral gives holomorphy in a complex parameter of Taylor
coefficients, commutation with a specified parameter derivative, and locally
uniform geometric coefficient bounds. The holomorphy proof is extracted from
`DLMF/Hypergeometric/Asymptotics.lean`; all inputs here are Mathlib-only.

# Extending the disk of convergence of a scalar power series

If a power series `∑ cₙ zⁿ` sums to `f z` on a small disk and `f` is complex differentiable
on a larger disk `‖z‖ < R`, then the same series sums to `f z` on the whole larger disk.
The proof compares the coefficients with Mathlib's Cauchy–Taylor expansion
(`Complex.hasSum_taylorSeries_on_ball`) through uniqueness of formal multilinear series;
the uniqueness argument follows `DLMF.Hypergeometric.scalarSeries_unique_ball`.
A reindexing lemma handles even series `∑ aₙ z^{2n}`.
The scalar-to-multilinear adapter and the Cauchy product lemma also support algebraic
operations on convergent power series; these specialize Mathlib’s analytic and sum APIs.

# Infinite products for hyperbolic sine and cosine

The normalized hyperbolic sine product follows from Mathlib's Euler sine product. Splitting its
factors into even and odd indices gives the hyperbolic cosine product, including its zeros by
locally uniform convergence. These proofs were moved from the DLMF elementary layer.

# Localizing zeros of holomorphic functions near approximate zeros

A quantitative, Newton–Kantorovich-type criterion for a function of a complex variable to have
*exactly one* zero in a closed disc around an approximate zero `z₀`: if the derivative of `f` stays
within relative distance `κ < 1` of a fixed nonzero number `c` on the disc `closedBall z₀ r`, and
`‖f z₀‖ ≤ (1 - κ) ‖c‖ r`, then the simplified Newton map `z ↦ z - f z / c` is a `κ`-contraction of
the disc into itself, so by the Banach fixed-point theorem `f` has exactly one zero there; the zero
lies within `‖f z₀‖ / ((1 - κ) ‖c‖)` of `z₀` and is simple.

The file also records elementary lower and upper bounds for `exp ζ - 1` near `0` (the model
function for zeros of exponential type, used together with Rouché's theorem) and the passage from
eventual pointwise localization to a sequence of zeros with a Landau bound, which is the form in
which asymptotic zero results (DLMF §§7.13, 9.9, 13.9) are stated.

Mathlib has no argument principle or Rouché theorem; for zero counting with multiplicity see
`TauCeti.rouche` in `TauCeti.Analysis.Complex.Conformal.Rouche`.

* `Complex.zloc_existsUnique_zero_closedBall`: exactly one zero in the closed disc.
* `Complex.zloc_exists_zero_norm_sub_le`: the zero lies within `‖f z₀‖ / ((1 - κ) ‖c‖)` of `z₀`,
  and its derivative is nonzero.
* `Complex.zloc_eventually_exists_zero_isBigO`: a sequence (or filter) version producing zeros
  `r k` with `r k - w k = O(ρ k)`.
* `Complex.zloc_norm_exp_sub_one_ge`: `‖ζ‖ / 2 ≤ ‖exp ζ - 1‖` for `‖ζ‖ ≤ 1/2`.

# Convergence of generalized continued fractions with field elements

Mathlib's `GenContFract` theory proves convergence mainly for simple continued fractions of
real numbers. This file supplies a Pincherle-type convergence theory for the continued fraction

  `h + a₀/(b₀ + a₁/(b₁ + a₂/(b₂ + ⋯)))`

with arbitrary partial numerators and denominators in a (normed) field, given by sequences
(`GenContFract.cfConv_ofFun`).

* `cfConv_det`: the determinant formula `A_{m+1}B_m - B_{m+1}A_m = (-1)^m ∏_{k ≤ m} a_k`.
* `cfConv_invariant`: a *backward solution* `w_k = b_k w_{k+1} + a_{k+1} w_{k+2}` pairs with the
  continuants: `A_{m+1} w_{m+1} + a_{m+1} A_m w_{m+2} = a₀ w₁ + h w₀` and similarly for `B`.
* `cfConv_error`: the exact error `h + a₀w₁/w₀ - A_{m+1}/B_{m+1}`.
* `cfConv_tendsto_of_minimal` (**Pincherle's theorem**, sufficiency): if the forward solution
  `G_m = (∏_{k ≤ m} a_k) w_{m+1}` attached to `w` is small compared with the denominators, the

* `cfConv_tendsto_of_ratio`: a checkable criterion: if eventually `q ‖a_{k+1} w_{k+2}‖ ≤ ‖w_k‖`

* `cfConv_tendsto_of_ratio_real`: the real analogue when `w_k` and `a_{k+1}w_{k+2}` have
  opposite signs and `|a_{k+1} w_{k+2}| ≤ |w_k|` (negative elements, Worpitzky-type).
* `cfConv_tendsto_of_ratio_pos`: the real analogue when `w_k` and `a_{k+1}w_{k+2}` have the

* `cfConv_continuants_of_back`, `cfConv_equiv_convs`, `cfConv_convs_smul_a0`: finite backward

* `cfConv_sfrac_bound`: the value region of an S-fraction `b_k = 1`, `a_k = c_k s²` (`c_k > 0`,

# The Euler–Maclaurin summation formula

For `f : ℝ → E` of class `Cᵖ`, `p ≥ 1`, and `n : ℕ`,

`∑_{k=0}^{n} f(k) = ∫₀ⁿ f + (f(0) + f(n))/2
  + ∑_{j=1}^{p-1} (-1)^{j+1} B_{j+1}/(j+1)! (f⁽ʲ⁾(n) - f⁽ʲ⁾(0))
  + (-1)^{p+1}/p! ∫₀ⁿ B̃ₚ(x) f⁽ᵖ⁾(x) dx`,

where `B̃ₚ(x) = Bₚ({x})` is the periodic Bernoulli function (Temme, *Special Functions*,
§1.1.3). Since the odd Bernoulli numbers beyond `B₁` vanish, the sign `(-1)^{j+1}` may be
dropped; we keep it, as it is what the proof produces.

The proof integrates by parts on each `[a, a+1]` against `Bₚ(x - a)`, using
`Bₚ₊₁' = (p+1) Bₚ` (`integral_eq_sum_bernoulliFun_add`), and sums over the unit intervals.

## Main definitions

* `periodicBernoulli`: the periodic Bernoulli function `B̃ₚ(x) = Bₚ(x - ⌊x⌋)`.

* `integral_eq_sum_bernoulliFun_add`: the one-interval identity.
* `sum_range_succ_eq_integral_add`: the Euler–Maclaurin formula with remainder.

# Almost-everywhere Fourier inversion and integral pairings on `L¹`

When a function and its Fourier transform are integrable, inversion holds almost
everywhere, without continuity of the original representative. Testing against smooth
compactly supported functions reduces this to Mathlib's inversion for Schwartz functions.
The resulting pairing requires integrability of only one of the Fourier transforms.

For functions in `L¹ ∩ L²`, the classical Fourier integral represents Mathlib's

# Fourier series of entire periodic functions

Let `F : ℂ → ℂ` be entire and `2π`-periodic. Shifting the line of integration (Cauchy's theorem
for rectangles, the vertical sides cancel by periodicity) shows that the Fourier integrals
`c_k = ∫₀^{2π} F(x) e^{-ikx} dx` decay faster than any exponential, and applying Mathlib's
`has_pointwise_sum_fourier_series_of_summable` on every horizontal line gives the expansion
`F(z) = ∑_{k ∈ ℤ} (2π)⁻¹ c_k e^{ikz}` for **every complex** `z`.

Tools for improper integrals `lim_{R → ∞} ∫₀^R f` that need not converge absolutely, as they
